metadata.practice_summary: Allison Parrish is a computational poet and programmer who uses word vectors, embedding spaces, and language models as poetic medium — treating the mathematical spaces that encode linguistic meaning as terrains to be explored, mapped, and traversed with the same intentionality a poet brings to choosing words on a page.
metadata.methodology: Parrish works at the intersection of computational linguistics, creative writing, and critical making. Her methodology involves: (1) building custom tools and software for navigating word embedding spaces (GloVe, word2vec, and custom-trained embeddings), (2) developing novel algorithms for traversing semantic space — e.g., finding paths through embedding space that move between concepts in aesthetically interesting ways, (3) treating the topology of embedding space itself as poetic material — distances, clusters, voids, and trajectories in vector space become compositional decisions, (4) extensive critical writing and teaching articulating why this matters as poetry rather than mere technical novelty. She teaches at NYU's Interactive Telecommunications Program (ITP) and has been deeply influential in the creative coding and electronic literature communities.

key_works.title: Articulations
key_works.description: A book-length computational poem generated by sorting and interpolating between lines from the Project Gutenberg poetry corpus using phonemic and semantic similarity in embedding space. Lines from different poems across centuries are brought into proximity based on their vector representations, creating uncanny juxtapositions and continuities. Published by Counterpath Press.
key_works.relevance: Demonstrates how embedding space navigation can recompose a vast corpus into new meaning — directly analogous to how A(DAI)'s graph of digital arts intelligence could be traversed to produce new configurations and insights.

key_works.title: Compasses
key_works.description: An interactive web-based tool and poetic work that allows users to navigate word embedding space using directional 'compasses' — semantic vectors that define trajectories through meaning space. Users can explore how moving in directions like 'more abstract' or 'more natural' transforms language.
key_works.relevance: Makes embedding space navigation tangible and interactive — users directly experience the topology of semantic space. A model for how A(DAI) users might navigate the knowledge graph as an experiential rather than informational interface.

key_works.title: Semantic Space is Not a Space (talk/essay)
key_works.description: A widely cited talk and essay where Parrish critically examines the metaphor of 'space' for word embeddings — arguing that embedding spaces have properties that defy spatial intuition (non-Euclidean geometry, high dimensionality, learned biases) and that poets must grapple with these properties honestly rather than treating vector space as a transparent medium.
key_works.relevance: Essential theoretical reference for A(DAI). If the Sense Room involves navigating embedding/graph space, Parrish's critical analysis of what it means to move through such spaces — and what spatial metaphors conceal — is indispensable.

metadata.commons_summary: Strongly commons-oriented. Parrish publishes code, Jupyter notebooks, and teaching materials openly (GitHub). Her work at ITP/NYU emphasises open pedagogy. Tools and libraries are shared for reuse. Academic and critical writing is freely accessible. The practice is embedded in open-source creative coding and electronic literature communities that value knowledge sharing.
metadata.governance_summary: Parrish works as an independent artist-researcher-educator. Creative decisions are made independently. Teaching and community engagement happen through NYU ITP and the broader creative coding/electronic literature communities. No formal collective or organisational governance structure.

metadata.practice_summary: Memo Akten is an artist and researcher working at the intersection of computation, AI, and human perception. His practice explores how neural networks and machine learning systems see, dream, and hallucinate — using deep learning as both tool and subject to probe questions about consciousness, perception, and the nature of intelligence.
metadata.methodology: Akten combines artistic practice with rigorous academic research (PhD from Goldsmiths, University of London on creative AI). He builds custom neural network architectures and training pipelines, often training models on specific curated datasets to create systems that generate visual, sonic, or textual output reflecting learned patterns. His methodology involves: (1) curating training data with intentionality — the dataset is an artistic choice, (2) designing or modifying neural network architectures to produce aesthetically and conceptually meaningful outputs, (3) developing real-time interactive systems that allow audiences to navigate or trigger AI-generated content, (4) rigorous conceptual framing through writing and talks. He has contributed to open-source creative coding tools (ofxMSAFluid, ofxMSAPhysics for openFrameworks) and published academic papers on creative AI.

key_works.title: Deep Meditations
key_works.description: A series of AI-generated meditation videos created by training neural networks on thousands of images and videos related to spirituality, nature, cosmos, and consciousness across diverse cultural traditions. The system generates continuous, slowly morphing abstract imagery with ambient sound that evokes a contemplative state. Presented as both installation and online series.
key_works.relevance: Demonstrates embedding space as artistic territory — the latent space trained on contemplative imagery from many traditions becomes a new kind of space to inhabit. Directly relevant to how A(DAI)'s graph of digital arts knowledge could become an experiential environment.

key_works.title: Learning to See
key_works.description: Real-time interactive installation where a neural network trained on specific datasets (ocean waves, fire, flowers, clouds) continuously reinterprets a live camera feed of visitors and objects. Whatever you show the camera, the neural network 'sees' it as the domain it was trained on — holding up your hand becomes waves, flames, petals. Explores how perception is shaped by training/experience.
key_works.relevance: Makes the concept of learned representation viscerally tangible — the audience directly experiences how a trained embedding space shapes perception. Powerful metaphor for how A(DAI)'s intelligence layer could reshape how we see connections between artworks and practices.

key_works.title: Distributed Consciousness
key_works.description: Large-scale immersive installation (shown at Barbican Centre and other venues) exploring AI perception and machine consciousness through multiple neural networks generating and interpreting imagery simultaneously. Multiple screens show how different networks perceive and hallucinate the same inputs differently.
key_works.relevance: Explores distributed intelligence — multiple AI systems with different training perceiving the same world differently. Relevant to A(DAI)'s concept of multiple perspectives on the same field of knowledge.

metadata.practice_summary: American Artist examines how knowledge systems, technology, and data encode racial power structures, using surveillance, operating systems, and corporate infrastructure as both subject and material. Their legal name change to 'American Artist' is itself an intervention into how search engines, databases, and naming systems construct identity.
metadata.methodology: American Artist works across installation, video, sculpture, and text to investigate how technology -- particularly data systems, surveillance infrastructure, and corporate platforms -- reproduces and encodes racial hierarchy. The name change (to 'American Artist' in 2013) is a foundational conceptual gesture: it disrupts search engine results, database categorization, and the assumptions embedded in naming conventions. Their research-based practice draws on critical race theory, media archaeology, and the material history of computing. Works often take the form of immersive installations that recreate or simulate the environments of technological power (server rooms, operating systems, surveillance networks).

key_works.title: My Blue Window
key_works.description: Installation featuring a custom operating system modeled on Windows XP's interface, displayed on monitors in a dark room resembling a server room or surveillance center. The work examines how operating systems structure perception and encode corporate/racial power, referencing both the 'Blue Screen of Death' and the historical blueness of surveillance/police systems.
key_works.relevance: Directly demonstrates how the infrastructure layer (operating system, interface design) is a site of power and meaning-making. Essential reference for A(DAI)'s thinking about how graph infrastructure is never neutral.

key_works.title: Black Gooey Universe
key_works.description: Essay and lecture series examining the graphical user interface (GUI) as a site of racial meaning. The white desktop, the black terminal -- American Artist reads the history of computing interfaces through the lens of race, arguing that the shift from command-line (black screen) to GUI (white desktop) mirrors broader racial politics of visibility and control.
key_works.relevance: Foundational theoretical text for understanding how interface design and data visualization encode racial assumptions. Directly relevant to how A(DAI) designs its own interfaces and graph visualizations.

key_works.title: Sandy Speaks
key_works.description: AI chatbot trained on the writings and statements of Sandra Bland, who died in police custody. The work raises questions about voice, representation, consent, and the ethics of training AI on the words of the dead -- particularly Black people who died at the hands of the state.
key_works.relevance: Raises critical questions about consent, data provenance, and the ethics of AI training data that directly challenge A(DAI)'s pipeline. Whose voices are encoded? Who consented? What does it mean to train a model on someone who can no longer consent?

metadata.practice_summary: Artist who treats datasets as artistic medium, hand-labeling thousands of training images as a form of craft practice. Her work foregrounds the labor, subjectivity, and provenance of training data, making visible the human decisions embedded in machine learning systems.
metadata.methodology: Ridler creates her own training datasets from scratch -- photographing, categorizing, and hand-labeling thousands of images (e.g., 10,000 tulip photographs for Myriad/Mosaic Virus). She trains GANs on these bespoke datasets, treating the entire pipeline from data collection to model training to output generation as creative acts. The labor of dataset creation is foregrounded as craft, drawing parallels to historical practices like botanical illustration and tulip mania speculation. She studied at the Royal College of Art and has a background in literature, bringing narrative and historical framing to technical processes.

key_works.title: Myriad (Tulips)
key_works.description: Installation displaying all 10,000 hand-photographed and individually labeled tulip images used to train a GAN. Each image is categorized by Ridler according to color, shape, and stripe pattern. The dataset itself is presented as the artwork.
key_works.relevance: Foundational example of dataset-as-artwork. Makes visible the subjective human labor inside machine learning. Directly models how hand-curated knowledge can function as primary artistic material.

key_works.title: Mosaic Virus
key_works.description: Three-screen video installation of GAN-generated tulips whose visual characteristics (stripe patterns, 'infection' level) are driven by real-time Bitcoin price data. References 17th-century Dutch tulip mania and the Tulip Breaking Virus.
key_works.relevance: Demonstrates relational/responsive composition -- artwork determined by external data input. The connection between financial speculation and botanical beauty is a graph-like conceptual link made generative.

key_works.title: The Shell Record
key_works.description: Work using hand-collected and labeled shell specimens to explore classification systems, taxonomy, and the relationship between natural variation and machine categorization.
key_works.relevance: Extends the dataset-as-medium approach to natural history and taxonomy, showing how classification systems themselves are creative and subjective acts -- directly relevant to how a knowledge graph curates and categorizes.

metadata.practice_summary: Pioneer of ambient and generative music who designs self-generating systems that produce endlessly non-repeating compositions. His practice centers on building frameworks that make music with minimal ongoing intervention — the artist as planner and programmer, then audience to the results.
metadata.methodology: Eno designs systems using incommensurable loops — multiple independent audio or visual tracks of different lengths that, when layered, produce combinations that never exactly repeat. Inspired by wind chimes and Steve Reich's tape pieces, he builds frameworks where elements recombine endlessly. His approach progressed from tape loops (Discreet Music, 1975) through MIDI-based generative systems (1990s) to software apps (Bloom, Reflection) and generative film (Eno documentary, 2024). He describes himself as 'a systems manipulator' rather than a musician, gravitating toward 'situations and systems that, once set into operation, could create music with little or no intervention.' His visual practice uses the same generative logic — 77 Million Paintings layers hand-painted slides via software to produce combinations requiring 10,000 years to exhaust.

key_works.title: Music for Airports (Ambient 1)
key_works.description: Foundational ambient album using tape loops of different lengths to create endlessly recombining compositions. Track '2/1' uses seven vocal loops and one piano loop of incommensurable lengths.
key_works.relevance: Establishes the core generative technique — independent loops with different periods producing non-repeating compositions — that directly models how relational elements in a Sense Room could recombine.

key_works.title: 77 Million Paintings
key_works.description: Generative software combining 296 hand-painted glass slides four at a time, with generative music, producing 77 million possible combinations. Software developed by Jake Dowie. Released as DVD/software and exhibited on the Sydney Opera House sails.
key_works.relevance: Demonstrates generative visual-sonic composition for inhabited spaces. The hand-made-to-algorithmic pipeline (paint on glass to software recombination) models how human-created art materials can be substrate for generative systems.

key_works.title: Reflection
key_works.description: Album released alongside a generative app (developed with Peter Chilvers) that creates an endless, endlessly changing version of the piece. Represents the most sophisticated of Eno's ambient generative experiments.
key_works.relevance: The app format puts generative composition directly in users' hands — a model for how Sense Room experiences could be distributed and co-inhabited.

metadata.commons_summary: Eno's generative apps (Bloom, Scape, Reflection) are commercial products. His music and installations operate within standard commercial art/music markets. However, his philosophical contributions to generative art are widely shared through lectures, writing, and the Long Now Foundation. The conceptual framework (generative systems, ambient as environmental art) has become commons knowledge even if specific implementations are proprietary.
metadata.governance_summary: Eno operates as solo artist with collaborators (Peter Chilvers for apps, Jake Dowie for 77 Million Paintings software, various musicians). Creative decisions are ultimately his. Long-term collaborations with institutions (Long Now Foundation, hospitals) involve some shared governance of permanent installations.

metadata.practice_summary: Chinese multimedia artist who builds virtual worlds and cinematic environments exploring the collision of rapid urbanisation, digital culture, and lived reality in contemporary China. Her work maps the psychic geography of a society caught between communist legacy, hypercapitalist acceleration, and digital escapism.
metadata.methodology: Cao Fei works at the intersection of documentary observation and speculative world-building. She embeds herself in specific social contexts -- factory floors (Whose Utopia), cosplay subcultures (COSPlayers), virtual communities (RMB City in Second Life), and Beijing's urban periphery (La Town) -- and constructs layered narratives that blend fiction, documentary, gaming aesthetics, and architectural modelling. Her later work uses VR and game engines to create persistent virtual environments. She collaborates with architects, programmers, and game developers. Represented by Vitamin Creative Space (Guangzhou) and Spruth Magers.

key_works.title: RMB City
key_works.description: A virtual city built in Second Life, combining iconic Chinese architectural forms (CCTV Tower, Oriental Pearl, factories) into a surreal digital metropolis. Functioned as a persistent online community where avatars could live, trade, and perform. Included RMB City Opera and RMB City: A Second Life City Planning.
key_works.relevance: Foundational example of art-as-virtual-infrastructure. A persistent world built as artwork that others inhabit and transform -- directly relevant to graph-curated generative environments where art is substrate rather than object.

key_works.title: Whose Utopia
key_works.description: Three-channel video filmed in an OSRAM light bulb factory in Guangzhou's Pearl River Delta, juxtaposing factory workers' assembly-line labour with their private fantasies -- dancing ballet, playing guitar -- staged on the factory floor.
key_works.relevance: Demonstrates Cao Fei's methodology of embedding in social systems and revealing hidden layers of desire and imagination within industrial infrastructure. Models how data from real systems (labour, production) can become artistic material.

key_works.title: Nova
key_works.description: Feature-length film and immersive installation (first shown at Serpentine Galleries) set in a virtual replica of a demolished Beijing neighbourhood. Uses motion capture, game engines, and CGI to create a ghostly digital archaeology of vanished urban space.
key_works.relevance: Shows how virtual world-building can preserve and recompose lost physical spaces. The work functions as a navigable environment rather than a linear narrative -- relevant to spatial, non-linear exhibition formats.

metadata.commons_summary: RMB City was open to public inhabitation within Second Life -- anyone could visit and participate. However, Cao Fei's work overall operates within the commercial gallery system (Spruth Magers, major museum exhibitions). The virtual worlds were commons-like in their social function but not in their licensing or governance. Her work critiques enclosure (factory labour, urban demolition) without necessarily building alternative commons infrastructure.
metadata.governance_summary: Cao Fei is the primary creative director of her projects, working with technical collaborators (programmers, architects, game developers) under her artistic direction. Her studio practice follows a solo artist model with project-specific collaborators.

metadata.practice_summary: Artist and educator who co-created the Processing programming language and co-founded Feral File. His practice explores art emerging from relational rules — defining systems rather than composing images — connecting 1960s conceptual art instruction-based practice to 21st-century generative computation.
metadata.methodology: Reas writes code to define systems of autonomous elements whose interactions produce emergent visual forms. Inspired by Sol LeWitt's instructional wall drawings, he translates written scores into generative software where the artist's role is to define relational rules rather than compose pictures. His Process series (2005-ongoing) explores instruction-based visuals where possibilities for interaction between elements are outlined in code, and structures evolve through element actions within given parameters. Later work (Ultraconcentrated, In Silico, Compressed Cinema) extends into machine learning, using GANs to compress and transform existing media. He also curates and builds infrastructure for digital art through Feral File.

metadata.practice_summary: Danielle Brathwaite-Shirley creates interactive digital archives and game-like environments that center Black trans experience, treating archiving as a radical act of survival and challenging who controls the narratives and data of marginalized communities.
metadata.methodology: Brathwaite-Shirley uses video game engines (primarily Unity) to build immersive, navigable environments that archive Black trans stories, histories, and experiences. The work is built through direct collaboration with Black trans people who contribute their stories, voices, and likenesses. The interactive format means visitors must make choices that implicate them in the archive -- asking whether they are an ally or not, and gating access to certain stories based on responses. The aesthetic draws on lo-fi game environments, glitch art, and DIY animation. The archival practice is explicitly political: it asks who gets to build archives, who is included or excluded, and what happens to data about marginalized people.

key_works.title: WE ARE HERE BECAUSE OF THOSE THAT ARE NOT
key_works.description: Interactive web-based and installation archive of Black trans lives, built in a game engine. Visitors navigate a 3D environment, encountering stories, testimonies, and histories of Black trans people. The work gates access based on the visitor's declared relationship to the community -- allies and community members experience different paths.
key_works.relevance: Core example of how archival infrastructure can be designed as artwork, with governance embedded in the visitor experience. Directly models questions about who accesses what data and under what conditions.

key_works.title: Resurrection Land
key_works.description: Video game installation where players navigate a world built from Black trans archives. The game mechanics embed ethical choices about witnessing, allyship, and complicity. Shown at major institutions including Tate, Serpentine, and international biennials.
key_works.relevance: Demonstrates how game mechanics can encode governance and ethical frameworks. The 'resurrection' metaphor -- bringing archived lives into active presence -- resonates with A(DAI)'s interest in living, evolving knowledge systems.

key_works.title: SHE KEEPS ME DAMN ALIVE
key_works.description: Interactive installation combining game engine environments with physical arcade-style interfaces. Visitors physically interact with custom-built controllers to navigate archives of Black trans experience.
key_works.relevance: Bridges digital archives with physical embodied interaction, demonstrating how data archives can be experienced spatially and haptically rather than just visually.

metadata.commons_summary: Brathwaite-Shirley's practice is deeply commons-oriented in spirit -- building shared archives for a marginalized community, centering collective memory over individual property. However, the commons is specifically defined: it belongs to the Black trans community, not to everyone equally. This is a model of selective commons -- open to the community it serves, with gatekeeping mechanisms for those outside it. This challenges universalist open-access models.

The artist makes the overarching structural decisions, but the archived community members shape the content. This is a hybrid of solo artistic direction and community-participatory content creation with embedded audience-responsive governance.

Their process is slow, deliberate, and attentive to the politics embedded in technical choices.

Their methodology is rooted in careful material consideration — choosing technologies that align with ethical commitments (low-energy, open-source, non-extractive). They maintain a critical perspective on AI, large-scale data harvesting, and platform capitalism, articulated through both artistic works and influential essays. Their process is slow, deliberate, and attentive to the politics embedded in technical choices.

relevance_to_sense_room.relevance_summary: Pipkin's practice of building commons-oriented tools as artworks directly models a mode of art-making where infrastructure and creative expression are inseparable — essential for a graph-curated exhibition treating system design as medium.
relevance_to_sense_room.art_as_substrate: Yes. Their generative text works, drawing tools, and game engines can function as substrate layers. Works like Lacework produce outputs that could be embedded in larger compositions.
relevance_to_sense_room.relational_composition: Partially. Some works (particularly generative text pieces) create meaning through relational juxtaposition of elements. The tool-making practice creates infrastructure that enables relational composition by others.
relevance_to_sense_room.self_recomposing: Several works are generative and produce different outputs on each encounter. Browser-based pieces often incorporate randomness and recombination. However, the emphasis is on considered, intentional generation rather than autonomous evolution.

works.title: The Barnacle Goose Experiment
works.description: A collaborative wiki-novel built in a custom engine where readers and writers co-create a branching, evolving narrative. Explores collective authorship and commons-based creative production.
works.relevance: Directly models collective, relational content creation — a community-authored graph of narrative where meaning emerges from connections and contributions.

works.title: Lacework
works.description: A generative drawing tool that creates intricate lace-like patterns through algorithmic processes, released as open-source software.
works.relevance: Exemplifies tool-as-artwork with commons orientation. The generative outputs are themselves artworks that could serve as visual substrate in a composed exhibition.

works.title: On Gathering (essay)
works.description: An influential essay critiquing large-scale dataset collection practices in AI/ML, arguing for ethical data gathering that respects consent and commons principles.
works.relevance: Provides critical theoretical framework for how A(DAI) should approach data provenance, consent, and the ethics of building a collective intelligence commons.

protocol_art_resonance.protocol_art_summary: Pipkin treats the design of tools, platforms, and infrastructure as artistic medium. The ethical and political commitments embedded in their software — open licensing, low energy use, non-extraction — are aesthetic choices as much as moral ones.
protocol_art_resonance.system_designed: Multiple open-source tools and game engines. The Barnacle Goose Experiment's collaborative wiki platform. Various generative text and drawing systems released as commons infrastructure.

commons_orientation.commons_summary: Deeply commons-oriented at every level. Open-source tool releases, critical writing against data enclosure, explicit advocacy for non-extractive technology. Their practice is one of the strongest examples of commons-as-medium in contemporary digital art.

governance_model.governance_detail: Solo practice with participatory elements. The Barnacle Goose Experiment distributes authorial governance to participants. Tool releases invite community contribution. No formal governance structure but strong ethical framework guiding decisions.

consent_and_authorship.consent_approach: Consent is a central concern. Their critical writing explicitly addresses consent in data gathering. Participatory works are designed with informed, voluntary participation. They advocate against scraping and non-consensual data collection.
consent_and_authorship.authorship_model: Solo for tools and essays, collaborative/distributed for participatory projects like Barnacle Goose. Open-source releases enable community co-authorship.

liveness_and_duration.temporal_detail: Generative works produce different outputs on each encounter. Web-based pieces are durational in that they persist and can be revisited. The Barnacle Goose Experiment evolves through community contribution over time.

data_materiality.data_sources: Self-generated datasets, hand-curated text corpora, participant contributions, public domain texts. Deliberately avoids scraped data from non-consenting sources.
data_materiality.data_provenance: Ethically sourced — consented, self-generated, or public domain. Pipkin is one of the most vocal advocates for ethical data provenance in the digital arts.

embedding_space_relevance.embedding_summary: Not a primary focus, and in fact Pipkin is critically skeptical of large-scale embedding/ML systems due to their extractive data practices. Some generative text work engages with semantic space at a smaller, more intentional scale.
embedding_space_relevance.multimodal: Yes — practice spans drawing, text, code, games, and writing, though not unified through embedding spaces.

exhibition_modality.spatial_description: Works primarily encountered through web browsers and screens. Some gallery installations and performative readings. The web is the primary exhibition space, consistent with commons principles of open access.

interoperability.composability: Moderate. Tools produce standard outputs (images, text files) that can feed into other processes. Open-source code is forkable and adaptable. Not explicitly designed as modular pipeline components but amenable to integration.
interoperability.technical_openness: Open source, documented, forkable

technical_approach.stack: JavaScript, Python, HTML/CSS, custom game engines, generative algorithms, minimal/low-dependency approaches reflecting sustainability commitments

network_position.scene_affiliation: Net art, indie games, critical tech art, digital commons movement, creative coding community. Connected to both art world and tech ethics discourse.
network_position.connections: Sam Lavigne (shared tool-making and commons ethos), Darius Kazemi (bot/generative art community), broader indie game and net art communities

potential_role_in_adai.role_detail: Pipkin's critical perspective on extractive technology and their commons-first practice provide an essential ethical compass for A(DAI). Their writing on data gathering directly informs how A(DAI) should approach consent and provenance. They could serve as a critical friend who tests whether A(DAI) lives up to its commons commitments.

metadata.practice_summary: Sam Lavigne creates tools, software, and data-driven artworks that interrogate surveillance, labor, policing, and corporate power. His practice treats data curation, recomposition, and tool-making as primary creative acts.
metadata.methodology: Lavigne works through what he calls 'Scrapism' — the creative repurposing of found data through web scraping, natural language processing, and computational recomposition. He builds open-source software tools (Videogrep, Runway) that function simultaneously as artworks and as instruments others can use. His process typically involves collecting large datasets from public or institutional sources, then applying algorithmic transformations that reveal hidden patterns or absurdities. He teaches at NYU's Interactive Telecommunications Program (ITP), embedding pedagogy into his practice.

key_works.title: Videogrep
key_works.description: Open-source command-line tool that searches through video dialogue transcripts and automatically creates supercuts based on search terms. Widely adopted by artists, journalists, and researchers.
key_works.relevance: Exemplifies tool-as-artwork and data recomposition as creative act. Its output is inherently relational — meaning emerges from the juxtaposition of found fragments.

key_works.title: Scrapism (book/methodology)
key_works.description: A methodology and book teaching web scraping as artistic practice — treating publicly available data as material for creative intervention and political critique.
key_works.relevance: Provides a theoretical and practical framework for data-as-material that aligns with A(DAI)'s approach to field intelligence gathering and recomposition.

key_works.title: White Collar Crime Risk Zones
key_works.description: A predictive policing tool inverted to predict white-collar crime instead of street crime, using financial and corporate data. Created with Francis Tseng and collaborators.
key_works.relevance: Demonstrates how recomposing institutional data through a different relational frame reveals systemic patterns — a model for graph-based sensemaking.

metadata.commons_summary: Strongly commons-oriented. Nearly all tools are open source on GitHub. His pedagogical practice at NYU ITP further distributes knowledge as commons. The Scrapism methodology is explicitly designed to be adopted and remixed by others.
metadata.governance_summary: Primarily solo practice with frequent collaborations. Tools are released as open source but maintained primarily by Lavigne. Collaborative projects (like White Collar Crime Risk Zones) use informal collective decision-making.

metadata.practice_summary: American artist, programmer, and writer whose bot-art practice (under tinysubversions) pioneered Twitter-era computational creativity. Co-founded NaNoGenMo (National Novel Generation Month) in 2013 and Mastodon instance Friend Camp as community-infrastructure practice.
metadata.methodology: Prolific output of bots, generators, and small tools — 'Tiny Subversions' blog and GitHub are the primary venue. Recent practice focuses on small-scale decentralised social infrastructure (Mastodon, Hometown fork).

key_works.title: Two Headlines
key_works.description: Twitter (later Mastodon) bot that combines subject of one current news headline with predicate of another, posting hourly. The bot has run continuously for over a decade, producing a persistent low-level commentary on how news discourse works at the level of sentence-structure. Often cited as a foundational bot-art example because it does so much with such structural simplicity.

key_works.title: NaNoGenMo
key_works.description: Annual National Novel Generation Month — a parody of NaNoWriMo in which participants produce 50,000-word novels by computational means and share the code and output openly on GitHub. Co-founded by Kazemi, the event has become a durable community ritual for generative text practice, and its archives document a decade of experimental computational literature.

key_works.title: Hometown
key_works.description: Small-scale fork of Mastodon designed around intimate, local-first federation — an explicit counter-proposal to the scale-obsessed dominant social-media architectures. Kazemi maintains Hometown as infrastructural practice, arguing that decentralised social software is a design/aesthetics problem as much as a technical one. Widely adopted by small communities seeking non-viral social formats.

metadata.commons_summary: Deep commons orientation — essentially everything is open-source on GitHub, including platform experiments (Hometown Mastodon fork).
metadata.governance_summary: Solo practitioner; active in federated-social-web commons.

metadata.practice_summary: Refik Anadol creates large-scale data sculptures and immersive installations that use machine learning to process vast datasets — museum archives, nature recordings, urban data, neurological signals — transforming them into continuously evolving visual environments that reveal latent patterns invisible to human perception.
metadata.methodology: Anadol and his studio (RAS, ~team of multidisciplinary artists, architects, data scientists) train custom AI models using frameworks like NVIDIA StyleGAN2 ADA on massive datasets. They developed a proprietary Latent Space Browser (since 2017) to navigate high-dimensional embedding spaces and select outputs. Works often incorporate site-specific environmental inputs (light, sound, weather, movement) that modulate the generative output in real-time. The process typically involves: (1) ethically sourcing or partnering with institutions for large datasets, (2) training custom models on those datasets, (3) exploring the latent space for aesthetic possibilities, (4) creating real-time rendering systems that respond to environmental conditions. Recent work with the Large Nature Model involves training on 500+ million data points from nature.

key_works.title: Unsupervised — Machine Hallucinations — MoMA
key_works.description: Processed 138,151 images from MoMA's entire collection through StyleGAN2, displayed as a continuously evolving data sculpture in the museum's Gund Lobby. Over 3 million visitors; average viewing time 38 minutes. Acquired by MoMA as the first generative artwork in its permanent collection. Environmental data from the lobby modulated output in real-time.
key_works.relevance: Demonstrates how an institutional collection can become substrate for a living generative artwork. The model discovers latent relationships between 200 years of art — a machine-learning parallel to graph-based curation of artistic connections.

key_works.title: Large Nature Model (LNM)
key_works.description: The world's first open-source generative AI model dedicated to nature, trained on 500+ million ethically sourced data points from the Smithsonian, National Geographic, Natural History Museum London, and field recordings from 16 rainforest locations. Multimodal (images, audio, video, text). Debuted at World Economic Forum Davos 2024.
key_works.relevance: Directly relevant as infrastructure: an open-source, ethically sourced AI model that generates from nature data. The commons orientation of the model (open-source, institutional partnerships, ethical data collection) aligns with A(DAI)'s commons-first values. Shows how art practice can produce open infrastructure.

key_works.title: WDCH Dreams
key_works.description: Projected ML-processed visualizations of 100 years of the LA Philharmonic's digital archives onto Frank Gehry's Walt Disney Concert Hall. Architecture as screen, institutional memory as generative material.
key_works.relevance: Demonstrates building-as-canvas and institutional archive-as-material — the architectural environment becomes a generative system driven by cultural data.

metadata.commons_summary: The Large Nature Model is explicitly open-source, built on Meta's open-source Llama models, and trained on ethically sourced institutional data. Anadol has publicly advocated for the importance of open-source AI. However, the studio's commercial practice (gallery sales, commissioned installations, NFT releases through platforms like Feral File) operates within proprietary art market structures. Dataland is a private museum initiative. The practice is hybrid: commons-oriented infrastructure (LNM) alongside commercial art production.
metadata.governance_summary: Refik Anadol Studio (RAS) is led by Anadol as primary creative director, co-founded with Efsun Erkilic who handles operational leadership. The studio employs a multidisciplinary team but creative direction flows from Anadol. Partnerships with institutions (Smithsonian, Google, NVIDIA, Meta) shape data access and compute resources but not artistic decisions.

protocol_art_resonance.protocol_art_summary: Anadol's practice increasingly treats the construction of AI models and data pipelines as creative acts. The Large Nature Model is simultaneously an artwork, a research tool, and open infrastructure — the model itself is the artistic output as much as any visual rendering. Dataland (his planned AI museum) represents institution-building as creative practice.
protocol_art_resonance.system_designed: The Large Nature Model (LNM) — an open-source multimodal generative AI model for nature. The Latent Space Browser — a proprietary tool for navigating high-dimensional embedding spaces. Dataland — a museum and Web3 platform dedicated to AI art, opening Spring 2026 in Los Angeles in a Gehry-designed building.

commons_orientation.commons_summary: The Large Nature Model is explicitly open-source, built on Meta's open-source Llama models, and trained on ethically sourced institutional data. Anadol has publicly advocated for the importance of open-source AI. However, the studio's commercial practice (gallery sales, commissioned installations, NFT releases through platforms like Feral File) operates within proprietary art market structures. Dataland is a private museum initiative. The practice is hybrid: commons-oriented infrastructure (LNM) alongside commercial art production.

governance_model.governance_detail: Refik Anadol Studio (RAS) is led by Anadol as primary creative director, co-founded with Efsun Erkilic who handles operational leadership. The studio employs a multidisciplinary team but creative direction flows from Anadol. Partnerships with institutions (Smithsonian, Google, NVIDIA, Meta) shape data access and compute resources but not artistic decisions.

consent_and_authorship.consent_approach: Data is sourced through institutional partnerships (Smithsonian, Natural History Museum, MoMA) with explicit permission. For the Large Nature Model, Anadol emphasizes 'ethically harnessed' open-source data. Field recordings from rainforests are self-collected by the studio. No personal data from individuals is used as primary material (the MoMA work uses artwork metadata, not visitor data).
consent_and_authorship.authorship_model: Solo authorship credited to Refik Anadol, with studio acknowledged as RAS. Machine co-authorship is implicit — the AI models generate the visual output — but Anadol frames this as 'machine hallucination' rather than machine co-creation. The artist retains full authorial credit.

liveness_and_duration.temporal_detail: Installations render in real-time, continuously generating new visual states. Unsupervised incorporated live environmental data (light, sound, weather, movement) to modulate output. The Large Nature Model can generate indefinitely from its training. Works are designed to never repeat — each moment is unique. Duration in exhibition contexts ranges from months (Unsupervised ran almost a year at MoMA) to permanent installation.

data_materiality.data_sources: Museum collection metadata and images (MoMA's 138,151 works), nature imagery and audio (500M+ data points from Smithsonian, National Geographic, Natural History Museum London, 16 rainforest field recordings), architectural archives (LA Philharmonic's 100-year digital archive), EEG neurological data (Melting Memories), urban data, satellite imagery, coral reef images (135 million for Serpentine show).
data_materiality.data_provenance: Institutional partnerships with explicit permission for MoMA, Smithsonian, Natural History Museum, National Geographic. Self-collected field data from rainforests using LiDAR, photogrammetry, and audio capture. Public domain and openly licensed datasets. Anadol emphasizes ethical sourcing as a core value. The LNM is described as using 'the most extensive, ethically collected dataset of the natural world.'

embedding_space_relevance.embedding_summary: Central to the practice. Anadol's work is fundamentally about navigating and rendering latent/embedding spaces. The studio's custom Latent Space Browser (developed since 2017) allows exploration of 1,024-dimensional embedding spaces created by StyleGAN2 models. The 'machine hallucination' aesthetic is the visual manifestation of traversing these high-dimensional spaces. The Large Nature Model creates multimodal embeddings across image, audio, video, and text.
embedding_space_relevance.multimodal: Yes. The Large Nature Model is explicitly multimodal — trained on and capable of generating across text, images, audio, and video in a unified framework. Earlier works were primarily visual, but the practice is expanding toward full multimodal synthesis.

exhibition_modality.spatial_description: Works manifest as large-scale LED screens (Unsupervised: 24' x 24'), architectural projections (WDCH Dreams projected onto Gehry's building), and immersive room-scale installations. Dataland will be a 20,000 sq ft purpose-built museum. The scale is consistently architectural — the work occupies and transforms the space it inhabits rather than sitting within it as an object.

interoperability.composability: The Large Nature Model, as an open-source AI model, is inherently composable — its outputs can serve as inputs for other systems. The model itself can be fine-tuned or extended. However, individual installation works are self-contained and do not expose APIs or produce outputs designed for external consumption.
interoperability.technical_openness: Hybrid. The Large Nature Model is open-source (built on Meta's Llama). The Latent Space Browser and studio's proprietary tools are closed. Individual installations are closed systems. The practice straddles open infrastructure (LNM) and closed artistic production.

technical_approach.stack: NVIDIA StyleGAN2 ADA for generative models, Meta Llama for Large Nature Model foundation, custom Latent Space Browser for high-dimensional navigation, Google Cloud for sustainable compute, NVIDIA GPUs for training and inference, LiDAR and photogrammetry for field data collection, large-scale LED display technology, real-time rendering systems with environmental sensor integration.

network_position.scene_affiliation: AI art, data art, new media art, immersive/experiential art. Strong connections to both the commercial art world (major gallery representation, MoMA acquisition) and the technology industry (Google, NVIDIA, Meta partnerships). Bridges art world, tech industry, and institutional/museum contexts. Also connected to the Web3/NFT art ecosystem through Feral File and other platforms.
network_position.connections: teamLab (shared territory of large-scale immersive installations attracting mass audiences, though different technical approaches). Vladan Joler (both engage with AI infrastructure as artistic subject, but from opposite positions — Anadol celebrates ML aesthetics while Joler critically maps its extractive costs). Ian Cheng (both use real-time generative systems, but Cheng's are simulation-based while Anadol's are ML-based).

potential_role_in_adai.role_detail: Anadol's work demonstrates how large datasets can become living generative substrates — directly relevant to A(DAI)'s graph-based intelligence becoming exhibition material. The Large Nature Model's open-source, ethically-sourced approach offers a model for commons-oriented AI art infrastructure. However, the studio's scale, commercial positioning, and individual-genius framing may not align with A(DAI)'s collective, commons-first ethos. Most useful as a reference for: (1) how latent space navigation can reveal hidden connections in collections, (2) how open-source AI models can be artistic outputs, (3) how institutional data partnerships work in practice.

metadata.methodology: Writes JavaScript algorithms generating painterly compositions — flow fields, colour palettes, compositional variation. Writes extensively on generative aesthetics ('Aesthetically Programming', essays) and has helped shape the conceptual vocabulary of the field.

metadata.practice_summary: Avatar-artist practicing entirely as a virtual persona since 2012 — the artist is the avatar; there is no 'real' identity behind it. Work across CGI animation, social media performance, and commissioned games foregrounds digital-native identity as primary material.
metadata.methodology: Maintains avatar-consistent presence across platforms (Instagram, Twitter, commissioned work, gallery). Produces CGI animations and collaborations with musicians, brands, and institutions; the persona itself is part of the work's governance.

key_works.title: Club Rothko
key_works.description: Persistent virtual gallery-and-performance-space, originally in Second Life, through which Avedon curates exhibitions, hosts discussions, and stages performances. The space argues that a gallery is a social-technical assemblage whose digital instantiation is fully legitimate — not a 'virtual version' of a physical original. Over its decade-plus run it has become an infrastructural reference for avatar-native exhibition practice.

key_works.title: Home
key_works.description: Ongoing series of CGI self-portraits — each a rendered image, animation, or short loop of Avedon in domestic or gallery interiors — that insist that the avatar's self-portrait is as indexical as a photographic one. The series' long duration turns the avatar's persistence over time into its own content, a pointed counter-argument to the assumption that digital identity is weightless.

key_works.title: The Zizi Show (cameo, with Jake Elwes)
key_works.description: Collaboration with Jake Elwes for his AI-drag work 'The Zizi Show', in which Avedon's avatar performs as one of the cast of AI-generated drag performers. The collaboration extends Avedon's argument that avatar-presence and AI-generation occupy the same ontological register, putting her persistent character in dialogue with emergent generated ones.

metadata.commons_summary: Practice is avatar-native — commercial gallery, commissioned brand work, and institutional commission. Identity is the primary critical gesture.
metadata.governance_summary: Single persistent avatar-practice; represented by Transfer Gallery.

metadata.practice_summary: American-Belgian artist whose practice spans three eras of digital art: late-90s net.art (Entropy8Zuper!), 2000s independent games (Tale of Tales, with Michaël Samyn), and current decade digital sculpture, VR, and NFT. Few practitioners have as continuous a digital-native practice across media generations.
metadata.methodology: Each era defines its own methodology: Entropy8 was HTML-native narrative-surreal; Tale of Tales produced art games ('The Path', 'The Graveyard') as self-contained experiences; current practice builds 3D sculptures distributed across physical, digital, and NFT form, often referencing classical sculpture's history.

key_works.title: Entropy8Zuper!
key_works.description: Net.art and hypertextual Flash collaboration with Michaël Samyn that treated the browser as architectural and erotic space. Works including 'Skinonskinonskin' and 'Wirefire' used layered SWFs, evocative audio, and slow-revealing narrative to build intimate online environments at a moment when most web design was shedding such intimacy for utility. The practice was pivotal in establishing net.art as a medium of affect rather than only critique.

key_works.title: The Path
key_works.description: Commercial art game developed as Tale of Tales (with Samyn) that reframed Little Red Riding Hood as a meditation on rule-breaking, death, and feminine interior life. The game asked players to disobey its central instruction — don't leave the path — and punished conformity with vacuity. It became one of the canonical 'art games' of the late-2000s independent-games moment and helped establish the form as exhibitable beyond gaming contexts.

key_works.title: Minotaur sculpture series
key_works.description: Ongoing 3D-sculpture practice distributed across physical casts, high-resolution digital files, and NFTs. Harvey treats the figure of the minotaur as a stand-in for the hybrid body of the digital artist — classical sculpture's myth-figures reimagined in mesh geometry. Each work exists in multiple registers at once, proposing that digital-native sculpture can share the ontological weight of the physical tradition it converses with.

metadata.commons_summary: Net.art era distributed freely; Tale of Tales games were commercial; current practice mixes gallery, NFT, and open 3D-model release.
metadata.governance_summary: Solo/duo practice throughout; currently represented by bitforms.

metadata.practice_summary: Chinese multimedia artist whose gender-fluid avatar-based practice draws on Buddhist iconography, medical imaging, anime, and game engines. Represented China at Venice Biennale 2015; won Deutsche Bank Artist of the Year 2022.
metadata.methodology: Builds elaborate CGI universes centred around 'DOKU' — a non-binary digital incarnation — distributed across video, installation, game, music video, and live performance. Collaborates with musicians, animation studios, and game-engine specialists.

key_works.title: Uterus Man
key_works.description: Short animated film plus CGI action-figure character — a superhero whose skeleton is based on Lu Yang's own uterus — staged in the idiom of Japanese tokusatsu and anime. The work uses the body-horror and camp of those genres to detach the uterus from its traditional symbolic burden, proposing that reproductive organs can be computationally resculpted into speculative heroism. Widely shown in the Asia-Pacific digital-art circuit and foundational for Lu Yang's avatar-universe practice.

key_works.title: Delusional Mandala
key_works.description: Multi-channel video installation combining medical imaging, Buddhist iconography, and game-engine animation to stage consciousness as a diagnosable-yet-liberatory substrate. Selected for the Chinese pavilion at the 56th Venice Biennale, the work argued for a non-Western digital aesthetic rooted in religious image-making. A key moment in Asia-Pacific digital art's entry into major Western exhibition circuits on its own terms.

key_works.title: DOKU — Digital Alaya
key_works.description: Ongoing multi-media universe centred on 'DOKU', a non-binary digital avatar derived from Lu Yang's own motion-captured body and reworked across film, music video, installation, and live performance. The project proposes that gender-fluid digital embodiment is itself a cosmology — not a style — and draws on Tibetan Buddhist alaya-vijñāna (storehouse consciousness) for its metaphysical framing. Recipient of the Deutsche Bank Artist of the Year 2022 partly on its strength.

metadata.commons_summary: Gallery-commercial practice; some music-videos circulated widely on platforms.
metadata.governance_summary: Solo practitioner; represented by Société Berlin, Edouard Malingue (now Kiang Malingue).

metadata.practice_summary: Florian Hecker creates psychoacoustic sculptures and sound installations that use auditory illusions, spectral composition, and computational synthesis to alter listeners' spatial perception. His work treats sound as a sculptural material that operates directly on the perceptual apparatus.
metadata.methodology: Hecker works with advanced psychoacoustic research, computational sound synthesis, and spectral analysis to create sonic experiences that exploit the gaps and ambiguities in human auditory perception. He collaborates with scientists, philosophers (notably Reza Negarestani and Robin Mackay), and other sound artists. His process involves precise algorithmic composition using tools from computer music research, combined with rigorous spatial deployment in exhibition contexts.

key_works.title: Chimerization
key_works.description: Sound installation using chimeric sound objects that exploit auditory grouping and streaming to create perceptual fusions and fissions. Developed in dialogue with philosopher Reza Negarestani. Exhibited at Kunsthalle Wien and elsewhere.
key_works.relevance: Demonstrates how sound can create unstable perceptual objects that resist fixed categorization. Directly relevant to a Sense room that aims to compose through perceptual instability and emergence.

key_works.title: FAVN
key_works.description: Spatial audio work exploring auditory hallucination and chimeric perception, using multi-channel audio to create sound objects that exist only in the listener's perception. Presented at Old Selfridges Hotel, London.
key_works.relevance: A model for how sound can create virtual spatial objects through psychoacoustic means alone, without physical sculpture. Essential reference for the Sense room's sonic dimension.

key_works.title: Inspection II
key_works.description: Multi-part work including sound installation and performance exploring the relationship between acoustic signal, perception, and linguistic description. Collaboration with Negarestani on the concept of 'sound as concept.'
key_works.relevance: Demonstrates the intersection of computational sound synthesis, philosophy, and perceptual experience. A model for how art can operate at the boundary between sensation and cognition.

His work is not open-source or commons-oriented, though his collaborations with researchers contribute to shared knowledge in psychoacoustics and computer music.

consent_and_authorship.consent_approach: Hecker's work raises interesting questions about perceptual consent: his psychoacoustic works operate on listeners in ways they may not consciously control or choose. The experience is involuntary at the perceptual level. This is acknowledged as part of the work's meaning.
consent_and_authorship.authorship_model: Solo authorship with philosophical collaboration. Key works are developed in dialogue with Negarestani and Mackay, but Hecker is the named artist and primary creative decision-maker.

liveness_and_duration.temporal_detail: Installations run for exhibition durations with precisely composed sound that unfolds over time. Some works have fixed durations; others loop or evolve algorithmically. The perceptual experience shifts as the listener moves through the space and as their auditory system adapts.

data_materiality.data_sources: Algorithmically synthesized sound, psychoacoustic research data, spectral analysis, computational synthesis engines, acoustic measurements of exhibition spaces
data_materiality.data_provenance: Self-generated through computational processes. Sound material is synthesized rather than sampled. Psychoacoustic parameters drawn from published scientific research.

metadata.practice_summary: Iranian philosopher and writer whose theory-fiction 'Cyclonopedia' (2008) and subsequent rationalist-philosophical work ('Intelligence and Spirit', 2018) are heavily cited across digital-art and speculative-philosophy contexts. His writing functions for many practitioners as primary theoretical material.
metadata.methodology: Writes theory-fiction and systematic philosophy that blurs scholarly and speculative registers. Foundational influence on current thinking about AI, intelligence, and the computational.

key_works.title: Cyclonopedia: Complicity With Anonymous Materials
key_works.description: Theory-fiction in which a fictional archaeologist's manuscript merges with Lovecraftian horror, Middle Eastern oil politics, and Deleuzian philosophy to produce a singular hybrid text. The book popularised 'theory-fiction' as a genre and is a standing reference for artists seeking to fold speculative narrative into serious scholarly-philosophical material. Translated, reissued, and taught widely.

key_works.title: Intelligence and Spirit
key_works.description: Systematic philosophy arguing that genuine intelligence is a normative, inferential practice — and that artificial general intelligence, if possible, would have to be the construction of a normatively-bound mind rather than the scaling of pattern recognition. The book is cited in much contemporary AI-art writing as the most serious philosophical case for intelligence as socially-instituted rather than computationally-given.

key_works.title: The Corpus Project (with artists)
key_works.description: Ongoing collaboration with artists in which Negarestani's philosophical writing enters into direct textual dialogue with artwork — essays for exhibitions, commissions for installations, shared-authored publications. The format treats theory not as commentary but as co-material; has shaped how several AI-art practitioners engage with philosophical writing.

metadata.commons_summary: Extensively published through Urbanomic and academic presses; much writing accessible online. Work is heavily cited in digital-art theoretical discourse.
metadata.governance_summary: Academic/independent philosopher; currently faculty at The New Centre for Research & Practice.

metadata.practice_summary: British artist and musician whose algorithmic sound practice — as half of SND since 1996, and solo since — has been central to the Mego/Editions Mego and Sheffield-electronic circles. Writing and theoretical work extend the practice into academic and curatorial territory.
metadata.methodology: Uses custom algorithmic processes (often Max/MSP) to produce strict-rule compositions — stutter, modulation, rhythmic abstraction. Performs live with laptop; recorded output on Mego, Raster-Noton, The Death of Rave. Critical writing appears in The Wire, MIT Press, journals.

key_works.title: Multistability
key_works.description: Album-length solo statement — after a decade of duo work as SND — deploying strict algorithmic processes to produce stuttered, broken rhythmic material at the edges of what remains recognisably rhythmic. The record's rigour became a reference for a generation of algorithmic-music practitioners and helped crystallise a strand of computer music that refuses both the clean grid and the stochastic blur. Published by Editions Mego.

key_works.title: Manifestations
key_works.description: Commissioned sound-and-light installation that uses strict algorithmic relations between audio, lighting, and spatial configuration to produce a perceptual object that shifts rather than plays. The work extends Fell's rhythmic-algorithmic concerns into site-specific installation and is a reference point for sound-installation practice that refuses both ambient drift and narrative progression.

key_works.title: SND (with Mat Steel)
key_works.description: Long-running duo project whose minimal, algorithmic, micro-funk aesthetic across Mille Plateaux and Raster-Noton shaped the Sheffield/Mille-Plateaux sound and indirectly influenced broader minimal-electronic production. The duo's output insists that rhythmic complexity can emerge from strict constraint rather than accumulation — a compositional position that has been widely taken up.

metadata.commons_summary: Much theoretical writing available openly; music is commercial-label but on commons-adjacent independents.
metadata.governance_summary: Solo/duo practice; academic role (University of Huddersfield / Plymouth).

metadata.practice_summary: British experimental sound artist whose computer-music and noise practice since the 1990s has been central to the Warp / Editions Mego scene. 'Live Salvage' (2001), collaborations with Florian Hecker, and his own work on extreme computer-music synthesis are reference points.
metadata.methodology: Uses custom algorithmic synthesis, extreme-dynamic-range sound, and performance-as-event. Often collaborates with visual artists and other sound practitioners; central to Yasunao Tone, Aphex Twin, Russell Haswell / Florian Hecker axis.

key_works.title: Live Salvage 1997-2000
key_works.description: Double album of solo-performance recordings using custom synthesis and signal-processing systems, released on Warp. The record established Haswell's solo practice — already well-known from collaborations and no-fi performances — as rigorous compositional engagement with extreme dynamics and computational noise. A foundational document of the Warp-era computer-music-as-concert tradition.

key_works.title: Blackest Ever Black (with Florian Hecker)
key_works.description: Collaborative computer-music performance project with Florian Hecker, applying Xenakis-derived stochastic synthesis methods to live performance. The duo's work is widely cited in the algorithmic-computer-music lineage and extended the available performance-vocabulary of that tradition into extreme-dynamics territory.

metadata.commons_summary: Releases are commercial but via independent/experimental labels (Warp, Editions Mego).
metadata.governance_summary: Independent solo practice.

metadata.practice_summary: Lawrence Abu Hamdan is a sonic investigator and artist who uses sound as forensic, political, and spatial material. His practice treats audio evidence as a site of political struggle, making audible the power dynamics embedded in listening, voice analysis, and acoustic environments.
metadata.methodology: Abu Hamdan combines forensic audio analysis with artistic installation, working at the intersection of human rights investigation and contemporary art. He collaborates with organizations like Forensic Architecture and Amnesty International, using scientific audio analysis tools alongside artistic presentation. His process involves deep research into specific cases of political violence, border regimes, and surveillance, then translating acoustic evidence into immersive spatial installations and lecture-performances.

key_works.title: Walled Unwalled
key_works.description: Video and spatial audio installation exploring how walls have become listening devices and how sound travels through architectural barriers. Uses cases of earwitness testimony in legal proceedings. Won the Turner Prize in 2019.
key_works.relevance: Demonstrates how sound functions as spatial-political material that penetrates boundaries. A model for how the Sense room could use audio to create relational spatial experiences.

key_works.title: Earwitness Inventory
key_works.description: Installation cataloguing sounds described by witnesses in legal testimony from the Syrian civil war, creating an archive of sonic evidence that exists only in human memory and language.
key_works.relevance: Shows how sound can function as a relational database of experience, directly relevant to a graph-curated approach where audio signals carry intelligence about connections between events, spaces, and testimonies.

key_works.title: After SFX
key_works.description: Spatial audio installation exploring the sonic landscape of the Saydnaya military prison in Syria, reconstructed from earwitness testimony in collaboration with Forensic Architecture. Sound becomes the primary means of reconstructing a space that cannot be visually documented.
key_works.relevance: Sound as primary spatial and evidentiary material rather than supplement to the visual. Directly relevant to the Sense room's potential to privilege non-visual sensory registers.

metadata.practice_summary: Greek-French composer, architect, and mathematician (1922-2001) whose stochastic composition methods and the UPIC graphical composition system (1977) made him a foundational figure in computer music. UPIC — which allowed composers to draw sonic structures that the computer then realised — is one of the defining tools of algorithmic music.
metadata.methodology: Developed stochastic composition using probability distributions (Gaussian, Poisson, Markov chains) starting in the 1950s, initially computed by hand. UPIC was developed at CEMAMu, the computer-music research centre he founded. Deep entanglement with Le Corbusier's architectural practice informed his spatialised composition.

key_works.title: Metastaseis
key_works.description: Orchestral work composed using techniques derived from the graphical projections Xenakis developed as Le Corbusier's architectural collaborator, translating the architectural hyperbolic paraboloids of the Philips Pavilion into massed string glissandi. The piece is his first statement that musical composition could be geometric in substrate, and it predates and underwrites everything that follows — stochastic music, UPIC, the algorithmic composition tradition. Widely cited as the origin point of sonic-architectural thinking.

key_works.title: Philips Pavilion (with Le Corbusier)
key_works.description: Temporary pavilion for the Brussels World's Fair whose hyperbolic-paraboloid architecture and interior audio-visual work ('Poème électronique', with Varèse) co-produced a single audio-visual-architectural event. Xenakis designed the shell and contributed an interstitial piece ('Concret PH'). The work argues that architecture, composition, and computation share a single geometric substrate — the thesis the rest of his career operationalises.

key_works.title: UPIC system
key_works.description: Graphical computer-music system developed at CEMAMu allowing composers to draw sonic structures that the computer realises as sound. UPIC treats the drawing as score and the computer as executor, anticipating by decades the user-interface assumptions of contemporary digital-audio workstations. The first generation of computer music studios outside IRCAM/Stanford often traces directly to UPIC-style graphical-score thinking.

metadata.commons_summary: UPIC was academic-institutional; Xenakis's writings ('Formalized Music') are widely distributed. CCMIX (now Centre Iannis Xenakis) continues as public institution.
metadata.governance_summary: Academic / institutional practice (CEMAMu, Indiana University); legacy maintained by Centre Iannis Xenakis.

metadata.practice_summary: Austrian composer whose algorithmic-phonographic practice — 'Voices and Piano' transcribes famous voices into piano pulses; 'Talking Piano' makes a player-piano speak — occupies a unique position in contemporary computer music. Works also include site-specific sound installation and instrumental composition.
metadata.methodology: Algorithmic transcription of extra-musical material (speech, noise, landscape) into instrumental form. Uses player-piano, strict compositional systems, and deep conceptual framing. Strong theoretical writing accompanies the work.

key_works.title: Voices and Piano
key_works.description: Long-running composition cycle in which recorded spoken voices (writers, philosophers, revolutionaries, children) are transcribed into piano pulses performed synchronously with the original recording. The piano operates as a low-resolution analytic of the voice; the piece is a sustained investigation of what of speech remains when its pitched substrate is re-rendered as discrete pulses. One of the canonical works of algorithmic-compositional thinking.

key_works.title: A Letter from Schoenberg (Talking Piano)
key_works.description: Player-piano work in which the piano, driven by a high-resolution mechanical interface, 'speaks' a letter by Arnold Schoenberg — the instrument forced into phonemic duty by precisely-timed polyphonic attacks. The piece argues that speech and piano share a substrate that can be crossed by sufficient mechanical precision, and is one of the most-cited examples of the speech-as-sound tradition in contemporary computer music.

key_works.title: Weiss/Weisslich
key_works.description: Long-running series of sound installations and environmental works investigating noise, white-ness, and the edge between signal and environment. Ablinger's insistence on the unmeasured environmental sound as compositional substrate has shaped institutional sound-art curation internationally.

metadata.commons_summary: Extensive scores and writings distributed via his own site; new-music-institutional rather than purely commercial.
metadata.governance_summary: Independent composer; university teaching roles (Kunstuniversität Graz, Berlin).

metadata.practice_summary: Grimes launched Elf.Tech as an open AI voice platform allowing anyone to create music using her voice via a trained voice model, with a revenue-sharing agreement that splits royalties 50/50 with creators who use the tool commercially.
metadata.methodology: Grimes trained an AI model on her vocal recordings and released it publicly through the Elf.Tech platform. Users upload instrumentals or vocals, and the system transforms them into Grimes' voice using AI voice conversion technology. The project emerged from Grimes' public stance that she would 'split 50% royalties on any successful AI-generated song that uses my voice.' She collaborated with CreateSafe (the team behind the platform) to build the technical infrastructure. The approach treats the artist's voice as an open instrument -- a commercial parallel to Holly Herndon's Holly+ protocol art, but operating within mainstream music industry distribution channels (Spotify, Apple Music, etc.) rather than DAO governance.

metadata.practice_summary: Harm van den Dorpel is a Dutch-born, Berlin-based artist who uses evolutionary algorithms, machine learning, and blockchain technology to create artworks that evolve, mutate, and curate themselves. His practice treats curation and aesthetic selection as computational processes.
metadata.methodology: Van den Dorpel builds custom software systems that use evolutionary/genetic algorithms to generate and select visual compositions. His methodology involves defining fitness functions — aesthetic criteria encoded as algorithms — that guide generative processes toward outputs he finds interesting. He then intervenes as curator/selector within these evolutionary processes. His blockchain work extends this into on-chain curation, where provenance, ownership, and relational context are embedded in the artwork's technical substrate. He is deeply engaged with the intersection of aesthetics and computation.

key_works.title: Mutant Garden Seeder
key_works.description: A generative art system using evolutionary algorithms where digital organisms grow, mutate, and breed. Collectors can 'seed' new mutations from existing works, creating an expanding, evolving ecosystem of visual forms on the blockchain.
key_works.relevance: Directly models art-as-evolving-ecosystem — works that recompose based on collector actions and algorithmic mutation. The relational breeding mechanism mirrors graph-based composition.

key_works.title: Mutant Garden
key_works.description: An interactive web-based environment where users can breed and evolve digital organisms through an artificial life simulation with aesthetic selection. Precursor to the on-chain Seeder.
key_works.relevance: Demonstrates participatory evolutionary aesthetics where the audience directly shapes the evolution of artworks through selection — a model for audience-participatory graph curation.

key_works.title: Left Gallery
key_works.description: An online gallery and publishing platform co-founded by van den Dorpel that exhibited and sold digital art, pioneering early models for digital art commerce and curation.
key_works.relevance: Demonstrates protocol-art thinking — designing the infrastructure of art distribution and curation as creative practice. An early experiment in what on-chain curation would later become.

metadata.commons_summary: Complex relationship to commons. The evolutionary systems and some tools are shared openly, but the artworks are commodified through blockchain ownership. Left Gallery operated as a commercial platform. His work exists in the tension between open generative systems and blockchain-based scarcity/ownership.
metadata.governance_summary: Solo artistic practice with algorithmic co-governance — the evolutionary algorithms make aesthetic decisions within parameters set by the artist. Mutant Garden Seeder distributes some creative agency to collectors who can seed new mutations. Left Gallery involved collaborative curatorial decisions.

metadata.practice_summary: Steyerl creates video essays, installations, and lecture-performances that interrogate the politics of images, data, AI, and digital circulation. She is one of the most influential voices on the political economy of visual culture in the age of machine learning.
metadata.methodology: Steyerl works through essayistic film and lecture-performance, combining investigative journalism, critical theory, and visual experimentation. She frequently uses AI tools, 3D modeling, and data visualization as both subject and medium, exposing the power structures embedded in predictive technologies and image-making systems. Collaborates with teams of programmers, designers, and researchers at her UdK Berlin research center.

metadata.practice_summary: K Allado-McDowell is a writer and artist who co-founded Google's Artists + Machine Intelligence program and pioneered literary co-authorship with large language models, most notably in the book Pharmako-AI (2020), written in collaboration with GPT-3.
metadata.methodology: Allado-McDowell works through direct, improvisational dialogue with language models, treating the AI as a creative collaborator rather than a tool. The process involves iterative prompting, editing, and weaving together human and machine-generated text. They draw on traditions of ethnobotany, psychedelia, Indigenous knowledge systems, and speculative fiction to create hybrid texts that explore consciousness, ecology, and non-human intelligence.
