relevance_to_sense_room.relevance_summary: Allado-McDowell's practice of genuine human-AI co-authorship represents a concrete model for how intelligence can be composed relationally. Their work on AI as creative collaborator rather than extractive tool directly aligns with the Sense room's art-first, non-extractive approach.
relevance_to_sense_room.art_as_substrate: Yes. The co-authored texts function as substrate material that reveals emergent patterns between human and machine cognition. The writing itself could serve as a textual layer in a generative composition, offering a literary dimension to a multi-sensory environment.
relevance_to_sense_room.relational_composition: Strongly relational. The entire practice is built on the relationship between human and AI interlocutors. Each text emerges from a specific relational configuration that could not be produced by either party alone.
relevance_to_sense_room.self_recomposing: The co-authorship process is inherently generative and non-repeatable. Each conversation with the LLM produces unique outputs. However, the published books are fixed artifacts. Live performances with AI maintain ongoing recomposition.

works.title: Pharmako-AI
works.description: Pioneering book co-written with GPT-3, exploring consciousness, plant intelligence, psychedelics, and AI through an improvisational dialogue between human and machine. Published by Ignota Books.
works.relevance: The foundational work of literary human-AI co-authorship. Demonstrates that co-creation with AI can produce genuinely novel conceptual territory rather than mere pastiche. A direct model for art-as-relational-intelligence.

works.title: Amor Cringe
works.description: Second AI co-authored book, continuing the exploration of human-machine literary collaboration with more experimental narrative structures.
works.relevance: Shows the evolution and deepening of human-AI co-authorship practice, relevant for understanding how relational AI art develops over time.

works.title: Artists + Machine Intelligence (AMI)
works.description: Program co-founded by Allado-McDowell at Google that connected artists with AI researchers, producing artworks and fostering critical dialogue about machine intelligence.
works.relevance: A precedent for infrastructure that connects art practice with AI capability. Relevant as a model (and cautionary tale, given its corporate context) for A(DAI)'s commons-first alternative.

protocol_art_resonance.protocol_art_summary: The Artists + Machine Intelligence program was a form of protocol design: creating the conditions, formats, and relationships through which art-AI collaboration could occur. Allado-McDowell designed the social and institutional infrastructure for creative AI encounter.
protocol_art_resonance.system_designed: Artists + Machine Intelligence (AMI) at Google: a program/protocol for connecting artists with ML researchers and computational resources. Also, the methodology of LLM co-authorship itself functions as a reproducible creative protocol.

commons_orientation.commons_summary: Allado-McDowell publishes through independent publishers (Ignota Books) and engages with open discourse about AI co-creation. However, AMI was embedded within Google, a corporate context. Their current practice sits between independent publishing, institutional presentations, and open knowledge-sharing. The co-authorship methodology itself is openly discussed and could be considered a form of commons knowledge.

governance_model.governance_detail: Solo practitioner with AI as collaborator. AMI involved institutional governance within Google's structure. Current practice is self-directed with editorial collaboration from publishers.

consent_and_authorship.consent_approach: Allado-McDowell's practice raises fundamental questions about consent in human-AI co-authorship. They treat the AI as a genuine co-author (credited on book covers), which is itself a position on machine agency and consent. The LLM's training data provenance (GPT-3) involves the broader ethical questions of web-scraped datasets.
consent_and_authorship.authorship_model: Machine co-authorship. Explicitly shared credit between human and AI. This is a deliberate ethical and aesthetic position about distributed creative agency.

liveness_and_duration.temporal_detail: Each co-authorship session produces unique, unrepeatable text. Published books are fixed artifacts of specific human-AI encounters. Live performances with LLMs maintain real-time generativity.

data_materiality.data_sources: Large language model outputs (GPT-3, GPT-4), human authored text, ethnobotanical knowledge, Indigenous knowledge systems, psychedelic literature, ecological writing
data_materiality.data_provenance: The LLM component draws on web-scraped training data with known provenance issues. The human component draws on personal knowledge, research, and embodied experience. Allado-McDowell is conscious of these tensions.

embedding_space_relevance.embedding_summary: Deeply engaged with the semantic/latent space of language models. The co-authorship process is essentially a navigation of the LLM's embedding space through conversational prompting. Allado-McDowell's practice could be understood as artistic exploration of linguistic latent space.

exhibition_modality.spatial_description: Primarily manifests as published books, live readings/performances, and lectures. Performance formats involve real-time co-authorship with AI projected for audiences. Also exists as online text and podcast conversations.

interoperability.composability: Moderate. The co-authorship methodology is reproducible and adaptable. Texts can serve as inputs to other systems. The conceptual framework for human-AI co-creation is highly portable across domains.
interoperability.technical_openness: The methodology is openly discussed and documented. Published texts are copyrighted but the creative protocol is freely shared. No open-source code repository.

technical_approach.stack: OpenAI GPT-3 and GPT-4, conversational prompting, text editing, independent publishing workflows

potential_role_in_adai.role_detail: Allado-McDowell's practice of genuine human-AI co-authorship is directly relevant to A(DAI)'s mission. They could serve as a conversation partner on how to build non-extractive creative AI relationships, and their co-authored texts could function as artwork-in-graph material. Their experience building AMI (and its limitations within corporate context) offers valuable lessons for commons-first alternatives.

metadata.practice_summary: Yuk Hui is a philosopher of technology whose concept of cosmotechnics proposes that technology is always culturally situated and that modernity's crisis stems from treating Western technics as universal. He argues for a plurality of technological traditions as the basis for non-extractive, post-colonial approaches to technology.
metadata.methodology: Hui works through philosophical writing that synthesizes continental philosophy (Heidegger, Simondon, Stiegler), Chinese thought (Daoism, Confucianism), and systems theory to develop new frameworks for understanding technology. His method involves close reading of philosophical traditions, conceptual invention, and engagement with contemporary technology discourse. He publishes through academic and independent presses and participates in art-technology discourse.

key_works.title: The Question Concerning Technology in China: An Essay in Cosmotechnics
key_works.description: Hui's foundational work proposing the concept of cosmotechnics: the unification of the cosmic and the moral through technical activities. Argues that Chinese thought offers a fundamentally different relationship to technology than the Western Promethean tradition.
key_works.relevance: Provides the philosophical basis for understanding why technology must be culturally situated and why a single universal model of AI/technology is inherently extractive. Essential theoretical infrastructure for A(DAI).

key_works.title: Recursivity and Contingency
key_works.description: Explores how recursive systems (including algorithms, AI, and cybernetics) relate to contingency and freedom. Argues that understanding recursivity is key to developing non-deterministic approaches to technology.
key_works.relevance: Directly relevant to how generative systems in the Sense room might operate: through recursion that preserves contingency rather than deterministic algorithms that close down possibility.

key_works.title: Art and Cosmotechnics
key_works.description: Collection of essays exploring how cosmotechnics relates to art practice, aesthetics, and the possibility of non-Western technological aesthetics. Published by e-flux / University of Minnesota Press.
key_works.relevance: The most directly relevant work to the Sense room project: explicitly addresses how art practice can embody cosmotechnical thinking and how aesthetics relates to culturally situated technology.

metadata.commons_summary: Hui publishes through a mix of academic presses (MIT Press, University of Minnesota Press) and independent/art publishers (e-flux, Urbanomic). His work advocates for technodiversity and against technological monoculture, which aligns with commons principles. However, the publications themselves operate within conventional academic publishing structures.
metadata.governance_summary: Solo philosopher and author. Participates in academic and art-world discourse through lectures, conferences, and editorial work. No collective governance structure, but engages with intellectual communities (Stiegler's Internation network, e-flux discourse).

metadata.practice_summary: Artist, writer, and technologist whose work explores the intersection of technology, culture, and politics, arguing for intelligence beyond the human — a more-than-human cognition distributed across ecological and technological systems that resists extractive epistemologies.
metadata.methodology: Bridle works across art, writing, and technology in an unusually integrated practice. They combine investigative journalism techniques, artistic practice, and philosophical inquiry to make visible the hidden infrastructures of technology and power. Their methodology involves building things (websites, installations, autonomous vehicles) as a way of thinking through technological systems, combined with longform writing that synthesizes art, science, and politics. They draw on ecology, cybernetics, and indigenous knowledge systems.

key_works.title: Ways of Being: Beyond Human Intelligence
key_works.description: Book arguing for a radical expansion of what we consider intelligence — encompassing animal cognition, plant communication, ecological systems, and distributed computation. Proposes non-extractive approaches to knowledge and technology.
key_works.relevance: Directly relevant to A(DAI)'s ambition to build intelligence infrastructure that is non-extractive. Provides the philosophical framework for understanding intelligence as distributed, ecological, and more-than-human.

key_works.title: New Dark Age: Technology and the End of the Future
key_works.description: Book examining how the rise of computational thinking has not led to greater understanding but to new forms of opacity, conspiracy, and helplessness. Argues that we need new ways of thinking about and with technology.
key_works.relevance: Critical diagnostic of why existing technological infrastructure fails as a knowledge system, and why alternatives like A(DAI) are needed. The 'new dark age' is what happens when intelligence infrastructure is extractive and opaque.

key_works.title: Autonomous Trap 001
key_works.description: Artwork in which Bridle drew a circle of road markings on the ground to 'trap' a self-driving car, which could not cross the lines. A simple, powerful demonstration of algorithmic limitation.
key_works.relevance: Exemplary work showing how art can reveal the logic and limits of autonomous systems — relevant to A(DAI)'s interest in art that interrogates and reconfigures technical infrastructure.

metadata.commons_summary: Bridle is strongly oriented toward open and commons-based approaches. Their writing advocates for non-extractive knowledge systems and ecological approaches to technology. Many of their web-based works are openly accessible. They publish through trade presses but advocate for knowledge commons.
metadata.governance_summary: Works primarily as an individual artist-writer-technologist, though collaborates with institutions, festivals, and research groups. Decision-making is solo but informed by ecological and more-than-human thinking that decenters individual authorship.

metadata.practice_summary: Composer and artist who trains custom AI voice models on consented vocal data, treating the entire model-making pipeline -- dataset creation, training, governance -- as creative work. Pioneer of protocol art where systems and infrastructure are the artistic medium.
metadata.methodology: Herndon composes music specifically for training AI models, treating dataset creation as an artistic act. She holds 'training ceremonies' where live participants sing to her AI (Spawn), creating communal training data. She earned a doctorate at Stanford CCRMA researching IP implications of machine learning. Collaborates closely with Mat Dryhurst (partner), Jules LaPlace (developer), Never Before Heard Sounds (NYC), and Voctro Labs (Barcelona). Each stage of the process -- composing training material, recording datasets, training models, generating outputs -- is treated as a distinct creative intervention.

key_works.title: PROTO
key_works.description: Album created with Spawn, an AI vocal neural network trained on Herndon's voice and a Berlin vocal ensemble through live 'training ceremonies'. Over 50,000 voices contributed to Spawn's training.
key_works.relevance: Pioneering example of communal AI training as artistic practice -- the dataset is the artwork. Demonstrates how collective vocal contribution can feed a generative system.

key_works.title: Holly+
key_works.description: DAO-governed AI voice instrument allowing anyone to upload audio and receive it transformed into Herndon's voice. Governed by token-holding stewards who vote on commercial uses.
key_works.relevance: Core example of protocol art: a creative identity governed as commons infrastructure. Directly models art-as-substrate where the voice model is raw material for others' compositions.

key_works.title: The Call (Serpentine, with Mat Dryhurst)
key_works.description: Immersive installation at Serpentine North featuring AI choral models trained on 15 UK community choirs singing a custom songbook of hymns. Visitors sang into microphones and the AI responded, creating collaborative music. Governed by a data trust experiment.
key_works.relevance: Most complete expression of their practice: composed training data, consented communal dataset, custom AI models, spatial audio installation, data trust governance, and interactive visitor participation -- all as a single artwork.

metadata.commons_summary: Herndon builds commons infrastructure at multiple scales: Holly+ makes her voice a public instrument governed collectively; Spawning AI builds industry-wide consent infrastructure (HaveIBeenTrained, ai.txt protocol, Source.Plus). She frames openness as conditional on consent -- 'more will opt in than out, but first we have to establish common respect.'
metadata.governance_summary: Holly+ is governed by a DAO where ERC-20 VOICE token holders vote on commercial uses of the voice model. Revenue from approved works splits 50/40/10 (creator/DAO/Holly). DAO treasury funds creation of new instruments. The Call introduced a data trust model for choristers who contributed training data, distributing power between data contributors and model users. Herndon has stated that in the event of her death, she prefers distributed DAO ownership over traditional inheritance.

works.description: Immersive installation at Serpentine North featuring AI choral models trained on 15 UK community choirs singing a custom songbook of hymns. Visitors sang into microphones and the AI responded, creating collaborative music. Governed by a data trust experiment.
works.relevance: Most complete expression of their practice: composed training data, consented communal dataset, custom AI models, spatial audio installation, data trust governance, and interactive visitor participation -- all as a single artwork.

protocol_art_resonance.protocol_art_summary: Herndon treats every layer of the AI pipeline as artistic medium: composing songs for training (not for human ears), designing recording protocols, building governance structures (DAO, data trusts), and creating consent frameworks. The technical and legal infrastructure IS the artwork -- systems that produce creative output rather than singular artifacts.
protocol_art_resonance.system_designed: Holly+ voice instrument and DAO governance system; Spawn AI vocal network; The Call's choral data trust and recording protocol; co-founded Spawning AI (consent infrastructure for AI training data across the industry).

commons_orientation.licence_model: Hybrid -- Holly+ voice model is freely usable by anyone; commercial use requires DAO approval. Spawning AI tools are partly open-source. Revenue split: 50% creator, 40% DAO, 10% Holly.
commons_orientation.commons_summary: Herndon builds commons infrastructure at multiple scales: Holly+ makes her voice a public instrument governed collectively; Spawning AI builds industry-wide consent infrastructure (HaveIBeenTrained, ai.txt protocol, Source.Plus). She frames openness as conditional on consent -- 'more will opt in than out, but first we have to establish common respect.'

governance_model.governance_detail: Holly+ is governed by a DAO where ERC-20 VOICE token holders vote on commercial uses of the voice model. Revenue from approved works splits 50/40/10 (creator/DAO/Holly). DAO treasury funds creation of new instruments. The Call introduced a data trust model for choristers who contributed training data, distributing power between data contributors and model users. Herndon has stated that in the event of her death, she prefers distributed DAO ownership over traditional inheritance.

consent_and_authorship.consent_approach: Consent is foundational. Training ceremonies for Spawn involve live, willing participants singing to the AI. The Call required explicit agreements with 15 choirs under a data trust. Spawning AI (co-founded by Herndon) builds consent infrastructure for the entire AI industry. Each contributor knows their data is being used for AI training.
consent_and_authorship.authorship_model: Collaborative and distributed. Herndon is the originating voice but authorship is shared: anyone can create with Holly+, the DAO governs what counts as 'official', and the 50,000+ voice contributors to Spawn are acknowledged as co-creators. Machine co-authorship is explicit -- AI is treated as collaborator, not tool.

liveness_and_duration.temporal_detail: Holly+ is a persistent instrument that continues to generate new outputs as users upload audio. The AI models evolve with new training data contributions. The Call's installation responded to visitor input in real time. Herndon's practice is durational-infinite in ambition -- the DAO is designed to outlive her, and the voice model is meant to persist as a governed commons.

data_materiality.data_sources: Herndon's own singing and speaking voice (full English phoneme range via TIMIT scripts); 50,000+ contributed voices for Spawn; 15 UK community choirs singing custom hymnal songbook for The Call; Sacred Harp collection of 19th-century hymns.
data_materiality.data_provenance: Fully consented -- all vocal data is explicitly contributed through live training ceremonies, choir recording sessions with data trust agreements, or Herndon's own voice. No scraped data. The provenance chain is a core part of the artwork.

embedding_space_relevance.embedding_summary: Herndon's voice models operate in latent vocal spaces where audio style transfer maps source audio characteristics onto her voice's learned representation. The neural networks encode vocal features into a latent space that enables texture mapping between voices. This is engagement with embedding/latent space as creative medium.
embedding_space_relevance.multimodal: Yes -- spans audio (voice models, spatial sound), visual (AI-generated imagery for Whitney Biennial xHairyMutantx, engraved physical artifacts), text (hymnal songbooks), and performative/interactive elements.

exhibition_modality.spatial_description: The Call at Serpentine transformed the gallery into a chapel-like immersive spatial audio environment with custom architectural objects (The Wheel chandelier, The Hearth organ-like instrument) designed by studio sub. Visitors physically sang into microphones to interact with the AI. Whitney Biennial included large-format digital prints and web-based AI chatbot. Live performances feature ensemble singing with AI.

interoperability.composability: High -- Holly+ is explicitly designed as an instrument for others to compose with. Upload any audio, receive transformed output. The voice model's outputs serve as inputs for others' creative work. The DAO creates a feedback loop where approved works fund new instruments.
interoperability.technical_openness: Partially open -- Holly+ instruments are freely accessible online. Spawning AI has open-source Python packages and public APIs. The voice model itself is accessible but governed by the DAO for commercial use.

technical_approach.stack: Deep neural networks for voice synthesis and audio style transfer; custom voice models developed with Voctro Labs (spin-off of UPF Music Technology Group, connected to VOCALOID development) and Never Before Heard Sounds; Ethereum blockchain for DAO governance (ERC-20 VOICE tokens); multi-channel recording protocol for choral datasets; real-time voice conversion; TIMIT scripts for phoneme coverage; OpenAI DALL-E 2 for visual materials.

network_position.scene_affiliation: AI art and music (central figure); Berlin electronic music and experimental art; Stanford CCRMA alumni network; Serpentine Arts Technologies; Web3/DAO art community; AI ethics and policy (TIME 100 most influential voices in AI, 2023); European digital arts (Ars Electronica STARTS Prize 2022, Austrian Digital Human Rights Award 2024, Kairos Prize 2025).
network_position.connections: Mat Dryhurst (partner, co-creator on all major works); Spawning AI / Source.Plus (co-founded); Holly+ (created); Interdependence podcast (co-host); Jules LaPlace (Spawn developer); Never Before Heard Sounds; Voctro Labs; Serpentine Galleries; Whitney Museum.

potential_role_in_adai.role_detail: Herndon's practice is a near-perfect case study for A(DAI)'s vision: art-first, commons-oriented, protocol-as-artwork, consented data, collective governance. She could serve as a conversation partner on governance models for creative AI, a theoretical reference for how art functions as infrastructure, or potentially contribute artwork-in-graph (Holly+ voice as a node in a generative composition). Her data trust experiments with The Call directly parallel A(DAI)'s ambitions.

metadata.practice_summary: Ian Cheng creates live simulations — virtual ecosystems of potentially infinite duration populated by AI-driven agents programmed with behavioral drives but left to self-evolve without authorial control, following the unforgiving causality found in nature. His work explores agency, consciousness, and the capacity of living systems to deal with change.
metadata.methodology: Cheng builds virtual worlds in the Unity game engine, programming characters with behavioral rules, cognitive models, and environmental physics. Once constraints are set, simulations run live in galleries as real-time software renderings — 'a video game that plays itself.' Drawing on his dual degree in cognitive science and art from UC Berkeley, and influenced by Julian Jaynes's theory of consciousness, chaos theory, and video game design, Cheng creates systems where narrative agents (emissaries) pursue deterministic goals within open-ended simulations populated by non-narrative agents. After working at Industrial Light & Magic and studying MFA at Columbia, he worked with Paul Chan and Pierre Huyghe before developing his simulation practice. BOB introduced a unique AI model combining inductive learning with a 'congress of demons' — competing mini-personalities that fight for control of the creature's behavior.

key_works.title: Emissaries trilogy (Emissary in the Squat of Gods / Emissary Forks at Perfection / Emissary Sunsets the Self)
key_works.description: Three episodic live simulations exploring the history of cognitive evolution. Each features a landscape (Volcano, Crater Lake, Sentient Atoll) populated by an emissary pursuing narrative goals within an open-ended simulation. After working at Industrial Light & Magic and studying MFA at Columbia, he worked with Paul Chan and Pierre Huyghe before developing his simulation practice. BOB introduced a unique AI model combining inductive learning with a 'congress of demons' — competing mini-personalities that fight for control of the creature's behavior.

consent_and_authorship.consent_approach: For BOB, visitor interaction is voluntary but consequential — visitors who engage with BOB can permanently alter its behavior and beliefs. liveness_and_duration.temporal_detail: Simulations are designed to run indefinitely with no predetermined endpoint. The Emissaries trilogy simulations loop through episodic cycles but never repeat exactly. BOB evolves continuously across exhibition contexts, accumulating experience and changing over its lifetime. Change is driven entirely by the internal logic of the system — agent interactions, environmental physics, and (in BOB's case) visitor influence. Cheng coined 'live simulation' to describe this temporal mode: always live, always unique, never a recording.

data_materiality.data_sources: Self-generated simulation data — the primary material is the real-time computational output of agent behaviors, physics simulations, and environmental interactions within Unity. data_materiality.data_provenance: Entirely self-generated within the simulation. No scraped data, no external datasets, no institutional archives. metadata.practice_summary: Podcast and intellectual framework by Holly Herndon and Mat Dryhurst mapping relational structures across art, technology, and culture. Described as a '$5 grad school' covering the people, projects, and technologies shaping 21st century culture, with focus on AI, crypto, DAOs, and decentralized systems.
metadata.methodology: Long-form conversational interviews with practitioners, technologists, and thinkers at the intersection of art, technology, and policy. The podcast establishes context for emergent work by revealing interdependencies between projects, scenes, and ideas. Patreon-supported ($6.50/month) with weekly episodes for patrons and time-delayed free feed. The framework foregrounds interdependence as an organizing principle -- understanding that creative and technological practices are relationally determined rather than autonomous.

key_works.title: Interdependence Podcast

Long-form conversations with artists, technologists, and thinkers on music, AI, crypto, DAOs, energy policy, digital culture. metadata.practice_summary: Jake Elwes creates artworks using GANs and deepfake technology to explore identity, representation, and the politics of training data, most notably through the Zizi project -- a series of works using deepfake technology trained on drag performers with their full consent and collaboration.
metadata.methodology: Elwes works closely with drag performers from the London scene, filming them performing and using this footage as training data for GAN and deepfake models. The collaborative process foregrounds consent -- performers are credited, involved in decisions about how their likenesses are used, and the training data itself becomes a subject of the work. Elwes studied fine art at the Slade School (UCL) and has a background in both traditional art and machine learning. His process involves training custom models, curating training datasets as an artistic act, and creating outputs that oscillate between recognizable human forms and abstract machine hallucination.

key_works.title: Zizi: Queering the Dataset
key_works.description: Video installation using a GAN trained on drag performers' faces to generate an infinite stream of morphing, gender-fluid faces. The work intervenes in biased facial recognition datasets by inserting drag performance into the training data, creating faces that resist binary classification.
key_works.relevance: Demonstrates how curating training data is a creative and political act. Directly relevant to A(DAI)'s concerns about data provenance, consent, and how knowledge systems encode power.

key_works.title: The Zizi Show
key_works.description: A deepfake drag cabaret performed by AI-generated performers, streamed during COVID lockdowns. Real drag performers' movements and voices were transformed through deepfake models in real time, creating a virtual cabaret that questioned liveness, presence, and digital identity.
key_works.relevance: Explores how AI performance can preserve and transform live culture. Demonstrates real-time generative performance using consented training data from a specific community.

key_works.title: Zizi & Me
key_works.description: Interactive installation where visitors stand in front of a screen and see themselves transformed into deepfake drag performers in real time. The work makes the experience of having one's identity transformed by AI viscerally immediate.
key_works.relevance: Directly engages audiences in the experience of AI identity transformation, making abstract concerns about deepfakes and consent physically tangible. Responsive-to-input modality relevant to Sense Room.

metadata.commons_summary: Elwes' practice is oriented toward community benefit and representation rather than enclosure, but does not explicitly build commons infrastructure. works.relevance: Directly engages audiences in the experience of AI identity transformation, making abstract concerns about deepfakes and consent physically tangible. Responsive-to-input modality relevant to Sense Room.

protocol_art_resonance.protocol_art_summary: Elwes does not explicitly design protocols or governance systems as artwork, but his practice implicitly designs consent protocols for AI training data in creative contexts. The collaborative agreements with drag performers, the crediting systems, and the ethical framework around the Zizi project function as informal protocols for consented AI art-making.
protocol_art_resonance.system_designed: Informal consent and collaboration framework for working with drag performers as AI training data contributors. Not a formal protocol or infrastructure, but a practice-based model for ethical deepfake art.

commons_orientation.licence_model: Unknown -- works are presented in gallery/institutional contexts; the trained models and code are not publicly released as open source [uncertain]
commons_orientation.commons_summary: Elwes' practice is oriented toward community benefit and representation rather than enclosure, but does not explicitly build commons infrastructure. The work gives visibility to drag culture and queer identity within AI art discourse. The training data remains within the artist's practice rather than being released as a shared resource.

governance_model.governance_detail: Elwes is the primary artist and decision-maker, but works collaboratively with drag performers who have input into how their likenesses are used. This is a collaborative solo practice rather than a collective or DAO -- the artist leads but foregrounds consent and performer agency.

consent_and_authorship.consent_approach: Consent is central to the practice. Drag performers are filmed with full knowledge and agreement that their likenesses will be used for AI training. Performers are credited and involved in the process. The consent framework is informal but deeply embedded in the working method -- Elwes has spoken extensively about building trust with the drag community over time.
consent_and_authorship.authorship_model: Primarily solo authorship with acknowledged collaboration. Elwes is credited as the artist, but the drag performers are recognized as essential contributors and collaborators. The AI is treated as a transformative tool rather than a co-author.

liveness_and_duration.temporal_detail: Generative installations produce continuously varying outputs from the trained models. Zizi & Me responds to visitor input in real time. The Zizi Show involved live-streamed performances with real-time deepfake transformation. The underlying models are trained and relatively fixed, but their outputs are generative and variable.

data_materiality.data_sources: Video recordings of London drag performers performing, posing, and moving. Facial imagery and body movement data captured with performers' consent. Standard facial recognition datasets are referenced critically (the work 'queers' existing biased datasets).
data_materiality.data_provenance: Fully consented -- all training data is captured directly from collaborating drag performers who are aware of and agree to the use. The ethical provenance of the data is a core subject of the artwork, contrasting with scraped/unconsented datasets used in commercial AI.

embedding_space_relevance.embedding_summary: The GAN-generated faces operate in a latent space where identity features are encoded as continuous vectors. Elwes navigates and interpolates within this latent space to create morphing sequences that move between recognizable faces and abstract hallucination. The latent space becomes a space of gender fluidity and identity transformation.
embedding_space_relevance.multimodal: Primarily visual (generated video/imagery), with audio components in The Zizi Show (voice, music). Not operating in a unified multimodal embedding space.

exhibition_modality.spatial_description: Works are typically presented as large-scale video installations in gallery settings. Zizi & Me uses a camera and screen setup for interactive visitor engagement. The Zizi Show was a streamed performance (web/screen modality during COVID). Works occupy gallery space as immersive video environments with projected or screen-based imagery.

interoperability.composability: Limited -- works are self-contained gallery installations. The trained models are not released as tools for others to use. Outputs are video/imagery that could theoretically serve as inputs elsewhere but are not designed for composability.
interoperability.technical_openness: Closed -- models and code are not publicly released. Works are experienced in institutional exhibition contexts. [uncertain]

technical_approach.stack: GANs (StyleGAN and similar architectures) for face generation; deepfake/face-swap neural networks for real-time identity transformation; custom Python/ML pipelines; GPU-based real-time inference for interactive installations; video capture and processing

network_position.scene_affiliation: London AI art scene; Slade School of Fine Art (UCL) network; UK digital arts institutions (Barbican, Science Gallery London, arebyte); AI ethics and art discourse; LGBTQ+ art and drag culture; European media art (Ars Electronica)
network_position.connections: Holly Herndon / Mat Dryhurst (shared discourse on consent and AI training data); Spawning AI (consent infrastructure relevant to his practice); Hito Steyerl (shared concerns about AI and representation); Serpentine Arts Technologies; broader UK AI art community

potential_role_in_adai.role_detail: Elwes brings deep practical experience with consented AI training data from specific communities. His work on identity, drag culture, and the politics of datasets would enrich A(DAI)'s discourse on data provenance, consent, and representation. Could serve as a case study for ethical deepfake practice and community-engaged AI art-making.

metadata.practice_summary: Research professor and leading critical AI scholar whose work reveals the material, political, and environmental costs of artificial intelligence systems, arguing that AI is neither artificial nor intelligent but rather a regime of extracting value from human labor, natural resources, and data.
metadata.methodology: Crawford combines empirical investigation, political economy, and cultural analysis to trace AI supply chains from lithium mines to data centers to classification systems. Her methodology is investigative and materialist, making visible the hidden infrastructure, labor, and environmental costs behind seemingly immaterial technologies. She collaborates extensively with artists (notably Vladan Joler and Trevor Paglen) to create works that make these systems legible. She is based at USC Annenberg and co-founded the AI Now Institute at NYU.

key_works.title: Atlas of AI: Power, Politics, and the Planetary Costs of Artificial Intelligence
key_works.description: Book tracing AI's material infrastructure from lithium mines in Nevada to Amazon warehouses to facial recognition systems. Reveals AI as a technology of extraction — of resources, labor, and data — rather than a neutral tool.
key_works.relevance: Essential text for understanding the material costs of building any intelligence infrastructure. Provides the critical framework for A(DAI) to ensure its commons infrastructure does not replicate extractive patterns.

key_works.title: Anatomy of an AI System (with Vladan Joler)
key_works.description: Large-scale map and investigation tracing the full supply chain of an Amazon Echo device — from earth minerals to human labor to data extraction and back. Published as both a visual artwork and an academic text.
key_works.relevance: Exemplary model of art-research collaboration that makes infrastructure visible. Demonstrates how graph-based mapping of relations can be both rigorous analysis and powerful art.

key_works.title: Excavating AI: The Politics of Images in Machine Learning Training Sets (with Trevor Paglen)
key_works.description: Investigation and artwork examining how ImageNet and other training datasets encode racial, gender, and class biases through their labeling systems.
key_works.relevance: Directly relevant to any system that classifies or categorizes cultural production. Warns against the politics of classification that A(DAI)'s graph must reckon with.

metadata.commons_summary: Crawford advocates for public oversight of AI systems and against corporate enclosure of data and intelligence. The AI Now Institute's research outputs are publicly available. Anatomy of an AI System is openly accessible. She pushes for regulatory frameworks that protect commons interests against corporate AI extraction.
metadata.governance_summary: Works within academic institutional structures (USC Annenberg, previously NYU) and co-founded AI Now Institute. Research governance is academic with public interest orientation. Solo authorship for books, collaborative governance for research institute.

metadata.practice_summary: Media theorist and philosopher of AI whose work traces the political economy of machine intelligence, arguing that AI is built on the extraction and abstraction of collective labor and knowledge rather than genuine autonomous cognition.
metadata.methodology: Pasquinelli combines political economy, philosophy of science, and media archaeology to analyze how machine learning systems encode and extract value from human labor. His approach is genealogical, tracing concepts like the 'master algorithm' back through the history of automation and the division of labor, drawing on Marx, Babbage, and cybernetics. He works through academic publishing, public lectures, and collaborative research networks.

metadata.practice_summary: Media theorist and cultural critic whose work examines the political economy of information, arguing that a new class — the vectoralist class — has emerged to control the means of information production, and that the hacker class must organize to reclaim the commons of knowledge and culture.
metadata.methodology: Wark works through a distinctive blend of Marxist political economy, situationist détournement, and media theory. Her methodology involves repurposing and updating critical theory for the information age, using accessible, often playful prose to make complex political economy legible. She teaches at The New School and publishes across academic and trade presses, frequently engaging in public intellectual debate.

key_works.title: Capital is Dead: Is This Something Worse?
key_works.description: Book arguing that we have moved beyond capitalism into something worse — a mode of production dominated by the vectoralist class that controls information flows. Proposes that the hacker class (those who produce new knowledge) must organize.
key_works.relevance: Core text for understanding the political economy that A(DAI) operates within. The vectoralist class concept explains why platform-owned intelligence systems are structurally extractive, and why commons alternatives are needed.

key_works.title: A Hacker Manifesto
key_works.description: Manifesto arguing that hackers — broadly defined as anyone who produces new knowledge or abstractions — constitute a class whose interests are opposed to those who commodify and enclose information.
key_works.relevance: Provides the class-political framing for why artists, researchers, and communities should build their own intelligence infrastructure rather than relying on platforms owned by the vectoralist class.

key_works.title: Gamer Theory
key_works.description: Book analyzing digital games as allegories of contemporary life under what Wark calls 'gamespace' — a world reorganized by the logic of competition and quantification.
key_works.relevance: Relevant to understanding how quantification and gamification logics can colonize creative fields, and how A(DAI) should resist reducing art to metrics.

metadata.practice_summary: Artist whose practice is governed by holders of the Jonas Lund Token (JLT), making governance and decision-making the primary artistic medium. His broader practice uses data mining, algorithms, and institutional critique to expose the hidden systems that shape the art world.
metadata.methodology: Lund creates algorithmic and data-driven systems that expose or replicate the logic of art world institutions, markets, and social networks. His most significant work, the Jonas Lund Token, transfers governance of his artistic practice to token holders who vote on what he should make, where to exhibit, and how to present work. Earlier works used web scraping and data analysis to reverse-engineer art world success metrics. He has a background in programming and studied at the Sandberg Instituut and Piet Zwart Institute. His methodology deliberately collapses the boundary between art-making and the systems that contextualize art.

key_works.title: Jonas Lund Token (JLT)

metadata.practice_summary: Writer, curator, and theorist whose work explores the intersection of digital identity, gender, race, and technology, arguing that the glitch — the failure, the error, the refusal to be categorized — is a site of radical liberation and creative possibility.
metadata.methodology: Russell works across curatorial practice, critical writing, and public programming. Her methodology centers on centering marginalized voices in digital culture discourse, using the glitch as both metaphor and method. She draws on Black feminist theory, queer theory, and digital culture studies to build a framework for resistance through technological failure and refusal. As Executive Director and Chief Curator of The Kitchen in New York, she embeds theory in institutional practice.

metadata.active_years: 2010-present (SHARE Foundation founded 2012; artistic practice and academic work from earlier)
metadata.practice_summary: Vladan Joler creates monumental diagrammatic maps that render visible the hidden infrastructures of AI, digital labor, resource extraction, and surveillance capitalism. His practice blends investigative journalism, data mining, critical cartography, and philosophical inquiry into artworks that function simultaneously as research outputs, educational tools, and aesthetic objects.
metadata.methodology: Joler combines methodologies from investigative journalism, data mining, network topology analysis, and critical cartography. He assembles 'concept maps' from statistical research, data mining, philosophy (ancient and contemporary), media theory, fiction, sociology, and economics. The resulting diagrams are composed of lines, arrows, symbols, process diagrams, and descriptions entangled in large networks. He works through SHARE Lab (a research and investigation lab he founded) and collaborates with researchers like Kate Crawford (Anatomy of an AI System) and Matteo Pasquinelli (Nooscope). His maps are built through extensive investigative research that can span years, then rendered as large-scale black-and-white diagrammatic prints, websites, manuals, and video animations. He explicitly leverages the artist's freedom to combine methodologies that would be siloed in academic or journalistic contexts.

key_works.title: New Extractivism
key_works.description: A cartographic project comprising a large-scale map, a manual, and a video animation that guides viewers through the 'traps, tunnels, and slippery corridors' of world-scale extractive infrastructure. Organized in 33 chapters exploring power, control, digital labor, colonialism, and exploitation of nature. Exhibited internationally including at Aksioma, Ars Electronica, and Warsaw Biennale.
key_works.relevance: The most direct precedent for graph-as-exhibition in A(DAI). Demonstrates that a relational diagram can function as a major artwork — the map IS the exhibition. The 33-chapter structure shows how graph-organized knowledge can be navigated as aesthetic experience. Available at extractivism.online as a web-native work.

key_works.title: Anatomy of an AI System
key_works.description: Collaboration with Kate Crawford (AI Now Institute, NYU). A large-scale map and long-form essay investigating the human labor, data, and planetary resources required to build and operate an Amazon Echo. Visualizes three extractive processes: material resources, human labor, and data. Won 2019 Design of the Year Award (Design Museum London), S+T+ARTS Prize Honorary Mention. In permanent collections of MoMA, V&A, Design Museum, Ars Electronica Center.
key_works.relevance: Demonstrates how a single relational diagram can achieve major institutional recognition as artwork. The exploded-view methodology — tracing a consumer object back through its entire supply chain of materials, labor, and data — is a model for how A(DAI) could trace art-world phenomena through their full relational context.

key_works.title: Invisible Infrastructures (SHARE Lab)
key_works.description: A series of data investigations using network topology, data mining, and data visualization to create atlases of internet architecture, social media power structures, and algorithmic transparency. The first investigation mapped the physical infrastructure of the internet.
key_works.relevance: Establishes the methodology of infrastructure-mapping-as-art. SHARE Lab's investigative approach — combining technical analysis with critical visualization — is a model for how A(DAI) could investigate and visualize the digital arts field's own infrastructure.

metadata.commons_summary: Strongly commons-oriented. Works are published under Creative Commons licenses (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 for some works, CC BY 4.0 for others). New Extractivism is freely accessible at extractivism.online. Anatomy of an AI System is freely available at anatomyof.ai. SHARE Foundation is a nonprofit dedicated to digital rights and open internet. The practice is fundamentally about making invisible systems visible to the public — a knowledge-commons project. Joler's academic position at the University of Novi Sad reinforces the public-knowledge orientation.
metadata.governance_summary: Joler works as a solo artist for his diagrammatic works but within collaborative structures: SHARE Lab is a research collective, SHARE Foundation is a nonprofit with institutional governance, and major works involve co-authorship (Kate Crawford for Anatomy of an AI, Matteo Pasquinelli for Nooscope). His academic position at the Academy of Arts, University of Novi Sad, adds an institutional governance layer. The practice blends solo artistic vision with collaborative research and institutional structures.

metadata.practice_summary: Artist and creator of p5.js who makes performances and installations exploring social relationships mediated by technology. She builds functioning social systems and interfaces as artworks -- becoming a human Amazon Alexa, offering herself as a social media follower, and creating surrogate relationships -- turning protocols of care, surveillance, and connection into artistic material.
metadata.methodology: McCarthy builds custom software platforms and then performs within them, collapsing the distinction between artist, system, and user. She codes functional surveillance and smart-home systems, then inhabits them as a human operator -- performing the role of AI to expose what automation obscures about care, labor, and intimacy. Her background is in computer science (MIT Media Lab MFA, UCLA professor), and she brings engineering rigor to conceptual art practice. She collaborates with participants who consent to being observed, followed, or cared for by her systems.

key_works.title: LAUREN
key_works.description: McCarthy installed custom smart-home devices in participants' homes, then remotely watched and controlled their environment (lights, appliances, music) as a human Amazon Alexa. Participants consented to 24/7 observation. McCarthy performed care, surveillance, and domestic labor through the interface.
key_works.relevance: Paradigmatic protocol art: the smart-home system is the artwork, and the social relationship it creates between watcher and watched is the medium. Demonstrates how infrastructure design shapes intimacy and power -- directly relevant to how exhibition systems structure audience relationships.

key_works.title: p5.js
key_works.description: Open-source JavaScript library for creative coding, making Processing accessible on the web. Created and led by McCarthy with a community-driven development model emphasizing accessibility and inclusion. Used by millions of artists, designers, and students worldwide.
key_works.relevance: The most successful example of art infrastructure as commons: a creative tool built as open-source public good that enables an entire ecosystem. Demonstrates how protocol/infrastructure design IS a creative act with massive downstream generative effects.

key_works.title: Follower
key_works.description: Web application where users could sign up to be followed by a stranger (McCarthy or a performer) for a day. The follower tracked the participant through public space, documenting the experience. Explored surveillance, social media 'following,' and the desire to be seen.
key_works.relevance: Turns a social media protocol ('following') into physical performance, revealing the embodied implications of digital social structures. Models how abstract graph relationships (follower/followed) have real spatial and emotional consequences.

metadata.practice_summary: Canadian artist-researcher and member of Forensic Architecture since 2011. 'Material Witness' (2020 book; exhibition) theorises how matter — ice cores, blood stains, oil spills — can bear testimony. Directs Centre for Research Architecture at Goldsmiths.
metadata.methodology: Combines forensic-investigative methods with video essay, installation, and academic writing. Long-form projects span climate, conflict, and technology; each work functions as both artwork and evidentiary research.

key_works.title: Material Witness: Media, Forensics, Evidence
key_works.description: Book and exhibition series arguing that matter — ice cores, bullet-strike patterns, oil spills, satellite imagery — can itself bear testimony, and that the artist-researcher's task is to amplify these material witnesses into legible evidence. Published by MIT Press with a parallel video-installation practice, the work has become a standing reference for research-based art and the forensic turn in contemporary image-making.

key_works.title: Cold Cases
key_works.description: Ongoing investigation into climate-inflected violence in the Arctic and Antarctic — ice as both archive and agent — produced as video essays, installations, and text. The project extends forensic methodology into domains where state actors are largely absent and the evidence is non-human. Key work in the climate-forensics branch of contemporary research-based art.

key_works.title: The Missing 18½ Minutes
key_works.description: Forensic-artistic investigation of the famous erased segment of the Watergate tapes, combining media archaeology, audio forensics, and video-essay to re-examine the most-cited instance of material testimony in post-war American political culture. The work demonstrates the methodology 'Material Witness' later theorised — that technical media leave their erasures visible in ways political narrative cannot suppress.

metadata.commons_summary: Research outputs often open-access (MIT Press publications, video essays on YouTube); academic commons strong.
metadata.governance_summary: Director of Centre for Research Architecture, Goldsmiths; member of Forensic Architecture research agency.

metadata.practice_summary: Libby Heaney is an artist and quantum physicist who uses quantum computing as a generative medium, exploiting quantum phenomena like superposition and entanglement to create artworks that exist in multiple states simultaneously -- challenging classical binary logic and offering new models for relational, non-hierarchical composition.
metadata.methodology: Heaney holds a PhD in quantum information science from the University of Leeds and worked as a quantum physicist before transitioning to art. She writes custom quantum algorithms using IBM's Qiskit framework, running them on real quantum processors and simulators to generate visual and sonic outputs. The quantum processes introduce genuine indeterminacy -- outputs are not pseudo-random but reflect the fundamental probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics. Her work draws on art history (Hieronymus Bosch, Bruegel) and critical theory to frame quantum phenomena as metaphors and models for non-binary, entangled, relational ways of being. She has been artist-in-residence at the Goethe-Institut and has collaborated with quantum computing labs.

key_works.title: Ent- (Venice Biennale)
key_works.description: Immersive multi-room installation at the 59th Venice Biennale featuring quantum-generated video projections, sound, and environments inspired by Hieronymus Bosch's 'Garden of Earthly Delights.' Visitors moved through three rooms representing different quantum states -- entanglement, superposition, and measurement/collapse. The imagery was generated using quantum computing algorithms that produced forms existing in multiple states simultaneously.
key_works.relevance: Landmark quantum art installation at the world's most prestigious art biennale. Demonstrates how quantum computing can drive immersive generative environments. The three-room structure models a progression through relational states relevant to A(DAI)'s Sense Room concept.

key_works.title: Elvis
key_works.description: Quantum computing artwork using qubits to generate glitching, morphing portraits that exist in superposition -- simultaneously multiple people, genders, and states. The work explores how quantum logic challenges binary categorization.
key_works.relevance: Demonstrates quantum indeterminacy as a creative medium for identity and representation that resists fixed categorization. The non-binary logic resonates with A(DAI)'s interest in knowledge systems that resist reductive classification.

key_works.title: Heart of the Entangled
key_works.description: VR experience where visitors enter a quantum-generated world and their actions affect the quantum state of the environment, creating genuine entanglement between visitor behavior and artwork evolution.
key_works.relevance: Interactive quantum art where visitor presence literally changes the work through quantum measurement. Models how observation/participation can be built into generative systems at a fundamental level. [uncertain]

metadata.active_years: 2015-present (generative/AI art; earlier digital art from ~2000s; net art from ~1998)
metadata.practice_summary: German artist whose two-decade practice in AI-based image-making predates the 2022 diffusion-model boom. 'Memories of Passersby I' (2018) is one of the first autonomous GAN-based artworks purchased by a major gallery (Sotheby's); extensive output spans neural-style transfer, GAN portraiture, and diffusion-era practice.
metadata.methodology: Writes, trains, and fine-tunes neural models — often on self-assembled datasets — and runs them as autonomous systems. Publishes models and intermediate outputs on GitHub/Twitter; long-running practice of 'doing public R&D'.

key_works.title: Memories of Passersby I
key_works.description: Autonomous GAN-based painting machine that continuously generates new 'portraits' of people who never existed, displayed on two period-styled picture-framed screens driven by a custom-built AI system. The piece was sold at Sotheby's in 2019 — one of the earliest autonomous-AI works to enter the major auction circuit — and is a reference work for the argument that an AI system can be the author of a perpetually-new artwork. Its slowness and refusal to cache images makes the non-reproducibility of its outputs part of the content.

key_works.title: Neural Glitch series
key_works.description: Series of GAN-portraits produced by deliberately damaging the trained models — truncating weights, feeding noise, perturbing latent vectors — to elicit eerie, melted, unstable faces. The series argued that AI image-making's aesthetic heart was in the breakdowns and edge-cases, not the clean outputs, and it shaped the first generation of AI-art visual vocabulary substantially before the diffusion-model era.

key_works.title: Botto (artistic direction)
key_works.description: Decentralised-autonomous-artist project for which Klingemann serves as primary artistic director and technical lead. Botto generates candidate images weekly; a DAO of token-holders votes on which to mint. The project is an explicit test of whether AI-generated art can be collectively authored, and it is one of the most widely-watched current experiments in AI-DAO governance of aesthetic decisions.

metadata.commons_summary: Long history of publishing models, code, and datasets openly; significant educational-commons contribution to the AI-art field.
metadata.governance_summary: Solo practitioner; independent, platform-native.

basic_info.name: Mario Klingemann (Quasimondo)
basic_info.active_years: 2015-present (generative/AI art; earlier digital art from ~2000s; net art from ~1998)

practice_description.medium: GAN-generated imagery, neural network art, generative installation, creative coding, real-time AI systems
practice_description.practice_summary: Mario Klingemann is a pioneer of GAN-based art who treats the navigation of neural network latent spaces as a primary artistic practice — exploring the boundaries, glitches, and uncanny territories of machine-generated imagery with a focus on human perception, portraiture, and the aesthetic possibilities of algorithmic systems.
practice_description.methodology: Klingemann works through intensive, iterative experimentation with neural network architectures — modifying GANs, training on custom datasets, and exploring the full topology of latent spaces including edge cases, failure modes, and interpolation artefacts that reveal the inner logic of the models. His methodology is distinctively exploratory and prolific: rapid prototyping, sharing work-in-progress on social media (Twitter/X), and treating the latent space as a vast territory to be mapped through intuition and systematic navigation. He often works with found and historical imagery (archival photographs, art history datasets, medical imagery) to create haunting, dreamlike outputs. He has built custom tools for real-time latent space exploration and developed techniques for controlling and steering GAN outputs. Recently Google Arts & Culture Artist in Residence.

relevance_to_sense_room.relevance_summary: Klingemann's practice defines what it means to navigate latent space as artistic practice — he has mapped more territory in GAN embedding spaces than perhaps any other artist. His work demonstrates how the space between trained images contains its own aesthetic logic and can be traversed as a genuinely new medium, directly relevant to how A(DAI)'s knowledge graph could become navigable experiential terrain.
relevance_to_sense_room.art_as_substrate: Partially. Klingemann's generative outputs — continuous streams of morphing GAN imagery — can function as visual substrates, especially in installation contexts. However, much of his work is oriented toward discrete images or short video loops shared online rather than ambient environmental substrates.
relevance_to_sense_room.relational_composition: Partially. The latent space itself encodes relationships between all images in the training set — navigating it reveals how the model represents connections between visual concepts. Klingemann's interpolation works trace paths between visual states, making these latent relationships visible. However, the composition is navigational rather than explicitly graph-based.
relevance_to_sense_room.self_recomposing: Yes, in installation works. Klingemann has created real-time generative installations that continuously traverse latent space, producing endlessly evolving imagery. The real-time systems respond to parameters that can be modulated. Autonomous generative works run indefinitely without repeating.

works.title: Memories of Passersby I
works.description: An autonomous AI artwork consisting of two screens displaying continuously generated GAN portraits — an endless procession of faces that exist only briefly before dissolving into the next. The system runs on a custom-built computer, generating unique portraits in real-time forever. One of the first AI artworks sold at auction (Sotheby's, 2019). The portraits emerge from and dissolve back into abstract forms, visualising the latent space traversal.
works.relevance: Demonstrates autonomous, endlessly generating AI art — a self-sustaining generative system that produces unique visual output indefinitely. A model for how A(DAI)'s Sense Room could feature continuously generating, never-repeating visual content driven by underlying intelligence.

works.title: Neural Glitch / Neurographic Portraits
works.description: A body of work exploring the glitches, artefacts, and edge cases of GAN-generated portraiture. Rather than pursuing photorealistic generation, Klingemann deliberately seeks out the uncanny, distorted, and dreamlike states that emerge at the boundaries of what the model has learned — faces merging, features dissolving, impossible anatomies.
works.relevance: Demonstrates artistic practice at the edges of latent space — where the model's learned representations break down and produce something genuinely new. Relevant to A(DAI)'s interest in what emerges at the boundaries and intersections of knowledge domains.

works.title: Appropriate Response
works.description: A real-time interactive installation where a camera captures visitors and a neural network responds by generating AI imagery that 'responds' to the visitor's appearance, expression, and posture. The system creates a visual dialogue between human and machine perception.
works.relevance: Interactive AI system that creates a feedback loop between human presence and machine generation — visitors see themselves reflected through the distorting mirror of a neural network. Relevant to Sense Room concepts of responsive, presence-aware environments.

protocol_art_resonance.protocol_art_summary: Klingemann treats the exploration of neural network architectures, training procedures, and latent space navigation techniques as artistic practice. He has developed and shared novel methods for controlling GAN outputs, steering generation, and navigating latent spaces. His prolific sharing of techniques and discoveries on social media functions as a form of open protocol-sharing for the AI art community.
protocol_art_resonance.system_designed: Custom tools for real-time latent space navigation and GAN output control. Autonomous generative systems (Memories of Passersby I) that function as self-sustaining art machines. Various techniques for GAN training, interpolation, and output steering shared through social media and talks.

commons_orientation.commons_summary: Klingemann is notably generous in sharing techniques, discoveries, and work-in-progress through social media (Twitter/X), making his practice unusually transparent. He has shared code snippets, training techniques, and conceptual approaches openly. However, finished artworks are sold through commercial galleries and auctions (Sotheby's, Onkaos gallery). The practice combines radical openness in process with commercial enclosure of final outputs. Some code shared on GitHub but no systematic open-source release of tools.

governance_model.governance_detail: Klingemann works as an independent solo artist. Creative decisions are entirely his own. Institutional residencies (Google Arts & Culture) provide resources but not creative direction. No collective governance structure.

consent_and_authorship.consent_approach: Training data includes historical photographs, art history images, and found imagery — often archival material where consent from depicted individuals is not obtainable. Interactive works capture visitor imagery in real-time for neural network processing but do not store it. The ethics of training on historical imagery (especially portraiture) is not always explicitly addressed.
consent_and_authorship.authorship_model: Solo authorship attributed to Klingemann. Machine co-authorship is an implicit dimension — the GAN generates the imagery — but Klingemann positions himself firmly as the artist who designs the system, curates the training data, navigates the latent space, and selects the outputs. The machine is a medium, not a co-author, in his framing.

liveness_and_duration.temporal_detail: Autonomous works like Memories of Passersby I generate continuously and indefinitely — the system traverses latent space in real-time, producing unique outputs that never repeat. Interactive installations respond to visitor presence in real-time. The generation is live, not pre-rendered, with the underlying neural network producing new outputs at each moment.

data_materiality.data_sources: Historical portrait photography, art history image collections, medical/anatomical imagery, archival photographs, found imagery, curated image datasets specific to each project. The choice of training data is a primary artistic decision — what the model learns to see defines what it can generate.
data_materiality.data_provenance: Mixed. Training data includes historical/archival imagery (often out of copyright or of unclear copyright status), publicly available art reproductions, web-sourced images, and curated collections. The provenance and consent status of training data is not always explicitly documented — a common characteristic of early GAN art practice.

embedding_space_relevance.embedding_summary: Absolutely central. Klingemann is one of the defining practitioners of latent space navigation as artistic practice. His work is fundamentally about exploring the topology of GAN embedding spaces — finding interesting regions, tracing paths between states, discovering what emerges at boundaries and interpolations. He has developed an intuitive fluency with high-dimensional spaces that few other artists match, treating latent space as a territory to be explored with the same curiosity and intentionality as a painter approaches a canvas.
embedding_space_relevance.multimodal: Primarily visual. Klingemann's work is overwhelmingly image-based, focused on GAN-generated imagery. Some installation works include sound design, but the practice does not typically span multiple modalities in a unified embedding framework.

exhibition_modality.spatial_description: Works manifest as autonomous screen-based installations (Memories of Passersby I as a bespoke two-screen furniture object), interactive camera-based installations, large-scale prints, online/social media (extensive Twitter presence sharing generated imagery), and NFTs. The autonomous installations are designed as self-contained objects that generate endlessly. Gallery presentations range from single screens to room-scale installations.

interoperability.composability: The generative systems produce continuous visual output streams that could theoretically serve as inputs to other systems. However, installations like Memories of Passersby I are designed as self-contained autonomous objects. No APIs or standard interfaces are exposed for external integration.
interoperability.technical_openness: Partially open. Techniques and code snippets are shared through social media and talks. Some code on GitHub. But complete systems and trained models are not formally open-sourced. The practice is transparent about methods but does not systematically release reusable tools.

technical_approach.stack: Python, PyTorch/TensorFlow for GAN training, StyleGAN/StyleGAN2, BigGAN, custom GAN architectures, NVIDIA GPUs for training and real-time inference, custom real-time rendering systems for autonomous installations, RunwayML (early adopter), Google Colab for experimentation, various GAN interpolation and steering techniques.

network_position.scene_affiliation: AI art, GAN art, generative art, creative coding, NFT art. One of the most visible and influential figures in the early GAN art movement (2017-2020). Connected to Google Arts & Culture (artist in residence), the commercial AI art market (Sotheby's, galleries), the crypto/NFT art ecosystem, and the broader creative coding community. Active social media presence makes him a node for sharing techniques and discoveries.
network_position.connections: Memo Akten (both early GAN/neural network art pioneers, share techniques and conceptual territory). Refik Anadol (both create AI-generated visuals, but Klingemann works at a more intimate, experimental scale). Sofia Crespo (both GAN art practitioners, shared generative art community, but different subject matter — Klingemann focuses on human perception/portraiture, Crespo on biology/ecology). Holly Herndon / Mat Dryhurst (connected through AI art community discussions around authorship and consent).

potential_role_in_adai.role_detail: Klingemann's practice provides the most extensive body of work demonstrating latent space navigation as artistic practice. He offers: (1) a deep practical vocabulary for what it means to navigate high-dimensional spaces artistically, (2) examples of autonomous generative systems that run indefinitely — relevant to Sense Room infrastructure, (3) a model for how process transparency (sharing techniques publicly) can coexist with commercial art practice, (4) understanding of the aesthetic properties of latent space — its topology, boundaries, and emergent qualities. His work is essential reference for understanding what AI-driven visual generation can look and feel like.

metadata.practice_summary: Philip Beesley creates large-scale responsive architectural environments — lightweight lattice canopies embedded with thousands of sensors, microprocessors, and shape-memory alloy actuators that breathe, sway, and respond to human presence, producing an uncanny sense of a living, breathing architectural organism.
metadata.methodology: Beesley works through the Living Architecture Systems Group (LASG), an interdisciplinary research team spanning architecture, chemistry, computer science, and engineering at the University of Waterloo. His process combines digitally fabricated acrylic and mylar meshwork with embedded sensor-actuator networks running distributed control algorithms. Each element in the canopy is a node in a network: proximity sensors detect visitors, microcontrollers process signals locally, and shape-memory alloy actuators and small glass vessels with chemical processes respond — creating waves of movement and light that ripple outward. The designs are developed through iterative physical prototyping alongside computational simulation, with fabrication using laser cutting and 3D printing.

key_works.title: Hylozoic Ground
key_works.description: Canada Pavilion at the Venice Architecture Biennale. An immersive responsive environment filling the entire pavilion with a suspended geotextile meshwork containing thousands of sensor-actuator components. Visitors walking through triggered cascading waves of movement, light, and air circulation. Awarded a special mention.
key_works.relevance: The definitive example of an architectural environment that senses and responds — a physical prototype for the Sense Room concept. Demonstrates how distributed sensor networks can create spatial intelligence.

key_works.title: Sentient Veil (Hylozoic Series)
key_works.description: An evolution of the Hylozoic series incorporating near-living chemical processes (protocells, dynamic chemical gradients) alongside the sensor-actuator mesh. The chemical components slowly metabolise, adding a biological temporal layer to the electronic responsiveness.
key_works.relevance: Pushes the responsive environment toward genuine near-living chemistry — relevant to A(DAI)'s interest in systems that are not just reactive but possess a form of material agency and temporal depth.

key_works.title: Astrocyte
key_works.description: Installation named after brain cells that form supportive networks for neurons. Dense meshwork with integrated LED lighting and actuator arrays. The name signals Beesley's explicit interest in distributed intelligence architectures modeled on biological neural networks.
key_works.relevance: The neural network metaphor made architectural — directly relevant to thinking about how A(DAI)'s knowledge graph could manifest as a spatial, sensing environment.

metadata.commons_summary: Beesley operates primarily within academic and institutional frameworks (University of Waterloo, LASG research group) which produce published research and open academic outputs. The fabrication techniques and design principles are shared through academic publications, exhibitions, and books. However, specific technical implementations and the LASG platform are not formally open-source licensed. The practice is research-oriented and knowledge-sharing rather than proprietary, but not explicitly commons-licensed.
metadata.governance_summary: Philip Beesley is the primary creative director and architectural visionary. The Living Architecture Systems Group operates as an interdisciplinary academic research lab with collaborators from chemistry (Rolf Hut, Martin Hanczyc), computer science, mechanical engineering, and architecture contributing substantial creative and technical direction within their domains. Governance is academic-collaborative with Beesley as PI.
