metadata.practice_summary: American artist and educator who founded Rhizome in 1996 — the organisation that has more than any other institutionalised net.art and digital-art preservation. His own artistic practice includes 'Port Huron Project' (2006-8), a re-enactment of New Left speeches in situ.
metadata.methodology: Institution-building as primary practice (Rhizome), alongside photography, video, and re-enactment art. Tribe led Rhizome's early years of net-art acquisition and exhibition, building the infrastructure that shaped how net.art entered museum collections.

key_works.title: Rhizome (founding)
key_works.description: Founding act of Rhizome — now in its third decade as the leading institution for net-art and digital-art preservation — began as an email list run from Tribe's apartment and scaled into an artist-serving non-profit embedded in the New Museum. Tribe's founding contribution is institution-building treated as artistic practice: the creation of infrastructure that subsequently produces conditions for other artists' work. Few founding gestures in digital art carry more lasting structural weight.

key_works.title: Port Huron Project
key_works.description: Series of six live re-enactments of New Left speeches — SNCC, SDS, Black Panthers — staged in the American landscapes where the originals were delivered. The work uses performance, video documentation, and archival research to argue that the political speech-act can be re-activated rather than only remembered. An important work of early-2000s research-based political video art.

key_works.title: Dystopia Tracker
key_works.description: Collaborative, crowdsourced database pairing science-fiction predictions with current-events realisations — an archive of the futures-that-have-arrived as they arrive. The project treats predictive fiction as a corpus against which journalism can be read, and invites public contribution. Reflects Tribe's long-running interest in institution-as-artwork.

metadata.commons_summary: Rhizome is the landmark commons-oriented digital-art institution; Tribe's own later projects have mostly been open-access.
metadata.governance_summary: Founded Rhizome (non-profit); now academic (Brown University).

metadata.practice_summary: German feminist net-artist and theorist, co-founder of the Old Boys Network (1997, the first cyberfeminist collective). Practice combines artwork ('Female Extension', 1997), academic research (PhD on generative art and authorship), and activism.
metadata.methodology: 'Female Extension' submitted 289 fake female artists to a net-art competition to expose the gender gap in curated net-art shows. Subsequent practice treats authorship itself as contested site — generative net-art, writings on piracy, commons, and feminist tech.

key_works.title: Female Extension
key_works.description: Intervention into the 'Extension' net.art competition held by Hamburger Kunsthalle: Sollfrank submitted 289 fabricated female-artist profiles to a show that had otherwise received few entries from women, exposing both the infrastructural gender gap and the reception-logic of the net.art curatorial circuit. The piece is a foundational work of cyberfeminist net.art and is cited in virtually every scholarly survey of the field's institutional politics.

key_works.title: net.art generators
key_works.description: Series of browser-based generators that automatically produce new net.art works by recombining fragments from an archive of net.art material. The generators implicitly argue that authorship in net.art is already algorithmic and collective, and that the conventions of signature and original work are inadequate to the medium. They anticipate by two decades the generative-AI debates about authorship, training data, and recombinatorial aesthetics.

key_works.title: Giving What You Don't Have
key_works.description: PhD research project and artistic practice examining contemporary artists' engagement with copyright, free culture, and the politics of giving what you don't own. The work combines interviews, documentation, and artworks into an unfolding investigation, published openly. A rigorous synthesis of artistic and legal-theoretical material.

exhibitions: Zentrum für Kunst und Medien Karlsruhe (ZKM)
metadata.commons_summary: Long-running commitment to commons/piracy/feminist-tech discourse; writing and research are public-facing. Academic role at HFBK Hamburg.
metadata.governance_summary: Independent / academic practice; OBN operated as artist-led collective.

metadata.practice_summary: American married duo whose practice since the late 1990s spans net.art, sound installation, concert work, and writing. 'Blackness for Sale' (2001) auctioned Keith Obadike's blackness on eBay — a canonical net.art work on racial identity and platform commerce.
metadata.methodology: Works across multiple registers: net.art, sound installation, concert/opera (TREE OF FLOWERS, THE PLAYERS 2019), and scholarly writing (both are academics). Practice combines conceptual-art lineage with sustained engagement with African-American music, literature, and digital form.

key_works.title: Blackness for Sale
key_works.description: Net.art work in which Keith Obadike auctioned his 'blackness' on eBay, complete with a list of advantages and disadvantages of ownership; eBay removed the listing four days in, citing inappropriate content. The piece is a canonical net-art engagement with race, platform commerce, and the politics of categorisation, and is one of the most-cited works in surveys of early-2000s Black digital art.

key_works.title: The Sour Thunder, an Internet Opera
key_works.description: Web-distributed opera incorporating live performance, sound files, text, and user-contributed material into a distributed operatic form. Commissioned by Yale Cabaret and released across streaming and web, the work extended opera's conventions into net-native form and is an early and rigorous example of cross-modal Black-diasporic internet art.

key_works.title: Four Electric Ghosts
key_works.description: Multi-part concert-installation work combining live performance, electronics, and visual projection into a layered meditation on the electrical substrate of African-American music and memory. Commissioned by The Kitchen (NYC), the piece is representative of the duo's move from net.art into sustained concert-scale sound-installation work.

metadata.commons_summary: Net.art works remain freely accessible; academic writing widely distributed. Concert work is institutional.
metadata.governance_summary: Duo practice; both hold academic roles.

metadata.practice_summary: British net.art collective (1995-2010), founded by Graham Harwood, Mervin Jarman, Matsuko Yokokoji, and Richard Pierre-Davis. Their work interrogated race, class, and the digital divide through online tools and installation; 'National Heritage' (1996) and 'Color Separation' (2000s) are key works.
metadata.methodology: Developed tools (Linker, social-software platforms) that were distributed to marginalised communities; the tools were themselves the artwork. Deliberately worked outside mainstream gallery circuit. Mongrel's members continued in successor formations (YoHa — Harwood and Yokokoji).

key_works.title: Heritage Gold
key_works.description: Software artwork reskinning Adobe Photoshop as 'Heritage Gold' — a tool for applying and removing racial markings on photographs, with filters such as 'Coon Chicken' and 'Anglo-Saxon'. The piece is a foundational work of tactical-media software art, and is still taught as an example of how software can be treated as critical medium, not only as infrastructure. Made by the Mongrel collective (Graham Harwood, Mervin Jarman, Matsuko Yokokoji, Richard Pierre-Davis).

key_works.title: Linker
key_works.description: Community-authoring software distributed to immigrant and working-class groups in London and Jamaica for self-representation on the early web. Linker's argument was that net.art's serious project is not the gallery-facing artwork but the tool given to people outside the art economy's usual audience. Distributed with workshops rather than through galleries; a formative work of tactical-media commons practice.

metadata.commons_summary: Tools released openly; deep commitment to the commons and community-tech traditions.
metadata.governance_summary: Artist collective; disbanded ~2010, successor practice continued as YoHa.

metadata.practice_summary: Brazilian-Italian artist, critic, and organiser who moved concrete art into computation. Founded the Grupo Ruptura in São Paulo (1952), authoring the manifesto that set terms for Brazilian concretism. In the late 1960s, working with physicist Giorgio Moscati on an IBM/360 at the University of São Paulo's computing centre, Cordeiro produced the first substantial body of computer art in Latin America. His computer works — image processing of political and quotidian photographs (Lyndon Johnson, a farmer, a dead soldier, his daughter Gente) — treated the machine as a reading device that could dissolve and re-compose what a photograph encodes. He theorised this as 'arte concreta semântica' (semantic concrete art): the computer's capacity to operate on meaning, not only on form. Cordeiro died in 1973, at 48, just as his computer-art project was reaching international circulation via Cybernetic Serendipity and related touring exhibitions.
metadata.methodology: Worked in two parallel registers through the 1960s: Euclidean and post-Euclidean concrete painting in São Paulo studio practice, and computer-based image processing conducted at USP on IBM/360 hardware with line-printer and plotter output. The computer workflow involved photographic sources converted to numerical values, processed through custom FORTRAN-era programmes, and output as printed grids or plotter drawings. The human decisions — which image, which processing pass, how to re-present the output — were the authorship; the machine executed.

key_works.title: Derivadas de uma imagem (Derivatives of an Image)
key_works.description: Series of computer-processed portraits — a farmer, Lyndon Johnson, a dead Vietnamese soldier — each passed through iterative image-processing operations on IBM/360 hardware. The image degrades, reconstitutes, or mutates across the series, functioning as a study in how a computational operation carries or sheds political meaning.
key_works.relevance: Canonical within Latin-American computer-art history and a direct parallel to concurrent European computer-art experiments (Nake, Molnar), produced without Euro-American institutional connection. Establishes that 1960s computer art was a multi-continental phenomenon.

key_works.title: Gente
key_works.description: Grid of computer-processed portraits of Cordeiro's daughter, iterated through tonal and structural transformations. Distinct from Derivadas in its intimate, familial source material — a deliberate domestic register for the same computational methodology.
key_works.relevance: The most formally inventive of his computer works; widely reproduced in subsequent Latin American media-art histories.

key_works.title: Arteônica (curation + manifesto)
key_works.description: Exhibition and accompanying theoretical text (sometimes rendered Arte & Electrónica / Arteonica) organising a São Paulo presentation of computer-based practice. Cordeiro's introductory text argued for 'arte concreta semântica' as the correct frame for this work.
key_works.relevance: Primary theoretical document for Latin-American computer art's self-understanding. Cited alongside Cybernetic Serendipity as parallel 1968-71 global consolidation of the field.

metadata.commons_summary: Cordeiro worked within a shared university computing resource — access to the IBM/360 was governed by institutional rather than market logic — and his critical writing treated the computer as a public apparatus for re-reading political imagery. His organising (Ruptura manifesto, Arteônica curation) built shared frameworks rather than proprietary signatures.

full_profile.governance_model: Informal collective-authorship-by-proximity (with Moscati at USP; with Ruptura colleagues in São Paulo). No formal studio or foundation survived him. Posthumous governance is carried by his estate and by institutional holdings (MAC-USP, ICAA / MFAH documents, Getty Research Institute).
full_profile.consent_and_authorship: Authorship explicitly distributed in his writing: the artist chooses, the machine executes, and the political source (the photograph) carries meaning the work then tests. Contemporary reprints of Derivadas raise consent questions about the political source images (notably the Vietnamese soldier) that were not posed in 1969; any re-presentation today is handled with added contextual framing.
full_profile.liveness_and_duration: Static outputs (prints, plotter drawings) with long archival lifespan. The computational process that produced them is not live; it happened on hardware that no longer exists. Reconstructions of the code are possible but partial.

data_materiality.data_sources: Photographic sources (press photographs, personal archive). Numerical encoding handled on IBM/360 at USP. Output as line-printer tonal grids and plotter line drawings.
data_materiality.data_provenance: Source images traceable (Johnson press photo, Vietnam War press photo, family photographs). Processing code not preserved in accessible form; reconstructed inferences exist in scholarly literature (Priscila Arantes, Analivia Cordeiro).

full_profile.embedding_space_relevance: High — as a bridge node, expected to sit close to Nake, Molnar, Mohr in embedding space (shared vocabulary: algorithmic processing, iterative variation, concrete-art-into-computation), and also close to contemporary Latin American computational practice that the first-pass graph lacks.
full_profile.exhibition_modality: Originally: São Paulo gallery and Bienal de São Paulo circuit; Arteônica São Paulo; Cybernetic Serendipity (London, 1968; touring 1969-71). Currently: posthumous retrospectives at MAC-USP, Itaú Cultural; inclusion in MoMA's 'Information' (1970) in conversation with the moment's wider consolidation.
full_profile.sensory_register: Visual (black-and-white printed output, occasional colour). Structurally static — the work does not change once output.
full_profile.interoperability: Print output is media-archaeologically stable but not directly queryable as data. Code: lost or unreconstructable at the level of executable reproduction.
full_profile.technical_approach: FORTRAN-era image-processing on IBM/360 mainframe; custom routines developed with Moscati for tonal quantisation, iterative re-quantisation, structural re-ordering. Output hardware: line printer, pen plotter.
full_profile.protocol_art_resonance: Strong: Cordeiro's 'semantic concrete art' anticipates the protocol-art move of treating computational operations themselves as the primary artistic material. His insistence that the machine operates on meaning (not just pattern) prefigures contemporary AI-art discourse.
full_profile.potential_role_in_adai: Bridge node. Anchors a 1960s non-Euro-American computer-art lineage. Carries the Latin American axis of the computer-art moment that Cybernetic Serendipity partly absorbed and partly missed. Expected to generate INFLUENCES edges to Nake, Molnar (same era, same lens via academic-media-art-history), and to later Brazilian digital practice once that enters the graph.
full_profile.temporal_status: historical (deceased 1973; active archive preservation ongoing via family and institutions)
uncertain: Exact dates for individual Derivadas instances (series published across 1969-71)
Attribution weight between Cordeiro and Moscati (consensus: Cordeiro authored, Moscati enabled technically; Moscati has been explicit about not claiming artistic authorship)
Which specific works travelled to Cybernetic Serendipity vs which appeared only in São Paulo (scholarship varies)
Status of the FORTRAN source code — likely lost; some reconstructions exist in academic literature but none claims to be complete
full_profile.relevance_to_sense_room: Historical anchor for a semantic-concrete-art reading of the room's practice: the room treats the graph as a computational operation on shared meaning, the same move Cordeiro named 'arte concreta semântica' fifty-five years earlier.

basic_info.name: Academic Media-Art History
basic_info.location: distributed (major hubs: Karlsruhe, Linz, Cambridge MA, Montreal, Melbourne, Donau-Universität Krems)

full_profile.description: The canonising logic of scholarly media-art history — the field consolidated by Oliver Grau's research networks, the Leonardo/MIT Press journal and book series since 1968, the MediaArtHistories conference circuit, ACM SIGGRAPH's historical record, and university programmes in digital humanities and media archaeology. This lens frames digital art through genealogy: who came before whom, what earlier technologies or ideas this work recovers or extends, how a specific practice fits a longer arc that includes pre-computer cybernetic art, concrete poetry, conceptual art, and scientific visualisation. It values provenance of ideas, cites other works carefully, and is structurally weak at immediately legible market or viral art — it waits. It is the slowest of the five lenses; its canonical judgements take decades to form, but they outlast the others. Pioneer-era practitioners (Cohen, Nake, Molnar, Schwartz, Mohr, Csuri, Komura) owe much of their current visibility to this lens rather than to market or immediate-institutional readings.
exemplars: Harold Cohen / AARON (bridge practitioner — academic coverage predates institutional market recognition)
Lillian Schwartz (bridge — Bell Labs + academic writing)
Waldemar Cordeiro (bridge — ICAA / Latin American academic archive)
Masao Komura / CTG (bridge — SIGGRAPH Pioneers + MediaArtHistories retrospectives)
Prema Murthy (bridge — Rhizome + academic feminist media writing)
Hito Steyerl (heavy academic citation; e-flux journal; Duty Free Art)
Matteo Pasquinelli (theorist — academic media-critical scholarship)
McKenzie Wark (theorist — critical media theory)
Legacy Russell (theorist — Glitch Feminism)
Yuk Hui (theorist — philosophy of technology)
full_profile.blind_spots: Very recent practice (the lens is slow; anything younger than ~5 years tends to be under-covered even when genuinely significant). Practice whose documentation lives only on social platforms or chat servers, which academic publishing cycles can't easily cite. Non-English-language scholarship — Spanish/Portuguese Latin American media-art scholarship, Japanese and Chinese academic circuits, are under-represented in the global-English canon this lens collapses into. Practitioners who refuse academic engagement.
full_profile.classification_logic: Apply this lens when the practitioner or work has substantial scholarly coverage — peer-reviewed articles, academic monographs, inclusion in conference proceedings (MediaArtHistories, SIGGRAPH historical papers, Leonardo journal), university teaching use — OR when the practitioner is themselves a working theorist whose writing is part of the academic corpus (Pasquinelli, Wark, Russell, Hui, Steyerl). Pair frequently with euro-american-institutional for blue-chip media artists, and with practitioner-self-report for theorist-practitioners.

basic_info.name: Asia-Pacific Institutional
basic_info.location: distributed (major centres: Tokyo, Yamaguchi, Seoul, Shanghai, Hong Kong, Singapore, Brisbane)

full_profile.description: The canonising logic of East- and South-East-Asian institutional circuits — NTT InterCommunication Center (ICC) Tokyo, YCAM Yamaguchi, Chronus Art Center Shanghai, Nam June Paik Art Center, Sharjah Art Foundation, M+ Hong Kong, Singapore Art Museum, Queensland's Gallery of Modern Art. Related to euro-american-institutional in form (museum acquisition, commissioned installation, survey exhibition) but distinct in inheritance: it traces a lineage from Paik, Gutai, and Mono-ha into contemporary media practice, and places different weight on collective practice, site-specific environmental art, and technologies developed in-region (NHK research partnerships, Sony R&D, Olympus imaging). It reads digital art through a commons-of-technique often rooted in corporate-R&D collaboration, not the lone-studio individualism the Euro-American institutional frame privileges. Japanese audiovisual canon (Ikeda, Kurokawa, Ikegami) sits centrally here. Chinese media-art canon (Cao Fei, Lu Yang, Xu Bing-adjacent) is rapidly consolidating via Chronus and M+.
exemplars: Ryoji Ikeda (NTT ICC, YCAM commissions; canonical within this lens)
Cao Fei (M+, Chronus; often co-read with Serpentine)
teamLab (through Japanese institutional path, distinct from its Western tour reading)
Lu Yang (Chronus, M+; bridge practitioner)
Ryoichi Kurokawa (NTT ICC, YCAM; bridge practitioner)
Masao Komura / Computer Technique Group (NTT ICC retrospective; bridge)

full_profile.blind_spots: Asia-Pacific practice that sits outside major Japanese/Chinese institutional circuits — Southeast Asia (Indonesian new media, Thai experimental), Pacific Islander practice, Korean digital art beyond the Paik-institutional axis. Informal-economy platform practice in the region that Euro-American markets don't track. Co-operative and collective practice which this lens tends to flatten into founder-attribution.
full_profile.classification_logic: Apply this lens when a practitioner has been acquired, commissioned, or critically canonised by a major Asia-Pacific institutional venue, OR when the practitioner's primary working context is an Asia-Pacific research-institution-adjacent commissioning circuit (NTT ICC residencies, YCAM lab projects, Chronus exhibitions). A practitioner showing at both Tate and NTT ICC usually carries both lenses — the two readings produce non-trivially different framings of the same work.

basic_info.name: Crypto Market-Native
basic_info.location: on-chain (Ethereum, Tezos, Bitcoin, Base, Solana) + associated platforms

full_profile.description: The canonising logic of on-chain markets and platforms — Foundation, Art Blocks, fxhash, SuperRare, Manifold, Objkt, Zora, Highlight, Verse. This lens reads practice through on-chain provenance: who minted what, on which contract, when, to whom. Editions, secondary sales, auction records, curator-seal platforms, and the history of a wallet address carry weight equivalent to exhibition records. It is native to generative art (Art Blocks, fxhash) and to artist-contract culture (Manifold), and it collapses authorship, edition, and market-price into a single chain of cryptographically-signed events. It excels at tracking participation, community formation around drops, and the economic life of a work. It is structurally incapable of reading pre-2014 practice and has a shallow grasp of critical contexts that lived off-chain. Its canonising speed is extraordinary — Fidenza became a genre reference within months of release — but its retention depends on continued market interest.
exemplars: Art Blocks (platform; the genre-defining on-chain generative art platform)
fxhash (Tezos generative-art platform)
Harm van den Dorpel (early adopter; chain-native practice)
Jonas Lund (system-native conceptual crypto work)
Sarah Friend (smart-contract-as-medium)
Fellowship (curatorial on-chain)
Feral File (curatorial digital editions)
Metalabel (collective on-chain publishing)
Tyler Hobbs / Fidenza (canon-forming within this lens)
Kevin McCoy / Quantum (first NFT; foundational on-chain history)
full_profile.blind_spots: Pre-2014 practice in its entirety. Work explicitly critical of market infrastructure (Rhizome-tradition net.art that refuses tokenisation). Practice where the artwork is off-chain but the artist is on-chain-active — the lens tends to read these as 'web2 artists who also mint' rather than recognise the primary body of work. Communities where provenance is deliberately collective or anonymous, which the lens flattens into wallet addresses.
full_profile.classification_logic: Apply this lens when a practitioner's primary body of work exists as on-chain artefacts, when their career legibility depends on platforms like Foundation / Art Blocks / fxhash, or when secondary-market activity is the documented history. Apply to on-chain platforms themselves. Multi-lens is expected: a practitioner canonised by both MoMA and SuperRare carries both euro-american-institutional AND crypto-market-native (Anadol, Beeple). A practitioner whose on-chain work is a minor thread carries this lens with lower weight or not at all.

basic_info.name: Euro-American Institutional
basic_info.location: distributed (major centres: New York, London, Basel, Karlsruhe, Berlin)

full_profile.description: The canonising logic of major Euro-American museums, kunsthalles, and flagship commissioning institutions — MoMA, Tate, the Whitney, Centre Pompidou, Serpentine, ZKM, HEK, Haus der Kulturen der Welt, major biennales. This lens reads digital art through the categories institutions have spent a century refining: the named practitioner as author, the discrete work as object (or timed performance), the exhibition as site, acquisition as validation, and the critical essay as afterlife. It tends to foreground works that translate into institutional formats — prints, editions, installations that travel, commissions that fit programme cycles. It is deeply literate in art-historical lineage and weak at reading work that lives natively on platforms or in network protocols. Institutions are slowly adapting: MoMA's acquisition of Anadol (2023), the Herndon/Dryhurst Holly+ commission (Serpentine), and Beeple's Christie's moment forced the lens to widen. But the logic beneath — the named maker, the primary object, the discrete exhibition — persists.
exemplars: Casey Reas (Processing; widely institutional since 2001)

full_profile.blind_spots: Practice that lives in platforms, DAOs, chat servers, or code repositories and never produces a discrete exhibitable object. Activism or tactical-media work where the institutional frame would neutralise the work's politics. Non-Euro-American institutional circuits (NTT ICC, YCAM, Chronus) which use related but distinct canonising logics. Anonymous or pseudonymous practice. Work where the primary audience was never meant to be the museum-goer.
full_profile.classification_logic: Apply this lens when the practitioner or work has been acquired, commissioned, exhibited, or critically canonised by a Euro-American flagship institution, OR when the practitioner's career legibility is primarily institutional (monograph published by museum press, retrospective held, major public collection). Multi-lens tagging is expected: most practitioners here will also carry practitioner-self-report, and some will carry academic-media-art-history. Absence of this lens on a strong practitioner node is itself a finding — surface it.

full_profile.description: The practitioner's own account of their work, lineage, and position. Per CLAUDE.md §Trust Model, self-report from an artist about their own practice carries the highest epistemic authority in A(DAI) — higher than curatorial framing, academic writing, or market activity. The artist knows which tool they actually used, who they were thinking about, what the work contests, and which readings misread it. This lens is the project's editorial commitment to treating the artist as a primary source, not a subject to be canonised about. It is structurally different from the other four lenses: those read the field from the outside-in (the institution, the market, the academy, the regional gatekeeper). This one reads from the inside-out. It is also, crucially, the one this graph has the least of at first-pass: almost all 59 existing practitioner JSONs were researched about artists by outside authors. The self-report lens is therefore scaffolded now, empty for most nodes, and will fill in over time as practitioners join and edit their own claims.
exemplars: Holly Herndon + Mat Dryhurst (Spawning; Holly+ — practitioners building their own infrastructure)
Grimes / Elf.Tech (artist-authored voice-model platform)
K Allado-McDowell (AI-collaborative practice theorised by the practitioner themselves)
Danielle Brathwaite-Shirley (artist-written accompanying texts drive the reading)
Tabita Rezaire (artist-led cosmology frames the work's meaning)
[scaffolded — the majority of this lens is intentionally empty at first-pass]
full_profile.blind_spots: Practitioners who are deceased, inactive, or uninterested in self-documenting. Practice where the artist deliberately refuses self-authorship (anonymous, pseudonymous, or collectively-authored-without-spokesperson work). Language barriers — self-report in non-English is under-represented until translation is part of the ingestion flow. Cases where the artist's self-account conflicts with documented facts — the lens does not auto-resolve conflicts; it holds both.
full_profile.classification_logic: Apply this lens when a significant portion of the practitioner-node's metadata was authored or closely reviewed by the practitioner themselves. In practice, at first-pass this means almost none of the existing 59 — flag the lens as scaffolded-empty and surface it as a gap. Populate progressively as practitioners join Layer 3 (the intimate layer in the seed-doc) and contribute their own claims. A practitioner with BOTH euro-american-institutional AND practitioner-self-report tags is epistemically stronger than one with institutional tagging alone.

references_consulted: CLAUDE.md §Trust model (practitioner self-report = highest authority)
CLAUDE.md §Principles #1 ('show the bias') and #18 ('the practitioner's sensing capacity is the primary intelligence source')
seed-doc Layer 3 (the intimate layer)

metadata.practice_summary: American artist often cited as a founder of computer art. His 1966 'Sine Curve Man' was among the first computer-generated artworks exhibited internationally, and he built computer graphics programmes at Ohio State University that trained generations of practitioners.
metadata.methodology: Programmed FORTRAN on IBM mainframes in the mid-1960s, using mathematical transformations to warp figurative drawings. Later developed real-time 3D animation tools at OSU's ACCAD. Practice spans analogue painting, 2D computer graphics, 3D animation, and print.

metadata.commons_summary: Academic practice; code and methods published via SIGGRAPH and OSU. ACCAD continues as institutional infrastructure.
metadata.governance_summary: University-based practice; founded ACCAD (Advanced Computing Center for the Arts and Design) at Ohio State.

practice_description.summary: Made computer-generated drawings and animations in the 1960s that now sit in the collections that define canons. Founded ACCAD at Ohio State — a bridge between art and computer science built when neither side recognized the other.

metadata.practice_summary: German mathematician and artist (1926-2016) whose February 1965 exhibition at Studiengalerie Stuttgart of plotter drawings generated on a Siemens computer is widely cited as the first exhibition of computer-generated art. His PhD 'Generative Computergrafik' (1969, supervised by Max Bense) is a foundational text of the field.
metadata.methodology: Programmed ALGOL on the Siemens 2002, outputting to a Zuse Graphomat Z64 pen plotter. Treated the algorithm as aesthetic substrate — the same procedural impulse that Frieder Nake shared; the two are closely associated. Industrial career at Siemens ran parallel to academic-artistic output.

key_works.title: Schotter (Gravel)
key_works.description: Plotter drawing of a grid of squares whose position and rotation are progressively randomised row-by-row, from orderly top to chaotic bottom. The piece is one of the most widely cited works of early computer art because it states the generative-art thesis at its minimum: rule plus controlled randomness produces emergent form. Schotter has been reimplemented thousands of times and functions as a pedagogical kernel for generative art from Processing to on-chain.
key_works.relevance: Embodies the generative-art thesis of rule + controlled randomness; foundational reference for subsequent generative art.

key_works.title: 23-Ecke (23-gon)
key_works.description: Plotter drawing from the February 1965 exhibition at Studiengalerie der Technischen Hochschule Stuttgart — widely cited as the first public exhibition of computer-generated art. The work constructs a 23-sided polygon through programmatic perturbation, instantiating the shift from computed geometry to computed aesthetic decision. Its primacy is the argument that computer art begins with the exhibition of algorithmically-produced form, not with the availability of hardware.

metadata.practice_summary: German artist and digital preservationist, preservation director at Rhizome (New York) and member of the net-art duo Bodenständig 2000. Has been central to institutional-scale digital art preservation via Webrecorder / Conifer and the Emulation-as-a-Service Infrastructure.
metadata.methodology: Splits practice between preservation infrastructure (Webrecorder tooling, Rhizome's emulation stack) and archival-artistic work. With Olia Lialina, maintains 'One Terabyte of Kilobyte Age' — a slow Twitter/Tumblr screenshot feed of archived GeoCities pages.

key_works.title: One Terabyte of Kilobyte Age
key_works.description: Collaborative project with Olia Lialina in which screenshots from the archived GeoCities webring are released on Tumblr and Twitter at a slow algorithmic cadence — roughly one image per twenty minutes — so that the amateur web of the 1990s returns into the contemporary feed as durational recovery. The work reframes the amateur web as serious cultural record, and the slow release as a preservation gesture against the attention economy's speed. A foundational reference for vernacular-web scholarship.

key_works.title: Webrecorder / Conifer
key_works.description: Open-source web-archiving suite developed at Rhizome that captures dynamic, interactive web pages as working preserved artefacts rather than flat screenshots. Espenschied has led much of its design, treating the preservation of artist-web-works as itself a form of practice. Webrecorder is now the dominant tool for artist-and-institution-led web preservation and is a significant infrastructural contribution to digital-art conservation.

key_works.title: Bodenständig 2000
key_works.description: Net.art duo with Sandra Hastenteufel producing MIDI-based, web-embedded performance and music-software pieces. Works such as 'Dear Jen' and the 'DOS-90' series treated amateur hardware and software — the MIDI format, the TextMate-era web — as expressive rather than transitional. The duo's outputs are among the earliest long-form net-native musical works.

metadata.commons_summary: Webrecorder and Conifer are open-source; One Terabyte of Kilobyte Age is open cultural research.
metadata.governance_summary: Preservation director at Rhizome (non-profit); duo practice with Olia Lialina.

metadata.practice_summary: Russian net.art founding figure — part of the original circle with Olia Lialina, Vuk Ćosić, JODI, and Heath Bunting — whose 1990s works treated the web as critical and formal medium. Later practice with 386DX staged the obsolescent PC as performance instrument; ongoing curatorial role in the Moscow net-culture scene.
metadata.methodology: Works across net.art object, performance, and curatorial practice. 'Form Art Competition' (1997) and the 'Easylife.org' platform instantiate the web-as-artwork argument foundational to net.art.

key_works.title: Form Art
key_works.description: Browser-native generative artwork using HTML form elements — checkboxes, radio buttons, drop-down menus — as primary visual material. Shulgin treats the form as the overlooked aesthetic substrate of the administered web, and Form Art competitions (1997) invited peers to submit works made only of these ostensibly utilitarian elements. The piece argues that bureaucratic UI is already expressive, and that net.art can locate its medium in the browser's structural vocabulary rather than in image or video.

key_works.title: 386DX
key_works.description: Long-running cybernetic-punk performance project in which an obsolete 386DX PC equipped with Microsoft SAM text-to-speech covers rock and punk songs live. The obsolete machine as performance instrument stages computational obsolescence as continuing labour rather than disposal; the covers' flat, affectless speech foregrounds the gap between machine-reproduced and live performance. The work has toured internationally for over two decades, treating a single ageing computer as durational co-performer.

key_works.title: Remedy for Information Disease
key_works.description: Early web-native work diagnosing informational overload as a somatic condition, predating most discourse on digital burnout by a decade. Structured as a mock-clinical protocol distributed via HTTP, the piece uses the medium's immediacy to enact rather than describe its subject. An important early reference for net.art's diagnostic mode.

metadata.commons_summary: All net.art works remain freely accessible; Easylife.org is an artist-run public archive of early net.art.
metadata.governance_summary: Independent practitioner; involved with MediaArtLab Moscow.

metadata.practice_summary: Mike Winkelmann's daily 3D-rendering practice 'Everydays', begun 2007 and uninterrupted since, became the substrate for 'Everydays: The First 5000 Days', sold at Christie's for $69M in 2021. That sale forced every major contemporary-art institution to revise its position on digital art and NFTs. His subsequent work spans monumental installation, the Beeple Studios exhibition space in Charleston, and continued daily renders.
metadata.methodology: One finished 3D render per day, every day, using Cinema 4D and Octane. Images are often satirical-political, drawing on current events, corporate iconography, and apocalyptic landscape. Stores and mints selected works as NFTs; also produces physical installation using kinetic sculpture and screens.

key_works.title: Everydays: The First 5000 Days
key_works.description: Collage of 5,000 daily digital artworks sold at Christie's for $69.3 million.

key_works.title: HUMAN ONE
key_works.description: Kinetic sculpture — four video screens in a box displaying a figure walking through changing digital landscapes, updatable by the artist.

metadata.commons_summary: Early work was given freely online (Creative Commons attribution); current market practice is commercial/NFT-gated. Source files for some Everydays have been released.
metadata.governance_summary: Sole practitioner, now operating Beeple Studios as an institution-scale venue in Charleston, SC.

practice_description.summary: The $69 million Christie's sale forced the art market to confront digital art as a financial reality. His Everydays practice — a new piece every day for 5,000+ consecutive days — predates crypto and gives the position staying power beyond one auction.

name: Pre-Process
metadata:
{"status": "draft", "description": "Ways of knowing...
Ways of seeing…

I can trace the origin of *Pre-Process* back to a Saturday afternoon in 2003 when I was sketching—first on paper, and then with code. I began by drawing circles, then connecting their center points, and then placing the circles in motion as coded animation. At that time, I was focused on *ideas* and not *images*—specifically, on dynamic systems and the ways a set of elements relate to each other within an imagined environment. I was working through questions about how to experience these systems and what might be an ideal (or interesting) way to engage with them. 

The ideas and code from this session later became the core of much of my subsequent work: including the foundation for the *Process* series of software, prints, and installations and the more recent *Process Compendium* works. *Pre-Process* pulls these origin points back into focus, develops them with what I’ve learned in the intervening years, and puts them on the blockchain to be archived. I consider the project a Rosetta Stone for my practice. It asks fundamental questions about the relationships between process and end result, including: Where is the aesthetic focus of a generative system? Is it deep within the code or within the picture the system creates?

Ultimately, *Pre-Process* emphasizes experiencing the origin of the system and then transitioning with it as it seeks, but never finds, equilibrium. The system is built around Element 1, the first that I created for the *Process* series:

*Element 1: Form 1 + Behavior 1 + Behavior 2 + Behavior 3 + Behavior 4
Form 1: Circle
Behavior 1: Move in a straight line
Behavior 2: Constrain to surface
Behavior 3: Change direction while touching another Element
Behavior 4: Move away from an overlapping Element*

*Pre-Process* is the origin of a long journey that I’m still on. It continues to ask essential questions and to encourage me to explore possibilities. Through it, I came to realize that I was ultimately more a picture-maker than a conceptual artist, or, the way I like to think about it,  I’m a “conceptual artist” with a small ‘c.’ I want the energy to be with the system (the ideas) *and* the surface (the picture) in equal measure. More directly, the work exists *between* the instructions, the performance and interpretation of the instructions, and the resulting images.", "work_type": "platform", "year_start": 2022, "year_end": 2022, "year_ongoing": false, "year_uncertain": false, "image_url": "https://media.artblocks.io/thumb/383000000.png", "image_license": "Art Blocks (verify per project license)", "image_source": "artblocks", "artblocks_contract": "0x99a9b7c1116f9ceeb1652de04d5969cce509b069", "artblocks_project_id": "383", "artblocks_token_id": "383000000", "artblocks_title": "Pre-Process", "artblocks_artist_name": "Casey REAS", "data_provenance": {"source": "artblocks-hasura", "fetched_at": "2026-04-21T13:45:48Z", "signal_id": "signal:artblocks-api-2026-04"}, "creator_practitioner_id": "practitioner:casey reas", "cdn_image_url": "https://pub-ebd869876a824a5e83dbb2fe42d03211.r2.dev/images/e0/e0d4f181602149c27572cbc5e112d8ede5a6ea1dbcfa6a7700f02f9038c504e4.png"}

name: Cytographia
metadata:
{"status": "draft", "description": "*Cytographia* is an elegy for species we will never know, or will never know again, expressed through generative illustrations from an imaginary book about imaginary organisms. The artwork depicts speculative cell structures whose appearances and movements arise emergently and in response to real-time user interactions. *Cytographia* was created using [p5.js](https://p5js.org/) (an open-source programming toolkit for the arts) and may run best in the Chrome browser on OSX.

An algorithmic "neoincunabulum of xenocytology", *Cytographia* presents an interactive diagram of a one-celled microorganism, styled to evoke a hand-drawn engraving. Every aspect of this illustration is generated through custom code, including the simulated behavior of the depicted creature, the poiesis of its anatomy, the calligraphic quality of its lines, the asemic letterforms of its labels, and the virtual "paper" on which it is rendered. *Cytographia*'s drawings may be exported as high-resolution PNG images, or in an SVG vector format suitable for pen-plotting on A4 paper.

The *Cytographia* project draws inspiration from several historically significant books that visually and methodically documented encounters with the unknown. These include Robert Hooke's *[Micrographia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Micrographia)* (1665), a landmark of scientific observation in which living cells were described for the first time; Edmund Fry's *[Pantographia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pantographia)* (1799), an attempt to compile exemplars of all the world's writing systems; Ernst Haeckel's [*Kunstformen der Natur*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kunstformen_der_Natur) (1899), a rich exploration of symmetry and structural hierarchy in natural forms; and Luigi Serafini's hallucinatory *[Codex Seraphinianus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Codex_Seraphinianus)* (1981), a visual encyclopedia of an artist's imagined world. The generative letterforms in *Cytographia* are loosely based on 16th-century typefaces by [Ludovico degli Arrighi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludovico_Vicentino_degli_Arrighi).

*Cytographia* represents a culmination of several enduring threads in Golan Levin's thirty-year *oeuvre* of interactive software art, including research into responsive blobs (e.g. [*Polygona Nervosa*](https://objkt.com/asset/hicetnunc/56312), 1997); artificial life (e.g. [*Obzok*](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oVOCKzE2fZk), 2001); the use of physics simulations in computational drawing (e.g. [*Floccus*](https://artbase.rhizome.org/wiki/Q3783), 1999) and the algorithmic generation of asemic writing systems (e.g. [*Alphabet Synthesis Machine*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alphabet_Synthesis_Machine), 2002).

*Cytographia* requires a modern browser with WebGL and hardware acceleration enabled. The recommended configuration for *Cytographia* is the Chrome browser on MacOS, in which the artwork is known to produce consistent and replicable results. The project responds to both mouse/touch and keyboard interactions. An index of *Cytographia*'s key commands can be displayed by pressing **h** (for "help"). These key commands provide access to functionality including file export; toggles that enable or disable various graphical options, potentially improving performance on some systems; and access to a playful "sandbox" mode, in which a collector or visitor can assemble the organelles of their own imaginary lifeform.", "work_type": "platform", "year_start": 2024, "year_end": 2024, "year_ongoing": false, "year_uncertain": false, "image_url": "https://media.artblocks.io/thumb/487000000.png", "image_license": "Art Blocks (verify per project license)", "image_source": "artblocks", "artblocks_contract": "0x99a9b7c1116f9ceeb1652de04d5969cce509b069", "artblocks_project_id": "487", "artblocks_token_id": "487000000", "artblocks_title": "Cytographia", "artblocks_artist_name": "Golan Levin", "data_provenance": {"source": "artblocks-hasura", "fetched_at": "2026-04-21T13:45:48Z", "signal_id": "signal:artblocks-api-2026-04"}, "creator_practitioner_id": "practitioner:golan levin", "cdn_image_url": "https://pub-ebd869876a824a5e83dbb2fe42d03211.r2.dev/images/57/574a0c82dfcf3c9a64a53d825edc02b4cd33e7b6e5f1990273607b1f79a2d209.png"}

name: Race Condition
metadata:
{"status": "draft", "description": "*🔈 Click anywhere to start the soundtrack 🔈*


***Race Condition*** is a racing game where you're flying through space at rapid speeds and see colors and shapes swoosh by. 


The game-objective is straightforward: you accelerate and try and stay on the road, if you miss a jump or a turn, you crash! The script determines the properties of your spaceship, acceleration, handling and max speed, as well as the map layout, including difficulty, color composition, and available power ups.


Once the series has been fully minted, a highscore of all the mints will be created on [racecondition.art](https://racecondition.art). The winners in each category will be awarded an additional Race Condition Winner NFT. The categories include but are not limited to fastest spaceship, most difficult level, easiest level, worst acceleration, and worst max speed.


In *Race Condition*, the winners are not determined by your driving skills, but by something outside of your control, the properties and features of your mint. Is your level more difficult than the others? Is your spaceship faster? Whether you are a winner in one of the categories is not really up to you, so enjoy the ride and race without pressure! 

**The Controls**
⬆️ or **W** to accelerate
⬇️ or **S** to decelerate (and cancel Nitro)
⬅️ or **A** to drive left
➡️ or **D** to drive right
**Space** to jump
**N** to activate Nitro
**M** or ⬇️ **S** to stop Nitro
**ESC** to open settings

Shortly after loading, the spaceship will start to race the map by itself in *self-driving mode*, where it can't crash. As soon as you press a key on your keyboard, it switches to *driving mode*.

**The Levels**
Race Condition has 21 different map generating algorithms, each with their own set of challenges and difficulty rating. The algorithms take into account the playability in combination with the difficulty and try to strike a good balance between the two. Each mint gets a difficulty rating and that determines which map pool is used for the creation of the level. The easy ones requires next to zero effort whereas the hard ones require a lot of skill in driving. The Easy Medium Hard means that it can select map algorithms from the complete pool.

**The Music**
The music is generated by first selecting a scale from a set of 14 predefined ones, combined with two oscillators / synth configurations, and spread across an imaginary step-sequencer, where the hash determines which steps should be activated or not, how long the sequencer should be, what BPM it should be, and when it step into the next phase of the step-sequencer, which results in some very nice chip-tune repetitive tracks. 

**Notes**
On mobile, the spaceship accelerates automatically and you turn left/right by tilting your device. You need to grant permission for this to work, if you decline, the spaceship will drive by itself in *self-driving mode*.", "work_type": "platform", "year_start": 2023, "year_end": 2023, "year_ongoing": false, "year_uncertain": false, "image_url": "https://media.artblocks.io/thumb/393000000.png", "image_license": "Art Blocks (verify per project license)", "image_source": "artblocks", "artblocks_contract": "0x99a9b7c1116f9ceeb1652de04d5969cce509b069", "artblocks_project_id": "393", "artblocks_token_id": "393000000", "artblocks_title": "Race Condition", "artblocks_artist_name": "Jonas Lund", "data_provenance": {"source": "artblocks-hasura", "fetched_at": "2026-04-21T13:45:48Z", "signal_id": "signal:artblocks-api-2026-04"}, "creator_practitioner_id": "practitioner:jonas lund", "cdn_image_url": "https://pub-ebd869876a824a5e83dbb2fe42d03211.r2.dev/images/65/65183c1f4853debe5552b8ef14b5bb316056bfa9869996545426c86136a43ddc.png"}

name: Cargo
metadata:
{"status": "draft", "description": "**Cargo** is a series of abstract paintings created with animated pixels that are constantly moving without ever repeating. It is painting new patterns on the fly in between macro and micro compositions with a duality of different rhythms and continuous synchronicity. The focus is alternately drawn to detail, then distracted by movement elsewhere and caught up in the overall picture. This rhythm turns the visual complexity into an active experience.

ASDF: “My work should offer individual ways of interpretation, or even allow one to find some self in it. It wants to inspire some thoughts about dynamics and systemics and also just mesmerize the audience, capture them in a little fantasy, or just for a brief moment in a state of satisfaction.”

Cargo is the latest work in Kim Asendorf’s ongoing work series of pixel pattern animations. Starting with [monogrid](https://monogrid.xyz) in 2021, and [Sabotage](https://sabotage.kim) in 2022, both highly conceptual series, therefore visually very raw and unimaginable. Asendorf discovered various interesting details in these works, which eventually became fundamental in his artistic expression.

Cargo is a real time WebGL software written in JavaScript and GLSL. At its core is a flip-flop render buffer, also known as feedback buffer. That means the animation is alternately rendered in two different frame buffers. This technique allows the usage of the previous frame of the animation as an asset in the current rendering, which allows for a series of reactive animation strategies.

An initial image with variable structures and patterns is rendered and subsequently loaded into the frame buffer. A fragment shader is used to apply a set of animation algorithms that make the pixel move and a set of reset algorithms that constantly try to recreate the initial image. The final animation happens in selected containers and is always a combination of two algorithms, one from each set. By regularly animating and partially resetting the pixels, a wide range of movement patterns appear.

Cargo is a responsive and pixel exact artwork and it will fill the screen on any display size, thus changing the total amount of used pixels accordingly. This results in the fact that the detail level in the artwork is changing depending on the dimensions. The overall structure is consistently stretching the x and y axis independently. Single containers scale along the dimensions and offer more pixels to render the patterns at a larger representation compared to a smaller representation. This behavior leads to a brilliance, perfect pixels, a crisp rendering with nothing like compression artifacts.

This software includes the [simplex noise](https://github.com/jwagner/simplex-noise.js) JavaScript implementation by Jonas Wagner and the [cellular noise](https://github.com/stegu/webgl-noise) GLSL code by Stefan Gustavson.", "work_type": "platform", "year_start": 2023, "year_end": 2023, "year_ongoing": false, "year_uncertain": false, "image_url": "https://media.artblocks.io/thumb/426000000.png", "image_license": "Art Blocks (verify per project license)", "image_source": "artblocks", "artblocks_contract": "0x99a9b7c1116f9ceeb1652de04d5969cce509b069", "artblocks_project_id": "426", "artblocks_token_id": "426000000", "artblocks_title": "Cargo", "artblocks_artist_name": "Kim Asendorf", "data_provenance": {"source": "artblocks-hasura", "fetched_at": "2026-04-21T13:45:48Z", "signal_id": "signal:artblocks-api-2026-04"}, "creator_practitioner_id": "practitioner:kim asendorf", "cdn_image_url": "https://pub-ebd869876a824a5e83dbb2fe42d03211.r2.dev/images/63/636ddfabd4219be08398b6d0b25657f14a792a39c592e31d6e582971602de89b.png"}

name: Gazers
metadata:
{"status": "draft", "description": "Since the dawn of humanity, the Moon's phases have fascinated humans, influencing any number of activities on Earth including ocean tides, seasons, harvests, migrations, hunting, crime, sleeping, sex, and has inspired countless works of art. The first lunar calendar, dated to 32,000 BC was discovered, drawn on animal bone in caves. It's believed hunters during the last Ice Age used these portable lunar calendars to anticipate the behavior of different animals like Mammoths. Since then, our Moon has been imprinted across all our ancient and modern cultures, even becoming the system from which our Gregorian calendar evolved from. In the present day, investors in crypto have used the Moon symbolically. 

What does it mean for all of us in crypto to be so ahead of our time, all while using the same metaphor of the Moon for the various measures of success and individual goals we collectively share in crypto? And how will the future appreciate our ambitions and perseverance within the present moment's growing pains on our way to mass adoption? These are some of the questions that Gazers ask.

On the surface, Gazers function as a lunar calendar, algorithmically synching closely with Moon phases in the sky, joining the blockchain with one of humanity's longest running lineages in art. Gazers seeks to create a community of collectors celebrating the change of our perceptions that happen over time, our collective goals in crypto, and our love of color theory, astronomy, and generative art. 

What we are building in blockchain and NFTs will primarily be for the benefit of the future. As such, this artwork was designed to pace itself and speed up its frame rate over time, scaling into anticipated advancements in technology that will steadily allow the artwork to run at faster speeds while at larger scales. Each NFT starts out with the assignment of a date from the past 20 years. These dates correspond to events that happened under particular New Moons that shaped my path as an artist. This is the Origin Moon trait and how Gazers is in part a conceptual self portrait. 

Starting from the Origin Moon, each New Moon that arrives will speed up the potential animation of the NFT. For example, an NFT with a 20 year old Origin Moon might run at 20 frames per second, appearing as an animation. But one with an Origin Moon fresh from the sale will run closer to 1 frame per second, appearing more like a slowly evolving painting. Every moment, the frame rate of the artwork speeds up fractionally, indecipherable to our eyes. Stacking these advancements over time creates a generational evolution of experience. There is something undeniably beautiful about everything speeding up within our lifetimes, but the Moon, high above us, continues to carry on at the same meandering rate of 29.53 days in each cycle. Much like these blockchain technologies and NFT markets, this artwork was designed to be collected by the present, but appreciated in a greater sense than we can even imagine by the future. 

I created Gazers to be like a living artwork, to be lived with, and to not only have the artwork evolve over time but also the appreciation and experience of viewers. As I coded the work, I imagined it hanging on the wall of collectors, a fixture in their physical space. Collectors might spend a moment admiring their work, walk away for a couple hours, and then come back to be delighted, noticing the most subtle of shifts. Each layer of the work consists of pattern designs. With the passage of time, the thickness of the layered lines pulse and the direction a design moves will advance or rotate, changing our perception of color in the most subtle and optical of ways. Each day at midnight, each layer receives a new set of rules in terms of how to rise or shine over the next 24 hours. The result is color that rises and sets, echoing the change of light in our sky.

My use of color has consistently been what I've been best known for across my 20 year artistic career. In all my work until now, I've made all the color and design choices as I've painted as a human in the moment. But in Gazers, I designed a complex system around color theory as I understand it, joining my talent for coding with my vision for color. 

Many NFT collectors of my work might be familiar with the additional experiences some of their NFTs unlock at my website. Rather than use a Gazers NFT to unlock a website, I decided this time to create rendering modes that unlock within the code over time. These additional modes of viewing are intended to help a collector better understand the architecture of their artwork's design and also benefit from greater enjoyment of it. The addition of these experiences should present an additional benefit to HODLing for some. 

Every 29 and a half days, we reach a Moon phase called the New Moon. This is when the dark side of the Moon is fully visible and no sunlight is reflected from the lunar surface back to Earth. In Gazers, each New Moon phase creates a New Moon design. In this artwork, the hash seed creates color theory and design rules. These rules are deterministic and dictate all the moons that will generatively be created into infinity. Time reveals our moons. Pairing time with deterministic generative code creates the ephemeral moment. We can all agree that looking at the Moon in the sky never seems to be the exact same experience twice, nor the exact same from different locations. I wanted to echo this nature in Gazers and emphasize the urgency and rarity of our present moment and how an artwork can capture this. 

As individuals, we all have our own version of the Moon and what reaching it means. Just as our goals change over time, often subtly, sometimes dramatically, so will our moons, creating a visual representation that might coincide with what's changing inside of us. In crypto, we are all ahead of our time. We are all gazers. And we are all waiting for our next Moon.", "work_type": "platform", "year_start": 2021, "year_end": 2021, "year_ongoing": false, "year_uncertain": false, "image_url": "https://media.artblocks.io/thumb/215000000.png", "image_license": "Art Blocks (verify per project license)", "image_source": "artblocks", "artblocks_contract": "0xa7d8d9ef8d8ce8992df33d8b8cf4aebabd5bd270", "artblocks_project_id": "215", "artblocks_token_id": "215000000", "artblocks_title": "Gazers", "artblocks_artist_name": "Matt Kane", "data_provenance": {"source": "artblocks-hasura", "fetched_at": "2026-04-21T13:45:48Z", "signal_id": "signal:artblocks-api-2026-04"}, "creator_practitioner_id": "practitioner:matt kane", "cdn_image_url": "https://pub-ebd869876a824a5e83dbb2fe42d03211.r2.dev/images/33/338dea9fcf5c233aae2b661fc89f5a949a37ed40902cbca844cd7f8d50068223.png"}

name: Solar Transits
metadata:
{"status": "draft", "description": "Solar Transits is a procedural exploration of the origins of astrophotography. Each image in this series depicts a randomly generated astronomical event but viewed through the lens of mid-to-late 19th century image capture techniques. The collection features a variety of rare alignments of stars, planets and moons, and are rendered in the spirit of the daguerreotype.

In June of 2012, I took a trip to Minneapolis to speak at the Eyeo Festival. Venus was going to transit while I was there. I was curious. I had not seen a transit before. At 5:09 pm on June 5th, a nearly imperceptible black circle began its march across the sun. Were it not a predicted mathematical certainty, it is doubtful anyone would have noticed. For six minutes, the light from the sun was 0.087% dimmer.

It is a significant thing to see an object silhouetted against the sun. We are so accustom to seeing our perfect circle of pure light that we can't help but to celebrate the occasions where something blocks the view. I still feel a little more excitement when a slight shadow shoots across the landscape on a cloudless day, the source being an extremely rare transit of a commercial jet liner.

Exponentially more rare is the planetary transit. When Venus hangs on the horizon, glowing against the night sky, it is all too easy to think it another star. Only when it is viewed in silhouette can its position in our universe be fully appreciated: orbitally locked like us, and forever drawing it's path around the sun. That tiny black circle effected me in a big way. The scale of the cosmos shifted into perspective. That doesn’t happen often. I was incredibly moved. It was an experience I will never forget. This project is an homage to that strange once-in-a-lifetime event.

As it turns out, I was very lucky to have seen it at all. In the time since my birth in 1972, a Venus transit has only happened twice. The 1st time was in 2004 but I lived in a part of the world where it was not visible. The 2nd time was in 2012. Unless I live to be 145 years old, there won’t be a 3rd time. There are a couple silver linings: the Great American solar eclipse is on April 8 2024, and Mercury will transit in 2032.

name: Recollection
metadata:
{"status": "draft", "description": "Recollection is released as part of reGEN, a special charitable auction of generative art to raise funds for Cure Alzheimer’s Fund, curated by Alex Estorick and Foteini Valeonti in collaboration with The Giving Block. 


It is curious how our memories can mislead. I vividly recall a childhood trek up Mt. Fuji with my parents through a foggy bamboo forest, and the image of my dad buying a walking stick from an older vendor. But as my mom later clarified, the adventure actually took place in a Tokyo park –– I’ve never even visited Fuji-san. Contemplating this blend of the real and the imagined has led me to create generative vistas whose clarity is eroded by the passing of time.


The landscapes in Recollection are understated and familiar: rolling hills, distant mountains, and sporadic clusters of trees or forests. There is a path through grass and stone –– sometimes clear but, at other times, overgrown and obscure. Many of these paths culminate at a portal, its purpose enigmatic. It is pure mystery, both inviting and unsettling. It is an obscuring void, a memory half-recalled.

Recollection is a meditation on the mysteries of the mind, and a tribute to the quest for understanding. It stands not only as a beacon of hope for those grappling with the disintegration of memory, but also a testament to the enduring pursuit of clarity in the midst of obscurity. While some details may fade with time, the essence — the emotions, the lessons, the significance — has the potential to regenerate through reflection, conversation, and creative expression.


Recollection is part of the reGEN initiative for Alzheimer’s research. For many, this cause is deeply personal and, I believe, it is no exaggeration to say that almost everyone has witnessed the effects of Alzheimer’s, be it within their own family or through friends. This project not only creates funding but also plays a pivotal role in amplifying awareness about Alzheimer’s disease. The opportunity to merge the joy of artistic expression with a mission that has tangible, real-world implications is profoundly inspiring.", "work_type": "platform", "year_start": 2023, "year_end": 2023, "year_ongoing": false, "year_uncertain": false, "image_url": "https://media.artblocks.io/thumb/475000000.png", "image_license": "Art Blocks (verify per project license)", "image_source": "artblocks", "artblocks_contract": "0x99a9b7c1116f9ceeb1652de04d5969cce509b069", "artblocks_project_id": "475", "artblocks_token_id": "475000000", "artblocks_title": "Recollection", "artblocks_artist_name": "Robert Hodgin", "data_provenance": {"source": "artblocks-hasura", "fetched_at": "2026-04-21T13:45:48Z", "signal_id": "signal:artblocks-api-2026-04"}, "creator_practitioner_id": "practitioner:robert hodgin", "cdn_image_url": "https://pub-ebd869876a824a5e83dbb2fe42d03211.r2.dev/images/6f/6fe22136f7f9e7152e8bb60ef4d194505c5f601b131924415caad3aeb2a5def8.png"}
