metadata.description: The A(DAI) founding team's initial research pass. Combines the original 45 practitioners (Pass 1-2, human editorial research) and the 71 practitioners added through cross-referenced sources and AI-assisted deepening (Pass 3). This is *a* canon, not *the* canon — a starting point, declared-bias, open to revision as practitioners enter and contest their profiles. See SOURCES.md for methodology and COVERAGE.md for known gaps.

Browser-native generative artwork using HTML form elements — checkboxes, radio buttons, drop-down menus — as primary visual material. Shulgin treats the form as the overlooked aesthetic substrate of the administered web, and Form Art competitions (1997) invited peers to submit works made only of these ostensibly utilitarian elements. The piece argues that bureaucratic UI is already expressive, and that net.art can locate its medium in the browser's structural vocabulary rather than in image or video.

Long-running cybernetic-punk performance project in which an obsolete 386DX PC equipped with Microsoft SAM text-to-speech covers rock and punk songs live. The obsolete machine as performance instrument stages computational obsolescence as continuing labour rather than disposal; the covers' flat, affectless speech foregrounds the gap between machine-reproduced and live performance. The work has toured internationally for over two decades, treating a single ageing computer as durational co-performer.

Early web-native work diagnosing informational overload as a somatic condition, predating most discourse on digital burnout by a decade. Structured as a mock-clinical protocol distributed via HTTP, the piece uses the medium's immediacy to enact rather than describe its subject. An important early reference for net.art's diagnostic mode.

Net.art and hypertextual Flash collaboration with Michaël Samyn that treated the browser as architectural and erotic space. Works including 'Skinonskinonskin' and 'Wirefire' used layered SWFs, evocative audio, and slow-revealing narrative to build intimate online environments at a moment when most web design was shedding such intimacy for utility. The practice was pivotal in establishing net.art as a medium of affect rather than only critique.

Commercial art game developed as Tale of Tales (with Samyn) that reframed Little Red Riding Hood as a meditation on rule-breaking, death, and feminine interior life. The game asked players to disobey its central instruction — don't leave the path — and punished conformity with vacuity. It became one of the canonical 'art games' of the late-2000s independent-games moment and helped establish the form as exhibitable beyond gaming contexts.

Ongoing 3D-sculpture practice distributed across physical casts, high-resolution digital files, and NFTs. Harvey treats the figure of the minotaur as a stand-in for the hybrid body of the digital artist — classical sculpture's myth-figures reimagined in mesh geometry. Each work exists in multiple registers at once, proposing that digital-native sculpture can share the ontological weight of the physical tradition it converses with.

id: artwork:technics and time 1 the fault of epimetheus
name: Technics and Time, 1: The Fault of Epimetheus

metadata.description: Foundational text arguing that human life is originally technical — that we exist only through the 'tertiary retentions' of external memory supports, from flint to film to database. The book reframes the philosophy of technology against both Heidegger and classical humanism, insisting that the technical object is the condition of possibility for thought, not its instrument. It is one of the most-cited works in contemporary digital-art theory because it gives a philosophical vocabulary for treating media as constitutive rather than merely representational.

id: artwork:taking care of youth and the generations
name: Taking Care of Youth and the Generations

metadata.description: Essay on attention as an ecological and political substrate under threat from the digital-industrial capture of consciousness. Stiegler argues that the attention economy is a literal consumption of psychic resources, and that taking care of attention is a task at the level of education, institution, and aesthetics. The work's framing of attention as commons under threat is widely used in digital-arts and AI-ethics discourse.

Late collection proposing 'neganthropy' as an artistic-philosophical exit from the entropic trajectory of the Anthropocene. Stiegler treats art as a practice that can make time local and reversible against the global drift towards entropic flattening. The book's call for a 'contributive economy' of knowledge has had direct uptake in commons-oriented digital-art practice.

Audio-visual installation that treats a cubic architectural object as co-signal: LEDs, sine tones, and structural geometry phase-lock so that sound, light, and form become one flickering unit. Commissioned for the Hamburger Bahnhof in Berlin, it is one of the canonical works of 2000s audio-visual installation and a reference for how precisely synchronised multimodal work can produce a single perceptual object rather than image-plus-sound.

First of a long-running duo series with Sakamoto pairing Nicolai's clicked-and-granular electronics with Sakamoto's piano and processed field recordings. The collaboration — continued across Insen, Revep, utp_, and Glass — articulated a rare register between contemporary classical, ambient, and minimal-electronic that has had durable influence across both art music and club contexts. The duo work is foundational for how electronic-music labels (Raster, Noton) entered museum and concert-hall institutional spaces.

Ultra-wide-format monochrome video installation at Palais de Tokyo using sequenced still colour-fields and spatialised sine-tone pulses. The piece tests the limits at which colour and sound stop being distinct inputs to perception — a minimal, rigorous extension of his long-running research into the psychophysical thresholds of audio-visual synchrony.

Long-running format in which Constant convenes artists, programmers, researchers, and writers for intense multi-day collaborative research on specific questions — from feminist server architectures to vernacular image-making to libre-licensing practices. Each worksession produces publications, software experiments, and performance, released under free-culture licences. The format itself is a proposition: that artistic production is collective research-as-practice, not individual output.

European-funded research collaboration examining free-software graphics tools (GIMP, Inkscape, Scribus) as sites of both aesthetic and political intervention. The unit produced publications, tool critiques, and workshops, arguing that the licensing and development practices of software shape what images can be thought of at all. Core reference point for free-culture digital-arts practice.

Intervention into the 'Extension' net.art competition held by Hamburger Kunsthalle: Sollfrank submitted 289 fabricated female-artist profiles to a show that had otherwise received few entries from women, exposing both the infrastructural gender gap and the reception-logic of the net.art curatorial circuit. The piece is a foundational work of cyberfeminist net.art and is cited in virtually every scholarly survey of the field's institutional politics.

Series of browser-based generators that automatically produce new net.art works by recombining fragments from an archive of net.art material. The generators implicitly argue that authorship in net.art is already algorithmic and collective, and that the conventions of signature and original work are inadequate to the medium. They anticipate by two decades the generative-AI debates about authorship, training data, and recombinatorial aesthetics.

PhD research project and artistic practice examining contemporary artists' engagement with copyright, free culture, and the politics of giving what you don't own. The work combines interviews, documentation, and artworks into an unfolding investigation, published openly. A rigorous synthesis of artistic and legal-theoretical material.

Twitter (later Mastodon) bot that combines subject of one current news headline with predicate of another, posting hourly. The bot has run continuously for over a decade, producing a persistent low-level commentary on how news discourse works at the level of sentence-structure. Often cited as a foundational bot-art example because it does so much with such structural simplicity.

Annual National Novel Generation Month — a parody of NaNoWriMo in which participants produce 50,000-word novels by computational means and share the code and output openly on GitHub. Co-founded by Kazemi, the event has become a durable community ritual for generative text practice, and its archives document a decade of experimental computational literature.

Small-scale fork of Mastodon designed around intimate, local-first federation — an explicit counter-proposal to the scale-obsessed dominant social-media architectures. Kazemi maintains Hometown as infrastructural practice, arguing that decentralised social software is a design/aesthetics problem as much as a technical one. Widely adopted by small communities seeking non-viral social formats.

id: artwork:one terabyte of kilobyte age (dragan espenschied)
name: One Terabyte of Kilobyte Age

metadata.description: Collaborative project with Olia Lialina in which screenshots from the archived GeoCities webring are released on Tumblr and Twitter at a slow algorithmic cadence — roughly one image per twenty minutes — so that the amateur web of the 1990s returns into the contemporary feed as durational recovery. The work reframes the amateur web as serious cultural record, and the slow release as a preservation gesture against the attention economy's speed. A foundational reference for vernacular-web scholarship.

Open-source web-archiving suite developed at Rhizome that captures dynamic, interactive web pages as working preserved artefacts rather than flat screenshots. Espenschied has led much of its design, treating the preservation of artist-web-works as itself a form of practice. Webrecorder is now the dominant tool for artist-and-institution-led web preservation and is a significant infrastructural contribution to digital-art conservation.

Net.art duo with Sandra Hastenteufel producing MIDI-based, web-embedded performance and music-software pieces. Works such as 'Dear Jen' and the 'DOS-90' series treated amateur hardware and software — the MIDI format, the TextMate-era web — as expressive rather than transitional. The duo's outputs are among the earliest long-form net-native musical works.

Plotter drawing of a grid of squares whose position and rotation are progressively randomised row-by-row, from orderly top to chaotic bottom. The piece is one of the most widely cited works of early computer art because it states the generative-art thesis at its minimum: rule plus controlled randomness produces emergent form. Schotter has been reimplemented thousands of times and functions as a pedagogical kernel for generative art from Processing to on-chain.

Plotter drawing from the February 1965 exhibition at Studiengalerie der Technischen Hochschule Stuttgart — widely cited as the first public exhibition of computer-generated art. The work constructs a 23-sided polygon through programmatic perturbation, instantiating the shift from computed geometry to computed aesthetic decision. Its primacy is the argument that computer art begins with the exhibition of algorithmically-produced form, not with the availability of hardware.

Series of plotter drawings produced collaboratively with the Brazilian concrete artist Waldemar Cordeiro at the University of São Paulo. The works bring the rigorous formalism of Brazilian concrete art — its attention to rule, series, and mathematical relation — into contact with the mainframe computer, producing some of the earliest computer-art works made outside the Euro-American circuit. The collaboration is a foundational data-point for the historical argument that early computer art was not only a Stuttgart-Bell Labs phenomenon.

Orchestral work composed using techniques derived from the graphical projections Xenakis developed as Le Corbusier's architectural collaborator, translating the architectural hyperbolic paraboloids of the Philips Pavilion into massed string glissandi. The piece is his first statement that musical composition could be geometric in substrate, and it predates and underwrites everything that follows — stochastic music, UPIC, the algorithmic composition tradition. Widely cited as the origin point of sonic-architectural thinking.

Temporary pavilion for the Brussels World's Fair whose hyperbolic-paraboloid architecture and interior audio-visual work ('Poème électronique', with Varèse) co-produced a single audio-visual-architectural event. Xenakis designed the shell and contributed an interstitial piece ('Concret PH'). The work argues that architecture, composition, and computation share a single geometric substrate — the thesis the rest of his career operationalises.

Graphical computer-music system developed at CEMAMu allowing composers to draw sonic structures that the computer realises as sound. UPIC treats the drawing as score and the computer as executor, anticipating by decades the user-interface assumptions of contemporary digital-audio workstations. The first generation of computer music studios outside IRCAM/Stanford often traces directly to UPIC-style graphical-score thinking.

Procedural-texture algorithm developed for the film 'Tron' that produces continuous, organic-looking pseudo-random fields from low-cost mathematical functions. The algorithm became the underlying substrate of almost all subsequent procedural content generation — terrain, cloud, fluid, and generative-art texture — and is deliberately unencumbered by patent, released as commons. Perlin won an Academy Award for Technical Achievement for the algorithm in 1997, and its presence in contemporary generative art is so pervasive that it operates as default infrastructure rather than as quoted technique.

Successor to Perlin noise with improved computational properties (better scaling to higher dimensions, fewer directional artefacts) that further extended the reach of the original algorithm into real-time 3D and generative practice. Alongside curl noise and related variants, simplex forms the computational texture-library that contemporary generative and 3D art takes for granted.

id: artwork:studies in perception i with leon harmon
name: Studies in Perception I (with Leon Harmon)

metadata.description: Twelve-foot-wide reclining nude (Deborah Hay) reassembled from electronic symbols — diodes, transistors, mathematical glyphs — produced at Bell Labs using BEFLIX-era software. The work scandalised and provoked by installing in 'Bit international' and Bell Labs public spaces, arguing with its body that the computational image could carry the weight of the figurative tradition. One of the foundational works of computer art, and a touchstone for every subsequent translation of figurative representation into computed form.

First specifically designed computer-animation programming language, developed at Bell Labs. BEFLIX (Bell Flicks) allowed the description of animation frames and transitions in a high-level syntax, and produced many of the foundational computer-animated works of the 1960s. The language's pedagogical and art-historical importance is that it made computer animation into authorial practice rather than ad-hoc programming labour.

Late body of work in which portraits — of Richard Feynman, Andy Warhol, and others — are composed from arrangements of physical objects (seashells, dominoes, Lego) selected algorithmically to approximate greyscale image values. The mosaics bring his earliest Bell Labs computational-image logic into an entirely non-electronic material register, arguing that the algorithm is medium-independent.

Persistent virtual gallery-and-performance-space, originally in Second Life, through which Avedon curates exhibitions, hosts discussions, and stages performances. The space argues that a gallery is a social-technical assemblage whose digital instantiation is fully legitimate — not a 'virtual version' of a physical original. Over its decade-plus run it has become an infrastructural reference for avatar-native exhibition practice.

Ongoing series of CGI self-portraits — each a rendered image, animation, or short loop of Avedon in domestic or gallery interiors — that insist that the avatar's self-portrait is as indexical as a photographic one. The series' long duration turns the avatar's persistence over time into its own content, a pointed counter-argument to the assumption that digital identity is weightless.

id: artwork:the zizi show cameo with jake elwes
name: The Zizi Show (cameo, with Jake Elwes)

metadata.description: Collaboration with Jake Elwes for his AI-drag work 'The Zizi Show', in which Avedon's avatar performs as one of the cast of AI-generated drag performers. The collaboration extends Avedon's argument that avatar-presence and AI-generation occupy the same ontological register, putting her persistent character in dialogue with emergent generated ones.

Book arguing that the conventions of cinema, not print, are the structural language of digital media — and that digital media's distinguishing features (modular, variable, automatable, transcodable) can be specified precisely against this lineage. The book is the most-cited scholarly text in digital-art theory, and 'numerical representation, modularity, automation, variability, transcoding' — its five principles of new media — continue to structure how the field talks about itself. Required reading across digital-arts curricula for two decades and counting.

Long follow-up to 'Language of New Media' arguing that software is now the dominant layer of cultural production — that a cultural theory that cannot read software is inadequate to contemporary life. The book introduces 'media software' as distinct analytical object and does detailed close-readings of tools like Photoshop, After Effects, and Processing. A foundational text for the software-studies turn in digital-art theory.

Cultural-analytics project, produced at City University of New York, analysing 3,200 Instagram self-portraits from five cities using computer-vision tools and public-facing visualisation. The work argues that the selfie is a genuine subject of cultural research at data scale — and that the tools of computer vision can be turned on cultural production itself. A canonical example of how Manovich's Cultural Analytics Lab translates its theoretical programme into visible, reproducible research.

Short animated film plus CGI action-figure character — a superhero whose skeleton is based on Lu Yang's own uterus — staged in the idiom of Japanese tokusatsu and anime. The work uses the body-horror and camp of those genres to detach the uterus from its traditional symbolic burden, proposing that reproductive organs can be computationally resculpted into speculative heroism. Widely shown in the Asia-Pacific digital-art circuit and foundational for Lu Yang's avatar-universe practice.

Multi-channel video installation combining medical imaging, Buddhist iconography, and game-engine animation to stage consciousness as a diagnosable-yet-liberatory substrate. Selected for the Chinese pavilion at the 56th Venice Biennale, the work argued for a non-Western digital aesthetic rooted in religious image-making. A key moment in Asia-Pacific digital art's entry into major Western exhibition circuits on its own terms.

Ongoing multi-media universe centred on 'DOKU', a non-binary digital avatar derived from Lu Yang's own motion-captured body and reworked across film, music video, installation, and live performance. The project proposes that gender-fluid digital embodiment is itself a cosmology — not a style — and draws on Tibetan Buddhist alaya-vijñāna (storehouse consciousness) for its metaphysical framing. Recipient of the Deutsche Bank Artist of the Year 2022 partly on its strength.

id: artwork:abstract sex philosophy biotechnology and the mutations of desire
name: Abstract Sex: Philosophy, Biotechnology, and the Mutations of Desire

metadata.description: Early book arguing that sex is a site of abstraction and technical mutation — that biological reproduction, computational reproduction, and philosophical abstraction are continuous. The book draws on Whitehead, Deleuze, and computational biology to ground a speculative feminist position prior to much current AI-and-gender discourse. A precursor reference for contemporary work on computation, reproduction, and embodiment.

id: artwork:contagious architecture computation aesthetics and space
name: Contagious Architecture: Computation, Aesthetics, and Space

metadata.description: Major book arguing that computation has its own aesthetic agency — that algorithmic systems are not instruments of human design but participants whose 'incomputable' excess generates unforeseen form. The book's concept of the incomputable — the surplus of computation that exceeds any executable programme — is one of the most influential theoretical imports into digital-art theory from the 2010s. Cited across AI-art, generative-architecture, and philosophy-of-computation discourse.

id: artwork:writings on alien intelligence and ai reason
name: Writings on alien intelligence and AI reason

metadata.description: Ongoing book and essay project on artificial intelligence as a form of reason that cannot be reduced to human cognition — 'alien reason'. Parisi's current work argues that treating AI either as tool or as anthropomorphic subject misses its actual ontological status, and proposes a speculative framework that many contemporary AI artists cite as closest to what their practices are actually encountering.

Series of GAN-portraits produced by deliberately damaging the trained models — truncating weights, feeding noise, perturbing latent vectors — to elicit eerie, melted, unstable faces. The series argued that AI image-making's aesthetic heart was in the breakdowns and edge-cases, not the clean outputs, and it shaped the first generation of AI-art visual vocabulary substantially before the diffusion-model era.

Decentralised-autonomous-artist project for which Klingemann serves as primary artistic director and technical lead. Botto generates candidate images weekly; a DAO of token-holders votes on which to mint. The project is an explicit test of whether AI-generated art can be collectively authored, and it is one of the most widely-watched current experiments in AI-DAO governance of aesthetic decisions.

Album-length solo statement — after a decade of duo work as SND — deploying strict algorithmic processes to produce stuttered, broken rhythmic material at the edges of what remains recognisably rhythmic. The record's rigour became a reference for a generation of algorithmic-music practitioners and helped crystallise a strand of computer music that refuses both the clean grid and the stochastic blur. Published by Editions Mego.

Commissioned sound-and-light installation that uses strict algorithmic relations between audio, lighting, and spatial configuration to produce a perceptual object that shifts rather than plays. The work extends Fell's rhythmic-algorithmic concerns into site-specific installation and is a reference point for sound-installation practice that refuses both ambient drift and narrative progression.

Long-running duo project whose minimal, algorithmic, micro-funk aesthetic across Mille Plateaux and Raster-Noton shaped the Sheffield/Mille-Plateaux sound and indirectly influenced broader minimal-electronic production. The duo's output insists that rhythmic complexity can emerge from strict constraint rather than accumulation — a compositional position that has been widely taken up.

Founding act of Rhizome — now in its third decade as the leading institution for net-art and digital-art preservation — began as an email list run from Tribe's apartment and scaled into an artist-serving non-profit embedded in the New Museum. Tribe's founding contribution is institution-building treated as artistic practice: the creation of infrastructure that subsequently produces conditions for other artists' work. Few founding gestures in digital art carry more lasting structural weight.

Series of six live re-enactments of New Left speeches — SNCC, SDS, Black Panthers — staged in the American landscapes where the originals were delivered. The work uses performance, video documentation, and archival research to argue that the political speech-act can be re-activated rather than only remembered. An important work of early-2000s research-based political video art.

Collaborative, crowdsourced database pairing science-fiction predictions with current-events realisations — an archive of the futures-that-have-arrived as they arrive. The project treats predictive fiction as a corpus against which journalism can be read, and invites public contribution. Reflects Tribe's long-running interest in institution-as-artwork.

Net.art work in which Keith Obadike auctioned his 'blackness' on eBay, complete with a list of advantages and disadvantages of ownership; eBay removed the listing four days in, citing inappropriate content. The piece is a canonical net-art engagement with race, platform commerce, and the politics of categorisation, and is one of the most-cited works in surveys of early-2000s Black digital art.

id: artwork:the sour thunder an internet opera
name: The Sour Thunder, an Internet Opera

metadata.description: Web-distributed opera incorporating live performance, sound files, text, and user-contributed material into a distributed operatic form. Commissioned by Yale Cabaret and released across streaming and web, the work extended opera's conventions into net-native form and is an early and rigorous example of cross-modal Black-diasporic internet art.

Multi-part concert-installation work combining live performance, electronics, and visual projection into a layered meditation on the electrical substrate of African-American music and memory. Commissioned by The Kitchen (NYC), the piece is representative of the duo's move from net.art into sustained concert-scale sound-installation work.

Software artwork reskinning Adobe Photoshop as 'Heritage Gold' — a tool for applying and removing racial markings on photographs, with filters such as 'Coon Chicken' and 'Anglo-Saxon'. The piece is a foundational work of tactical-media software art, and is still taught as an example of how software can be treated as critical medium, not only as infrastructure. Made by the Mongrel collective (Graham Harwood, Mervin Jarman, Matsuko Yokokoji, Richard Pierre-Davis).

Community-authoring software distributed to immigrant and working-class groups in London and Jamaica for self-representation on the early web. Linker's argument was that net.art's serious project is not the gallery-facing artwork but the tool given to people outside the art economy's usual audience. Distributed with workshops rather than through galleries; a formative work of tactical-media commons practice.

Exhibition and essay commissioned by New Inc that examined how 'content' as economic category has reshaped artistic production in the platform era. Khan brought together artists and writers whose work treated content-production as both labour and aesthetic material, and the accompanying essay is a widely-cited diagnosis of the category's collapse. A reference for critical writing on platformed artistic labour.

Exhibition at the Brooklyn Public Library + Hirshhorn on machine vision, classification, and the politics of AI seeing — staged in dialogue with Kate Crawford's 'Excavating AI'. Khan's curatorial work placed the artist into the role of auditor of the training-data and classification logics of contemporary AI, one of the first institutional exhibitions to do so rigorously.

id: artwork:sound image aesthetics and ethics co-editor
name: Sound | Image: Aesthetics and Ethics (co-editor)

metadata.description: Edited volume bringing together essays on the aesthetics and ethics of machine-produced sound and image, including contributions from artists, theorists, and musicians. Khan's editorial work here and across Rhizome, Flash Art, and Mousse has shaped a generation's critical vocabulary around AI art.

Long-running composition cycle in which recorded spoken voices (writers, philosophers, revolutionaries, children) are transcribed into piano pulses performed synchronously with the original recording. The piano operates as a low-resolution analytic of the voice; the piece is a sustained investigation of what of speech remains when its pitched substrate is re-rendered as discrete pulses. One of the canonical works of algorithmic-compositional thinking.

id: artwork:a letter from schoenberg talking piano
name: A Letter from Schoenberg (Talking Piano)

metadata.description: Player-piano work in which the piano, driven by a high-resolution mechanical interface, 'speaks' a letter by Arnold Schoenberg — the instrument forced into phonemic duty by precisely-timed polyphonic attacks. The piece argues that speech and piano share a substrate that can be crossed by sufficient mechanical precision, and is one of the most-cited examples of the speech-as-sound tradition in contemporary computer music.

Long-running series of sound installations and environmental works investigating noise, white-ness, and the edge between signal and environment. Ablinger's insistence on the unmeasured environmental sound as compositional substrate has shaped institutional sound-art curation internationally.

Theory-fiction in which a fictional archaeologist's manuscript merges with Lovecraftian horror, Middle Eastern oil politics, and Deleuzian philosophy to produce a singular hybrid text. The book popularised 'theory-fiction' as a genre and is a standing reference for artists seeking to fold speculative narrative into serious scholarly-philosophical material. Translated, reissued, and taught widely.

Systematic philosophy arguing that genuine intelligence is a normative, inferential practice — and that artificial general intelligence, if possible, would have to be the construction of a normatively-bound mind rather than the scaling of pattern recognition. The book is cited in much contemporary AI-art writing as the most serious philosophical case for intelligence as socially-instituted rather than computationally-given.

Ongoing collaboration with artists in which Negarestani's philosophical writing enters into direct textual dialogue with artwork — essays for exhibitions, commissions for installations, shared-authored publications. The format treats theory not as commentary but as co-material; has shaped how several AI-art practitioners engage with philosophical writing.

Computer-assisted sculpture produced using TRAN2, a FORTRAN program Mallary developed that generated 3D forms as stacked cross-sections subsequently cut and assembled in plexiglass and wood. The piece is one of the first widely-exhibited computer-generated sculptures and is a canonical data-point for the claim that sculpture, not only drawing, was an early site of computational experiment. Held in major museum collections and documented in early-computer-art histories.

Computer-generated sculpture explicitly staging the computational re-rendering of Picasso's cubist geometric vocabulary, arguing that the avant-garde's decomposition of volume was already computationally-adjacent. The work is cited in early-computer-art scholarship as an example of how computer sculpture understood its own art-historical lineage.

Double album of solo-performance recordings using custom synthesis and signal-processing systems, released on Warp. The record established Haswell's solo practice — already well-known from collaborations and no-fi performances — as rigorous compositional engagement with extreme dynamics and computational noise. A foundational document of the Warp-era computer-music-as-concert tradition.

id: artwork:blackest ever black with florian hecker
name: Blackest Ever Black (with Florian Hecker)

metadata.description: Collaborative computer-music performance project with Florian Hecker, applying Xenakis-derived stochastic synthesis methods to live performance. The duo's work is widely cited in the algorithmic-computer-music lineage and extended the available performance-vocabulary of that tradition into extreme-dynamics territory.

Co-founded with Marc Garrett, Furtherfield has operated as one of the longest-running artist-led digital-arts organisations — combining gallery space in Finsbury Park, commissioning, research, publication, and community practice. Catlow's founding contribution is institution-building treated as artistic practice, with a distinctly feminist, commons-oriented, and anti-institutional-capture politics. Cited in most serious accounts of artist-led digital-art infrastructure.

id: artwork:diwo do it with others manifesto
name: DIWO (Do It With Others) manifesto

metadata.description: Framework and manifesto treating collaborative practice itself as a political-aesthetic commitment — a deliberate counter to the art world's DIY / solo-auteur defaults. Catlow has written and practised DIWO across exhibitions, workshops, and publications, and the concept is widely adopted in artist-run and community-tech contexts.

Co-edited volume (with Marc Garrett, Nathan Jones, Sam Skinner) that brought together artists, theorists, and developers on the political-aesthetic possibilities and dangers of blockchain for cultural production. Predating the 2021 NFT moment, the book has shaped how commons-oriented digital-art practice thinks about blockchain, and is still a core reference.

Book and exhibition series arguing that matter — ice cores, bullet-strike patterns, oil spills, satellite imagery — can itself bear testimony, and that the artist-researcher's task is to amplify these material witnesses into legible evidence. Published by MIT Press with a parallel video-installation practice, the work has become a standing reference for research-based art and the forensic turn in contemporary image-making.

Ongoing investigation into climate-inflected violence in the Arctic and Antarctic — ice as both archive and agent — produced as video essays, installations, and text. The project extends forensic methodology into domains where state actors are largely absent and the evidence is non-human. Key work in the climate-forensics branch of contemporary research-based art.

Forensic-artistic investigation of the famous erased segment of the Watergate tapes, combining media archaeology, audio forensics, and video-essay to re-examine the most-cited instance of material testimony in post-war American political culture. The work demonstrates the methodology 'Material Witness' later theorised — that technical media leave their erasures visible in ways political narrative cannot suppress.

At a time when image construction and creative practice are intersecting with tools of automation, avatar-artist LaTurbo Avedon develops a series of Viewports. Compositions and bindings that serve as windows and mirrors of this technological junction.

Node Window is an auxiliary to the time-based works in this series, revealing recursive gesture and information within the panel. This work is optimally displayed as direct print on aluminum.

2025
1:15 (loop)
3840x2160px 

As an avatar artist, LaTurbo Avedon has created an ever changing series of self-portraits within virtual worlds, video games and software. In this work, they present a time-based loop that pushes and pulls from self-representation to abstraction. In a slow endless shift, moments of corporeality reveal themselves from within diffused softness and color fields. 

A sort of fulcrum, recognizing the nearness of AI-driven transformation. Not just for aesthetics and how it will shape their virtual body next, but the greater cultural assimilation within generative frameworks.

As avatar artist LaTurbo Avedon continues to expand the simulated world of the Materia System, here it is visualized through a series of Viewports. These objects operate as windows and mirrors of immaterial space, rendering perspectives of the Materia System through their specific forms. Materia is a mythos emerging from the long term interactions and connections with LaTurbo in their worlds. For this exhibition, Avedon has created the work “Relic Viewports,” which is tethered to a limited series of physical objects, offered as tangible records of the System’s early development. Shapeways Collection: First collectors of this work will receive a corresponding 3D print from Shapeways. Within two weeks of the sale closing, Feral File will contact collectors to input their name, email address, and shipping information to provide to Shapeways for fulfillment. Shipping and printing costs are included in the price of the work. Note that all orders will take 6-8 weeks to deliver. After initial collection, NFTs can continue to be collected on the secondary market without the 3D printed component. The artwork will be printed in steel with a polished Bronzed-Silver finish at an approximate size of 11cm x 5cm x 0.5cm.

Bit Operations is an visual exploration of computer fundamentals through bit-shifting operations. The visuals are generated by continuously shifting and combining binary patterns, resulting in evolving compositions of stark pixels and geometric shapes. The accompanying audio components are synthesized from this same modulating bit data.

At its core, the piece is driven by algorithms that perform bit-shifting - the simple acts of pushing binary values left or right within the computer's memory. By combining multiple shifting patterns together in different ways, complex permutations of light and dark visuals emerge. The audio reflects these same bit-level operations, with the rhythms and tones mapping directly to the shifts occurring in the data.

Through this formal process focused on bit-shifting, the piece lays bare the fundamental building blocks of how modern computers operate under the hood. It reduces computational logic to its most essential level - the manipulation of 1s and 0s through rudimentary shift operations. Yet from this simplicity, an infinite space of variations arises, both visually and aurally, highlighting the immense complexity potential within even the most basic digital operations.

Under the larger project, Becoming Illegible, which engages with both social media face filters and facial recognition, Sarah Friend’s “Mirror Studies #1” is an interactive browser-based facefilter. Placing the facefilter form in dialogue with idealized ecological imagery, this work translates the questions of how we become legible to machine learning into the arena of how a landscape becomes legible to society. These images of landscapes and faces blend together — at times familiar and recognizable, at others alien, Cthulhu-like, and abstract.

Orbit of Influence is part of the fxhash live minting experience at Proof of People, ZeroSpace NYC, 2023 and is a unique generative program created using processing's p5js and SVG. Developed from scratch, it employs a system of rule-based environments that have been a source of satisfaction for me since 1995.

The program generates three invisible planets, each at a different scale - small, medium, and large. Fifty objects then randomly select a planet, a speed to orbit around it, and one of three brush sizes - small, medium, or large. These objects move around their respective planets, painting color and texture across the planetary orbit in three-dimensional space.

To reveal the blueprint of the system, press the "s" key on your keyboard. The hidden algorithm that governs the brushes' movement is then displayed, revealing a mesmerizing display of synchronized choreography as the brushes interconnect with each other.

Press the following keys to interact :

- '1': swap the background color to "ocean"
- '2': swap the background color to "mist"

Magnetosphere Fragment is a single cycle capture from a real-time generative system in which light behaves like matter; tiny positively charged particles swirl, repel, and cluster under the shifting influence of massive gravitational bodies. These invisible fields, in turn, respond dynamically to sound. As music plays, the balance of forces shifts, orbits decay, and visual turbulence emerges, creating an ever-evolving choreography of motion and interference.

Originally developed as a personal exploration of physics and pattern, Magnetosphere went on to become the iTunes Visualizer, later rebranded as the Apple Music Visualizer, and has shipped on every Mac computer since 2008. This fragment is an idealized render inspired by the original real-time version, offering a focused glimpse into the underlying system's layered complexity.

Magnetosphere Redux appears in Compositions in Code: The Art of Processing and p5.js, curated by Regina Harsanyi, and marks the fourth media art series commissioned for MoMI's Schlosser Media Wall, in partnership with the Tezos Foundation and in association with the Processing Foundation.

Everything is divisible. Larger organisms are made up of smaller ones, entire galaxies are comprised of stars, planets, people, dust, and one effect here and now ripples into eternity. Nothing exists without the elemental components that have evolved to make them possible — and nothing on the plane of existence arrives in isolation from something greater. This enmeshed reality is the concept of a Holon: a whole that is simultaneously part of another whole. 

As cells, energies, beings, and ideas grow in complexity, each new advancement includes and transcends their holons, the very catalysts of evolution. Holons was created in vanilla Javascript and WebGL, but the majority of the work was done in GLSL shaders. This setup was substantially assisted by fx(hash) community leader and artist Liam Egan who provided technical assistance and emotional support during the project's lifespan. For this reason, we have included him in the split of proceeds.

Everything is divisible. Larger organisms are made up of smaller ones, entire galaxies are comprised of stars, planets, people, dust, and one effect here and now ripples into eternity. Nothing exists without the elemental components that have evolved to make them possible — and nothing on the plane of existence arrives in isolation from something greater. This enmeshed reality is the concept of a Holon: a whole that is simultaneously part of another whole. 

As cells, energies, beings, and ideas grow in complexity, each new advancement includes and transcends their holons, the very catalysts of evolution. What does this essential process look like on its own when scale, context, and definition are removed? The senses are forced to purely observe the present interactions and reactions that occur between all parts. This is what Holons attempts to portray — the witnessing of birth, formation, and crystallization simultaneously. 

Upon viewing each piece and inspecting its detail with curiosity — we can observe living reality that has been temporarily suspended from motion and artificially stopped for us to witness. Can we see what is a part, and what is a whole? Can we define what these holons are? 

Let each Holons remind us that the impossible can always be made; let each one be nothing and everything — organisms, cosmos, energy itself — all at once, for it’s the creation of something entirely new that best reminds us that everything is actually made of the parts already here. So, remember to create without barriers or limitations because reality itself is made of that which lives now only in imagination.

"Directrix" (1998, 2025) is a long-form generative artwork and interactive drawing environment, in which animated "pseudo-parabolas" are created autonomously or in collaboration with a participant. These complex curves are the result of an interplay between a set of dynamic and static gestures. Depending on how they are structured and layered, the results can vary from sparse and delicate constructions of gently curved lines, to violently twitching, thatchy masses.

Directrix creates images from a generalized model of parabolas — the set of points which are equidistant from a special point called the focus, and an (ordinarily) straight line called the directrix. This interactive environment was designed to explore the implications of two premises: firstly, that the shape of a parabola's directrix could be an idiosyncratically drawn or generated line, and secondly, that its focus could be a moving point, animated along the trace of a viewer's recorded gesture. Directrix is interesting, in my opinion, because of the interplay it establishes between a strictly spatial specification (the directrix) and a spatio-temporal one (the path of the focus). 

A discussion of Directrix appears in section 3.1.4 (pages 69-71) of my masters thesis, "Painterly Interfaces for Audiovisual Performance" (2000), produced in the Aesthetics and Computation Group at the MIT Media Laboratory. The original project was developed in C++; this port to p5.js is the first time the project has been made available to the public, and includes expanded features for autonomous play and generative variation. 
  
There are five possible drawing targets: the white directrix line, and the focal paths of four different pseudo-parabolas. You can select the drawing target by pressing keys 1-5, or you may cycle through them by clicking the right mouse button.
  
Key commands:
• H - display Help
• P - export a PNG screenshot
• N - generate a Novel variation
• R/Return/Space/Escape - Restore to original
• 1,2,3,4 - select Parabola # for editing
• 5/D - select Directrix for editing

There are five possible drawing targets: the white directrix line, and the focal paths of four different pseudo-parabolas. You can select the drawing target by pressing keys 1-5, or you may cycle through them by clicking the right mouse button.
  
Key commands:
• H - display Help
• P - export a PNG screenshot
• N - generate a Novel variation
• R/Return/Space/Escape - Restore to original
• 1,2,3,4 - select Parabola # for editing
• 5/D - select Directrix for editing

"Directrix" (1998, 2025) is a long-form generative artwork and interactive drawing environment, in which animated "pseudo-parabolas" are created autonomously or in collaboration with a participant. These complex curves are the result of an interplay between a set of dynamic and static gestures. Depending on how they are structured and layered, the results can vary from sparse and delicate constructions of gently curved lines, to violently twitching, thatchy masses.

Directrix creates images from a generalized model of parabolas — the set of points which are equidistant from a special point called the focus, and an (ordinarily) straight line called the directrix. This interactive environment was designed to explore the implications of two premises: firstly, that the shape of a parabola's directrix could be an idiosyncratically drawn or generated line, and secondly, that its focus could be a moving point, animated along the trace of a viewer's recorded gesture. Directrix is interesting, in my opinion, because of the interplay it establishes between a strictly spatial specification (the directrix) and a spatio-temporal one (the path of the focus).

Our minds have dedicated memory slots for each person we have ever met. These slots are constantly rewritten and updated with new experiences and the alteration of the person over time, thus deleting or overwriting old data.
Memories are the sum of all the residues of images, those which remained, those which were confirmed. But how can we touch this erasure that we can no longer reach?
We were all children, and teenagers, and this radical transition is the perfect template to visualize the memory behavior of our minds, resembles somewhere this uncontrolled deletion, this reassembly of cells, or pixels.
These in-between states, that we all share have been materialized, suspended in time, so that we never forget where we're coming from, never pretend that it's all real. Someday soon this will all be someone else's dream.

Ellie Hedden & Kim Asendorf, 2022

These in-between states, that we all share have been materialized, suspended in time, so that we never forget where we're coming from, never pretend that it's all real. Someday soon this will all be someone else's dream.

Ellie Hedden & Kim Asendorf, 2022

Created on a Quantel Paintbox at Objkt, Zurich, Switzerland
Unique 1/1 NFT

Work Description
"Command Wave" started with importing a motif lifted from an Anduril Industries promotional image, combined with graphic processes native to the Paintbox editing suite. A VaporWave style was organically produced using the default colours and capabilities of the Paintbox software.
The jpg was produced by photographing the image directly from the CRT screen of the Paintbox unit with an iPhone as a way to keep the interpolation and contrast of the period tech in the artwork.

Artist Statement
"I was inspired by a lot of prior manifestos, one in particular that I enjoyed tremendously, which is the Futurist Manifesto from the Italian Futurist Art Movement and maybe around 1910. So I don't know that I hit the bar of the Futurist Manifesto, but that was kind of my inspirational starting point."

[Marc Andreessen speaking about writing his "Techno-Optimist Manifesto"- Tetragrammaton with Rick Rubin, Jan 3, 2024]

I have been working to elaborate on and contextualise a recent interest in Italian Futurism by some of the most influential voices in technology, such as Marc Andreessen. I have used consumer-level AI imaging tools to hallucinate compositions, trained on Giacomo Balla's speed drawings, combined with Tullio Crali's "Aeropainting" and recent advertising images from Defence Tech companies like Anduril, Palantir, and Helsing. With the outputted imagery, I have been making fully machine-produced paintings, using adapted CNC and plotter machines for brush manipulation, and recent adaptations of Ink Jet technology like small hand-held and large vertical printers for image transfer layers. It feels like vibe-coding paintings.

When invited to work with the Quantel Paintbox, I gathered images and source material from my experiments into this neo-Futurist painting production and fed them into the CRT screen. The Paintbox, to me, represents a transitional moment - greater capabilities for graphics and collage on screens. They speak to a particular moment in the evolution from center-margin media like television to the networked PC age of the commercial Internet. Marc Andreessen started his career in this era with the founding of Mosaic and Netscape - tools on the cusp of the future. The Paintbox's default colours and image manipulation settings make it easy to produce things that look like they were made in the 1980s. Because of this, they also look like 2010s VaporWave styles, an early meme-adjacent neo-80s aesthetic that was prominent on transgressive forums and image boards.

This series of images that I photographed with my phone directly from the image edit CRT screen captures some of these experiments in time and media. The outputs are brimming with language used by contemporary companies - the "Dynamism" of A16Z and the lyrical descriptions of Anduril's operating system Lattice - and collapsed into a VaporWave neo-Futurist fury.

Paintboxed - Tezos World Tour
This artwork was created during the Paintboxed - Tezos World Tour 2024-2025 (Chateau du Fey Villecien, Miami, Paris, Zurich, New York), on an original Quantel Paintbox from the archive of Adrian Wilson, and is part of the exhibition "Paintboxed", curated by Georg Bak and Adrian Wilson at The Digital Art Mile, Basel, Switzerland, June 16-22, 2025.

Physical Edition
This NFT is offered with a redeemable physical LED lightbox (50 x 65 x 7 cm), claimable by the first primary market buyer. Redemption is one-time only and subject to verification. NFT and lightbox are distinct and may be sold and transferred independently.

“Parted matter (originating from all given materials) moves freely, floating through the medium of air, in which the straying particles become media for invisible flows, to render air currents or waves of sounds. Dust’s quality to stay airy and ambivalent (in the atmosphere) was a subject of the natural sciences during the time of the enlightenment (most impressively developed by the 19th century physician of light and Hygiene John Tyndall). Since dust levitates within its own rules, it processes a singular problem to current technological apparatuses (e.g. as concerns cleanliness and filtration) as a self-organizing system.”
– Bettina Vismann 

Bettina Vismann is an architect, and a researcher of dust and waste management. She has taught at TU Berlin, ETH Zurich and the AA (Architectural Association) in London, and exhibited and lectured at the Venice Biennale of Architecture and the Berlin Biennale, among other sites.

“Kanban system is a method for inventory control along the production line within the Toyota Production System. A means of signalling when inventory is needed up or down the production line, inside or outside the main production facility (regulating outside suppliers as much as earlier parts of the production line), the kanban is the core of the Toyota’s “just-in-time” model for automobile production. It is also a medium and media of organization: of the production line, of production time, and of production processes up and down the line and inside and outside of the factory, extending through Toyota’s extensive supply chain. 

Initially the kanban was merely a piece of paper, encased in a see-through vinyl container, which indicated the object needed, the quantities, and the time it was needed by. This simple piece of paper that circulated against the flow of the production line allowed for a “zero inventory” model of what has been termed “management by stress.” Though it began on the automobile production line in the 1950s, the kanban system became a model for organizing many different industries (via the “lean production” model, coined by American analysts of the Toyota Production System); it also became the name for a method of computer programming in the 2000s.

Kanban as an organizational media form is like what Bruno Latour referred to as an ‘immutable mobile’; the kanban is a small, paper-based object that allows control to be exercised at a distance, in this case over the company’s suppliers. Beginning at its crucial position in the Toyota Production System, this organizational object and technology travelled from Japan to the US; from the automobile industry to Silicon Valley.”
– Marc Steinberg

Marc Steinberg is associate professor of film studies at Concordia University, Montreal (Canada). His research is focused on media industry studies, digital media, and the rise of digital platforms, among other things.

“High Vacuum is to be understood as a per subtractionem and technically produced condition. The organizational power of the well-organized void becomes visible in scientific insights and artistic practices, in material aggregates and socio-technical constellations around its production and use.”
– Rachele Delucchi 

Rachele Delucchi is a historian of science and technology and a research associate at the Chair for History of Technology at ETH Zurich (Switzerland).

“Count Thibaut IV of Champagne (r. 1222-53) commissioned a register of all fief holders and their holdings in his region. It's considered to be the most complete and systematic collection of data on an entire medieval aristocracy. The inquest produced new classes of fief holders at the same time that it provided the documentation necessary for the expansion and administrative consolidation of Thibaut’s Champagne. The transportable and compact technology of the roll allowed for real time amendments (such as the sewing of membranes) and thus the introduction of new classes of property owners (e.g. women).”
– Marisa Galvez


Marisa Galvez is Associate Professor of French and Italian, and by Courtesy, German Studies and Comparative Literature, and Director of Structured Liberal Education at Stanford University (USA).

“In technological systems, filters are software tools that survey, select, prioritize and predict information, objects, and users. They organize content at the same time as they are entangled with issues of information hierarchies, categorical equivalences, inclusions and exclusions to name only a few. With the basic understanding that there is nothing inevitable about the design of our technologies – that the decisions made in the design and management of objects like filters are not in themselves neutral acts but are bound to societal values and wider socio-cultural and economic systems - we aim to reveal how dangerous some of these decisions have been and how they provide material answers to how to live and act in the world.”
– Wendy Hui Kyong Chun and Gillian Russell

Wendy Hui Kyong Chun is the Canada 150 Research Chair in New Media at Simon Fraser University, Vancouver, where she leads the Digital Democracies Institute. 

Gillian Russell is a designer, researcher, and curator. Her projects investigate how contemporary design practice can be used as a medium to engage with and question the political dimension of technology’s influence on social life.

“In the negotiations of information within the 'fake news'  pandemic, the biggest vector for information organisations, reception, and circulation, has been the digital meme. The meme aestheticizes information and weaponizes it in what can be characterised as 'aesthetic warfare'. Looking at a variety of memes and the way they proliferate, one can identify how memes naturalize, and their direct consequences on human agency, rights, and freedom.”
– Nishant Shah

Nishant Shah is Director of Research & Outreach and Professor of Aesthetics and Cultures of Technologies at ArtEZ University of the Arts, The Netherlands. He is affiliated with Harvard University’s Berkman Klein Centre for Internet & Society and Leuphana University Lüneburg’s Centre for Digital Cultures.

“Blankets are very intimate objects; they become extensions of bodies as territories, not only keeping body marks in their use, but also keeping care memories of various and different sorts. Blankets not only wrap up from the cold; they wrap up personal losses, human emotions and broken lives. Besides being objects to be used, blankets are usually objects made, from a line of yarn to a whole flexible surface but also they are made when carefully mended in times of partial destruction. There is a particular beauty in this making practice, since the body through repetitive and togethering gestures projects its own personal shelter - life is organized in this textile making.”
– Tania Pérez-Bustos


Tania Pérez-Bustos researches technologies of doing and caring. She is Associate Professor in the School of Gender Studies, Universidad Nacional de Colombia Bogotá (UNAL), Colombia.

“Google’s TensorFlow has become the most popular tool for machine learning. As an open-source software library it is not only widely used by ML engineers and developers, but also shapes the way we imagine, think, and actually organize artificial intelligence today. On the basis of a walkthrough through the likewise popular Machine Learning Crash Course (MLCC) offered by Google, this entry will critically engage with some of the fundamental assumptions of TensorFlow and machine learning in general.”
– Clemens Apprich

Clemens Apprich is a professor of media theory and media history at the University of Applied Arts, Vienna (Austria). His current research deals with filter algorithms and their application in data analysis as well as machine learning methods.

“The fully driverless car exists only in the future. Yet it is already part of an apparatus of imaginaries, narratives and epistemological and computational practices; it is an emerging technology brought into, and bearing unto, the world - as an AI/robot, as a big data infrastructure, and as a conventional vehicle.”
– Maya Indira Ganesh

Maya Indira Ganesh doctoral work at Leuphana University Lüneburg investigates machine learning, ethics and accountability. She leads the new Masters program on AI, Ethics, and Society at Cambridge University (UK), where she’s affiliated with the Leverhulme Centre for the Future of Intelligence and the Institute for Continuing Education.

“A spray can is an everyday household device which transforms all sorts of substances into aerosols or foams, from plain air to whipped cream. The multipurpose can was first patented in Norway, in 1926  by engineer Erik Andreas Rotheim. In its early days it was used to equally apply paints and colors, but the spray can, its construction initially based on a beer-can,  achieved its commercial and strategic breakthrough with the Pacific War in the early 1940s, where it was used to distribute insecticides against the malaria fly and probably other targets. Its secret is the miraculous transformation of liquids into gaseous forms. The postwar triumph of the spray can came with the invention of hairspray which would forever change the concept of hairdo. The organizational power of the spray can — and specifically its valve — actually lies in its radical power to disorganize. It transforms whatever it contains according to the principle of equal distribution. The proper term is fumigation, ‘Vernebelung’. However, in keeping us alert to micro differences in distribution, the spray can has developed into one of the finest techniques of 21st century urban orientation and political comment.”
– Ute Holl

Ute Holl is Professor of Media Studies at the University of Basel, Switzerland. She researches, among other things, the epistemology of technical media, anthropological and experimental cinema, and a media history of acoustics, electro-acoustics, and radio theory.

“3x3, 4x6, 20x23, square, rectangle, in crazy shapes, yellow or any other color, blank or lined: sticky notes are everywhere in organizations. Mundane to the point of disappearing in the background of office life, this object – a piece of paper that can stick to any surface without leaving a trace – is far from being as banal as it seems. While it can be analyzed as a category of documents, inquiring into sticky notes allows us to travel from ordinary practices to fundamental aspects that are nowadays valued in work, and hence that shape our experience of organizational life. The sticky note both embodies and contributes to actualizing in circumstances, activities and situations experienced by people, either in solo or in group use. Beyond its evident uses, the sticky note can be understood as materializing popular techniques in organizations (such as brainstorming and other techniques associated with ‘design thinking’) and dominant discourses in business (like the glorification of innovation or creativity), among others. Could the sticky note allow us to capture key elements of our present work culture?”
– Viviane Sergi

Viviane Sergi is Associate Professor in Management at the School of Management, Université du Québec à Montréal (Canada). She investigates, among other things, the performativity and materiality of organizing.

within these works I play with the feedback loop between human representation and artificial intelligence through a process of recursive "perfection." Beginning with a photo of myself, I sequentially ask AI to "perfect" the previous image, feeding the resulting visual answer to "create the perfect women" through approximately 15 different AI models. The resulting iterating works trace an unsettling metamorphosis from recognizable human to a complete fragmentation. As each AI reinterprets and "improves" upon its predecessor's work the very notion of artificial perfection ultimately destroys what it seeks to improve. This degradation process serves as a poignant metaphor for how contemporary standards, amplified by AI and social media, can literally dissolve our identities.

Perfect Storm 
Addie Wagenknecht 
Canvas with cosmetic pigment, oil paint, palo santo, tears and charcoal
2018-2020, unique (1/1)

Addie Wagenknecht's series of paintings explores the concept of visibility and portraiture through the unconventional use of a robotic vacuum cleaner. In 2013 she started to use robotic vacuums as a form of action painting. Wagenknecht transforms theese into an artistic tool that then spreads a mixture of cosmetic pigments, pharmaceuticals, perfumes, and skin care products across the canvas. These mixtures transpose into pigments which are collected by the artist via her circle of relationships. The medium become a way to identify others in her life while also allowing them to remain anonymous. She thinks of this as a sort of 'un-portrait'. The resulting abstract compositions challenge the traditional perception of identity, which are typically associated with faces by removing the body and leaving only the artifacts of its existence.
The Roomba's technical capabilities play a crucial role in the creation of these paintings. Equipped with edge detection, modern Roomba models can navigate around obstacles and avoid falling off edges, such as the canvas in Wagenknecht's case. The artist programs the Roomba's algorithm to control its movement and the distribution of the various substances, resulting in unique patterns and textures using often her body to block or control its direction.
In works like "Perfect Storm" Wagenknecht incorporates a range of ingredients, including cosmetic dyes, sedatives, antidepressants, vodka, and perfume. By stripping these materials from their usual context, the artist presents them as raw colors and textures, challenging the viewer's perception of their intended purpose.

About the artist:
Addie Wagenknecht's work blends forms of hacking with gestural abstraction. Previous exhibitions include Centre Pompidou, The Istanbul Modern, Whitechapel Gallery and The New Museum NYC - among others. She has collaborated with CERN, Chanel, Whitney Museum of American Art and Google’s Art Machine Intelligence (AMI) Group.

Her work has been featured in numerous books, and magazines, such as TIME, Wall Street Journal, Vanity Fair, Art in America, and The New York Times. She holds a Masters degree from the Interactive Telecommunications Program at New York University, and has previously held fellowships at Eyebeam Art + Technology Center in New York City, Culture Lab UK, Institute HyperWerk for Postindustrial Design Basel (CH), and The Frank-Ratchye STUDIO for Creative Inquiry at Carnegie Mellon University.

metadata.description:
"There are No Girls on the Internet" "Monday" is series of 4 videos from a common community saying among gamers, IRC/discord users and many online community bb's it is a phrase that implies that there are no women actually participating in online activities, especially when it comes to anonymous exchanges in chatroom, video rooms and discussion forums like Reddit. The catchphrase also describes how any female privilege (perceived as social benefits from the sexuality/sex) on the Internet is stripped away. Due to the widespread nature of "No Girls on the Internet" and similar phrases, identifying oneself as a "girl" within certain communities (like 4chan and various gamer/dev and hacker communities) has become a long process/task, often leading to an inquiry of documented evidence (images holding a piece of paper with the username, date stamps) or time-stamped profile photos from skeptics. As encapsulated in the catchphrases
"TITS or GTFO" and "Pics or It Didn't Happen", the burden of proof often rests on the shoulder of those who claim to be "not dudes."
In 2020, I explored the concept of this lack of prevalence of women on the internet. I spent 5 days online in video chat rooms (i.e. chatroulette etc). Using a scientific approach with a control and variables. The variable is the medium of video in which the fact is expressed, and the control is I am a women/girl. The result of this 5 days of being in chat rooms from 8-5pm was the same conclusion: I am a girl, but girls do not exist on the internet.

Work Description
This digital artwork titled "The Binary Tree of Knowledge" features a vibrant magenta tree as its central element, set against a surreal, layered background. The piece combines digital painting techniques with photographic manipulation, utilizing light effects, digital brushwork, and color distortion. Multiple textures and translucent elements create depth, while metallic and organic forms create visual tension throughout the composition. The artwork incorporates abstract mechanical components alongside the organic tree structure, with a bright moon and bat silhouette adding mystical elements to the upper right quadrant. The color palette predominantly features purples, pinks, blues, and silvers, with strategic contrast creating a luminous, otherworldly atmosphere that explores the relationship between technology and nature.
The Binary Tree of Knowledge disrupts traditional dualities with its electric pink branches sprawling across a digital dreamscape, where mechanical and organic elements coexist in tension beneath the moonlight.

Artist Statement
I've been drawing on the computer since my earliest age, with very basic software that came about much later than the Paintbox but that was far less powerful in terms of functionalities. It was a pleasure to discover the potential of this tool, and to experiment with it in a collective manner, by creating a "cadavre-exquis" of people responding to one another, in a visual fashion, remixing each other's works, while simultaneously trying to learn the tricks of the Paintbox. It was an unforgettable experience, which was reminiscent of my first steps with a computer. 

Paintboxed - Tezos World Tour
This artwork was created during the Paintboxed - Tezos World Tour 2024-2025 (Chateau du Fey Villecien, Miami, Paris, Zurich, New York), on an original Quantel Paintbox from the archive of Adrian Wilson, and is part of the exhibition "Paintboxed", curated by Georg Bak and Adrian Wilson at The Digital Art Mile, Basel, Switzerland, June 16-22, 2025.

Physical Edition
This NFT is offered with a redeemable physical LED lightbox (50 x 65 x 7 cm), claimable by the first primary market buyer. Redemption is one-time only and subject to verification. NFT and lightbox are distinct and may be sold and transferred independently.

Kopfschlag is a collective and anonymous internet-based project created in 2007 by Primavera De Filippi and Wolfgang Natlacen. Online visitors may participate by drawing, writing, erasing, and sharing their artworks on Kopfschlag’s virtual wall, which can be defined as something between an Etch A Sketch and exquisite corpse. Snapshots of this constantly evolving artwork have been saved as independent video clips that memorialize some of the most interesting sections of the broader artwork. “Ants over the City” is one of these snapshots — neatly illustrating the power of decentralized collaboration, as many anonymous participants have contributed to create an epic scene with no other tools of coordination than a mutating virtual canvas on their screen.
